Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in the field of healthcare, with applications ranging from diagnosis to treatment planning. However, the limited availability of labeled data and the complexity of medical images pose significant challenges in developing accurate and efficient segmentation models. In this paper, we propose a novel hierarchical self-supervised learning approach for medical image segmentation based on multi-domain data aggregation. Our method leverages the inherent spatial and temporal hierarchies in medical images to learn a hierarchical representation of the image data, which is then used to improve the performance of a supervised segmentation model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results with significantly fewer training resources. Our work provides a valuable contribution to the field of medical image segmentation, enabling the development of more accurate and efficient models for clinical use.

Abstract: Multi-organ segmentation is a crucial task in medical imaging analysis, which requires accurate classification and separation of different organs within an image. This has traditionally been accomplished through intensive training on large datasets with labeled examples. However, we propose an alternative approach using semi-supervision and co-training to improve multi-organ segmentation accuracy while significantly reducing required labeling overhead. Our proposed method involves learning joint representations from multiple data types (MRI, CT) simultaneously using deep planning networks that allow incorporating prior knowledge on organ hierarchy and spatial constraints. The model also utilizes unlabeled images to enhance inter-class relationships and generate pseudo-labels to augment limited supervision during learning. Quantitative results demonstrate improvement in segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods with less than half the necessary annotated cases as well as reduced domain gap due to cross-modal interactions.

In this paper, we introduce the notion of principal sub-manifolds, a generalization of the concept of sub-manifolds that provides for a more robust and efficient manner of modelling complex data systems. Principal sub-manifolds are defined as a set of points in a high-dimensional space that are linked by a set of locally linear mappings, rather than a single global map. This provides for the representation of complex structures such as bifurcations, folds, and self-intersections, which cannot be captured by conventional sub-manifold models. We propose an algorithm for estimating principal sub-manifolds from data, which incorporates the notions of dimension reduction and manifold learning. The algorithms first identifies a set of locally linear mappings that approximate the data, and then utilizes these mappings to establish a set of principal sub-manifolds that capture the fundamental structure of the data. We demonstrate the impact of our algorithms on many artificial and real-world datasets, and demonstrate that it outperforms conventional sub-manifold learning techniques in terms of consistency and complexity. The paper also demonstrates the mathematical properties of principal sub-manifolds, including their topological and mathematical structure. We show that principal sub-manifolds have a well-defined notion of dimension, which can be applied to study their properties and behavior. We therefore obtain a relation between principal sub-manifolds and other mathematical objects, such as Whitney stratifications and M-polyfoldons, which allows a deeper knowledge of their nature and relationships. Overall, this paper provides a new and effective tool for modelling complex data systems, and shows its relevance through a variety of technologies. The theory of principal sub-manifolds has significant consequences for a broad variety of fields, including computer vision, image processing, and machine learning, and we believe it to be a useful tool for scientists and educators in these areas.

The paper provides a novel method to image segmentation using adversarial networks. The proposed technique, called Points2Polygon, utilizes weak labels and contextual information to create more realistic segmentations than conventional pixel classification tools. The model is trained in an end-to-end fashion with an adversary network that allows the generation of coherent and realistic polygonal segments. Experimental findings on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods while providing more annotated information. Overall, this research demonstrates a promising approach for robust and efficient semantic segmentation using limited supervision.

BiSeNet has been proved to be a popular two-stream network for real-time segmentation. However, its principle of adding an extra path to encode spatial information is time-consuming, and the backbones borrowed from pretrained tasks, e.g., image classification, may be inefficient for image segmentation due to the deficiency of task-specific design. To handle these problems, we propose a novel and efficient structure named Short-Term Dense Concatenate network (STDC network) by removing structure redundancy. Specifically, we gradually reduce the dimension of feature maps and use the aggregation of them for image representation, which forms the basic module of STDC network. In the decoder, we propose a Detail Aggregation module by integrating the learning of spatial information into low-level layers in single-stream manner. Finally, the low-level features and deep features are fused to predict the final segmentation results. Extensive experiments on Cityscapes and CamVid dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by achieving promising trade-off between segmentation accuracy and inference speed. On Cityscapes, we achieve 71.9% mIoU on the test set with a speed of 250.4 FPS on NVIDIA GTX 1080Ti, which is 45.2% faster than the latest methods, and achieve 76.8% mIoU with 97.0 FPS while inferring on higher resolution images.

Abstract: A key challenge in medical image analysis is transferring knowledge from one imaging modality to another, as each modality presents unique characteristics and challenges. Most current approaches rely on domain adaptation or network architecture variations specific to the target modality which can limit their generalizability and applicability across different datasets. In this study, we propose a novel framework that leverages adversarial training to facilitate network-agnostic knowledge transfer between modalities using only a limited amount of labeled data. We demonstrate effectiveness of our approach on two benchmark tasks, liver segmentation in CT and MR images, achieving state-of-the-art results with minimal modifications to existing models. Our findings highlight the potential of domain agnostic learning strategies for improving model applicability and reducing transfer requirements.

A teenager has been arrested on suspicion of hacking into the CIA director's private emails, the FBI has confirmed. The boy, thought to be 16, was held on suspicion of Computer Misuse Act offences after officers searched a property in the city. Police have also arrested and bailed a 16-year-old from London, a 15-year-old from Nuneaton and a 16-year-old from Derby. The arrests came after a court order was served on Google to release details of the IP addresses of the computers from which the emails were sent. A statement released by the CIA today said that it was aware of media reports about the arrests. It added: "The CIA is aware of the reports and is working with the FBI on the matter." The arrests came as a new round of 14,000 emails sent by CIA director David Petraeus were made public by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Among the emails, which were sent between 2004 and 2012, were some sent by Paula Broadwell, the authorised biographer who was also Petraeus's lover. Ms Broadwell, 40, sent the emails to Jill Kelley, a 37-year-old married mother-of-three from Tampa, Florida, who was said to have had a close relationship with the CIA director. Kelley reportedly told the FBI that she was receiving harassing emails from a woman, and the agency then found out that the woman was Ms Broadwell, sparking the FBI investigation. The emails were sent between Mrs Kelley and General John Allen, who was the top US commander in Afghanistan until last week, as well as Ms Broadwell. A further 20,000 messages are due to be released over the coming weeks. Petraeus, who was director of the CIA until his resignation in November, is said to have had an affair with Ms Broadwell, who has written a book about him.

Deep learning models continuously break new records across different NLP tasks. At the same time, their success exposes weaknesses of model evaluation. Here, we compile several key pitfalls of evaluation of sentence embeddings, a currently very popular NLP paradigm. These pitfalls include the comparison of embeddings of different sizes, normalization of embeddings, and the low (and diverging) correlations between transfer and probing tasks. Our motivation is to challenge the current evaluation of sentence embeddings and to provide an easy-to-access reference for future research. Based on our insights, we also recommend better practices for better future evaluations of sentence embeddings.

In this paper, we present CHASE, a novel approach to visual tracking that leverages the power of differentiable neural architecture search (NAS) to optimize the tracking performance. Unlike traditional tracking methods that rely on hand-crafted features and pre-defined architectures, CHASE uses a cell-level differentiable neural network to learn a robust and adaptive representation of the target object. The proposed method consists of two main components: a cell-level differentiable neural network, and a tracking loss function that is designed to optimize the tracking performance. The cell-level differentiable neural network is trained to learn a robust representation of the target object by optimizing a novel tracking loss function that encourages the network to produce a stable output in the presence of occlusions, illumination changes, and other challenges. The tracking loss function is designed to be differentiable with respect to the network's architecture, allowing us to use backpropagation to optimize the network's parameters. We use a combination of gradient descent and evolution strategies to search for the optimal architecture that maximizes the tracking performance. We evaluate CHASE on several challenging benchmarks, including the PASCAL Visual Object Tracking (VOT) dataset, the Temple-Color-Tracking (TCT) dataset, and the LaSalle-Color-Tracking (LCT) dataset. Our experiments show that CHASE outperforms several state-of-the-art tracking methods, including deep learning-based methods, and achieves a high success rate in various challenging scenarios. The main contribution of this paper is the introduction of a novel differentiable neural architecture search method for visual tracking, which allows the network to adapt to changing object appearance and learn a robust representation of the target object. The proposed method has important implications for a wide range of applications, including object tracking in videos, autonomous driving, and robotics.

Apple has been criticized for placing its own apps at the top of the App Store search results. While Apple denies the accusations, an analysis of search terms showed that users seem to agree with them: App Store searches are sending more people to their own app pages than competitor's. According to data from SimilarWebApp Annie (similarweb.com), in January 2017 there were 40 million global daily app store queries on Google or Baidu - up 30 year-over-year and nearly half coming direct traffic (appstorequery.com). This equates to roughly 773 billion total searches per month, meaning "direct traffic" should have accounted for around one third of those searches. But it doesn't... The problem here isn't that companies like Amazon can afford some paid ads - rather, they need a way to reach customers immediately when shopping online is no longer an option. The rise of voice-commerce provides brands with new opportunities since customers will now buy products by simply speaking into their mobile devices. According toVoiceLabs, retailer sales via Siri tripled between 2014-2017. As this trend continues, retailers must adapt quickly or risk losing out on valuable customer engagements.

In applied image segmentation tasks, the ability to provide numerous and precise labels for training is paramount to the accuracy of the model at inference time. However, this overhead is often neglected, and recently proposed segmentation architectures rely heavily on the availability and fidelity of ground truth labels to achieve state-of-the-art accuracies. Failure to acknowledge the difficulty in creating adequate ground truths can lead to an over-reliance on pre-trained models or a lack of adoption in real-world applications. We introduce Points2Polygons (P2P), a model which makes use of contextual metric learning techniques that directly addresses this problem. Points2Polygons performs well against existing fully-supervised segmentation baselines with limited training data, despite using lightweight segmentation models (U-Net with a ResNet18 backbone) and having access to only weak labels in the form of object centroids and no pre-training. We demonstrate this on several different small but non-trivial datasets. We show that metric learning using contextual data provides key insights for self-supervised tasks in general, and allow segmentation models to easily generalize across traditionally label-intensive domains in computer vision.

What is more, these alterations cause complex behaviors that might not have been apparent before. Unfortunately, with enough images, it may be very difficult to explain their interrelationship; especially if we can find them (through some other technique), it could nearly surely be incomplete. One method to resolve this issue is based on machine learning techniques [1], and specifically computational models [2]. We introduce a generative model (a class-based stochastic neural network) that produces pictures by creating arbitrary sequences of possible images. While probabilistics are very effective, they only take human experience and knowledge into account, while our generative neural network gives advantage in an ad-hoc fashion as long as information is available about the scene's features when creating an image. It can not succeed while being trained with small amounts of data because pictures are too frequently used to represent anything completely different from what was shown first. For example, pictures which include objects from other cultures will not resemble English ones, resulting in confusing data when using machine learning techniques. The aim of this work is also to identify semi-supervised linguistic segmentations which use ficklenet without specifically allowing the user to input language data nor to provide images to further evaluate quality. To accomplish this, instead of training all visual domains, we compute samples from a preselected subset. To support this technique, we implement an optimal evaluation of a weakly supervised hierarchical Bayesian network using Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). As an alternative to SGD we show how a high energy Stochastic Gradient Gaussian Filter (S gdp ) can overcome both local minima found in traditional neural nets and allow much better convergence than traditional Gaussian filters. However, unlike traditional SGD, our sparse gradient descent implementation can handle noise, thereby removing one key feature often identified with unsupervised deep learning schemes. The following page relates to a new method for the determination of the different parts of the brain from the magnetic-resonance images. The method is called Holistic Decomposition Convolution. The HDC method consists of two stages: the first, the Holistic Decomposition, and the second, the convolution by means of the convolutional neural networks. In the first stage, the magnetic resonance image is decomposed into a set of spatial and intensity basis functions, obtained by a novel optimization process, which reproduce the essential structure of the image and which, by means of them, we represent the original image in a more concise and information-rich way. In the second stage, a 3D convolutional network is applied to the decomposed image, taking advantage of the spatial and intensity information of the basis functions, and this network learns the association between the decomposed image and the corresponding semantic label. We have tested the performance of HDC on a set of 3D MR images and compared it with the performances of the most advanced methods. The results obtained show that, in terms of the accuracy of the segmentation, the method HDC is superior to the other methods, demonstrating the importance of the use of the Holistic Spatial and Intensity Relations in the segmentation of 3D MR images. The main contributions of this paper are the introduction of a novel method of 3D MR image segmentation based on the Holistic Decomposition and the processing of a convolutional neural network. The development of a novel optimization process for obtaining the basis functions that capture the essential structure of the 3D MR images. The demonstration of the efficiency of the method HDC in capturing the Holistic Spatial and Intensity Relations in 3D MR images and improving the accuracy of the segmentation. The proposed method has the potential to improve the accuracy and speed of 3D MR image segmentation and has the possibility of having a great impact on various medical applications, such as the detection of tumors, the characterization of the lesion, the localization of the brain.

The sentencing of David Gilroy, who killed Edinburgh woman Suzanne Pilley, is due to take place next Wednesday. Earlier this week permission was also granted to film the proceedings. Twitter use has been allowed before in a Scottish court but it will be the first time a sentencing at the High Court in Scotland has been filmed. Gilroy was found guilty by a jury last month of murdering 38-year-old bookkeeper Ms Pilley. She disappeared in May 2010 but her body has never been found. Prosecutors believed that Gilroy, 49, buried his former lover in a "lonely grave" in a remote part of Argyll. Gilroy will be sentenced on Wednesday 18 April. During the filming, the camera will focus on the judge - no one else will feature in the footage except the macer and the clerk. Gilroy himself will not be filmed. Live updating on Twitter from a Scottish court was allowed for the first time for the sentencing of former MSP Tommy Sheridan in January 2011. However, guidance issued at the end of last year confirmed journalists in Scotland would not be allowed to use live text-based communication without specific clearance. Journalists south of the border have been told by the Lord Chief Justice to "twitter as much as you like."

Once upon a time there was a young girl named Alice who lived in a small town near the sea. She had grown up with tales of epic heroes and grand adventures, but she never felt like she could relate to them. One day, while walking along the beach, Alice stumbled upon an old book that changed her life. It was a collection of classic stories rewritten from the viewpoint of a teenage girl. Alice eagerly opened the book and was immediately drawn into the world of the characters. She read about the brave Odysseus facing the perils of the sea, Snow White's struggles against the wicked queen, and Romeo and Juliet's forbidden love. As she read, Alice began to understand the protagonists in a way she had never been able to before. Alice was so moved by the stories that she decided to take on a challenge of rewriting some of her own favorite classics. With each new story, Alice found herself becoming more confident and empowered. She realized that her voice mattered and that she could make a difference. Alice's rewrite of the classics became wildly popular. People all over the world were inspired by her stories and many young women found comfort in knowing that they weren't alone in their struggles. Alice's stories have been passed down through generations, inspiring countless young people to find their own courage within themselves. Alice's legacy will live on forever as a reminder that we can always rewrite our own stories.

The impact of Bi implantation on the conductivity and the thermopower of GeTe, Ge-Sb-Te, and Ga- La-S films is investigated. The enhanced conductivity appears to be notably sensitive to a dose of an implant. Incorporation of Bi in amorphous chalcogenide films at doses up to 1x1015 cm-2 is seen not to change the majority carrier type and activation energy for conduction process. Higher implantation doses may reverse majority carrier type in studied films. Electron conductivity was observed in GeTe films implanted with Bi at a dose of 2x1016 cm-2. These studies indicate that native coordination defects present in amorphous chalcogenide semiconductors can be deactivated by means of ion implantation. A substantial density of implantation-induced traps in the studied films and their interfaces with silicon is inferred from analysis of the space-charge limited current and capacitance-voltage characteristics taken on Au/amorphous chalcogenide/Si structures.

> Abstract. With advances in endoscopic capsule imageing technology, multi-dimensional images with three- dimensional resolution (magnific view) are now available. A significant part and main goal of these new colourectal polyp diagnosis techniques is to differentiate between benign lesions versus malignant lesion or cancerous tumours that may lead to life-threatening illnesses such as colon carcinoma if undetected or missed. While this can be accomplished manually by an expert gastroenterologist through frame-by-frame visualisation technique in conjunction with magnification videos taken during routine procedures there remains concerns towards manual image processing due to the labour intensive task associated with it not to mention subjective error rates involved based on individual knowledge level that can significantly impact clinical decision making process.. In addressing these challenges we propose novel deep convolutional neural network frameworks termed ROI_Unet and its counterpart ROI_UNet+ where these network's architectures allow for localised training and testing allowing for precise segmentations particularly useful for target region localised analysis at tumour margins using a variety of inputs i.e. RGB endoscope images (RGB), depth (Depth). The experimental results showcasing high accuracy performances relative to current stateofthe art approaches along with a highly reduced inference time further motivates this investigation into 2Dvs3D and 3D endoscopy frames classification models which have been recently explored thus far however without including realworld multi modal dataset containing both 3D and 4D information captured via depth sensors.

The paper "On some categorical-algebraic conditions in S-protomodular categories" explores the relationship between categorical algebra and algebraic geometry in the context of S-protomodular categories. The authors investigate certain categorical-algebraic conditions that are inherent in S-protomodular categories and their relationship to the geometry of the associated algebraic objects. The paper begins by introducing the concept of an S-protomodular category, a generalization of the notion of a protomodular category that allows for the presence of a non-trivial notion of "S-duality." The authors then examine the relationship between S-protomodular categories and other categorical structures, such as abelian categories and derived categories, and explore the ways in which these structures can be used to study the properties of S-protomodular categories. The main focus of the paper is on the study of certain categorical-algebraic conditions that are inherent in S-protomodular categories. In particular, the authors investigate the notion of "admissibility" and its relationship to the geometry of the associated algebraic objects. They show that admissible objects in an S-protomodular category have a well-behaved theory of "S-duality," which allows for a rich and flexible way of studying the properties of these objects. The authors also explore the relationship between admissibility and other categorical-algebraic conditions, such as "tilting" and "cotilting," and show how these conditions can be used to study the properties of S-protomodular categories. They also demonstrate how the theory of admissible objects can be used to construct new examples of S-protomodular categories and to study the properties of existing ones. Overall, the paper provides a detailed and systematic study of the categorical-algebraic conditions inherent in S-protomodular categories, and demonstrates the power and flexibility of these conditions in the study of algebraic geometry. The results and techniques presented in the paper will be of interest to researchers in algebraic geometry, categorical algebra, and related fields, and will provide a foundation for further study and exploration in this area.

The use of computer vision technology has gained a significant amount of popularity in Recent years, particularly with regards to real-time object recognition. One important application of such technology is in the Field of 3D reconstruction, where researchers are constantly seeking new and improved techniques for detecting Facial landmarks and fitting these landmarks to corresponding shapes within an image. This paper presents a novel method for real-time facial landmark detection that uses deep Regression networks to estimate shape models and directly output results within a set time frame of milliseconds. This process allows for unprecedented accuracy and efficiency compared to traditional methods, which rely On feature extraction or template matching algorithms. The proposed approach Involves training two Deep neural networks: one that estimates facial landmarks using Convolutional features, and another network that fits the detected landmarks to Each individual face’s unique configuration through a nonlinear deformation model. By utilizing this hybrid method, we can achieve accurate super-realtime landmark detection with minimal computational overhead. Through extensive testing, our technique demonstrates superior performance compared to both existing state-of-the-art approaches as well as offline benchmarks. We believe that This Research will have significant implications for various applications ranging from security surveillance systems, wearables, and virtual reality, among others. Overall, this paper provides a valuable contribution to advancing the field of real-time computer vision, while exploring new avenues to improve upon current landmark detection and deformable shape estimation techniques.

> > Abstract: Path tracing and label propagation both suffer from incomplete recovery in complex images often occurring around boundary objects whose appearance highly deviates from other structures, such as fibre termini or neuropil regions. In this work, we introduce Reinforce Proofreader (RLcor): an interactive proofreader that enables crowdworkers to review image segmentations by learning reinforcements with only few human corrections on a well-known connectome. By design, our algorithm learns what partitions are difficult to recover accurately while iteratively reinforcing workers' correction at the corresponding locations. We show how RLcor’s self-learning mechanism can effectively alleviate tedious labour input during ground truth validation through two major phases: 1) refining unground-truth labels based on its own prediction; and 2) identifying uncertain pixels requiring expert attention so as to accelerate path tracer's processing over complicated structures via an active masking strategy; thus enabling significantly better performance than previous approaches. As an illustrating application, we apply three state-of-the-art methods on D. melanogaster brain datasets including Path Tracker, DeepPath and Interactive deepPath.

Attack: Lee Keeley, 38, grabbed the unnamed woman and hit her head against a wall before stamping on her head and chest in a courtroom . An ex-boyfriend flew into a furious rage and attacked his former partner in the middle of a courtroom. Lee Keeley grabbed the unnamed woman and hit her head against a wall before stamping on her head and chest at Lincoln County Court, after a judge ruled against him in a civil matter. The 38-year-old defendant chased her round the courtroom and tore out clumps of her hair after losing his temper in January. A court heard Keeley launched a chair at his ex-girlfriend before he started attacking her and barristers had to step in to break the pair up. The victim suffered a cut to her right ear, bruising and swelling to the ear, a grazed cheek as well as bruised ribs. Last Thursday, Keeley appeared before another judge at Lincoln Crown Court and admitted assault occasioning actual bodily harm. He was jailed for two years and given an indefinite restraining order, preventing him from contacting his former partner. Sentencing, Judge Michael Heath said: 'I understand your disappointment but your behaviour after the decision was outrageous.' A court heard Keeley, from Lincoln, had become increasingly agitated during the hearing and then erupted as Judge Richard Toombs announced the decision. Shocking scene: Keeley chased the woman round the courtroom at Lincoln County Court (above) and tore out clumps of her hair after losing his temper when the judge ruled against him in a civil matter in January . Keeley, who had represented himself, began arguing with the judge then turned on his ex-partner. David Outterside, prosecuting, said Keeley shouted an insult at the woman before adding: 'He then picked up a chair and threw it at the victim but missed her. 'He then chased after her. Twice they ran round and round the court as he tried to get hold of her.' The court heard Keeley later told police he went into a rage when the decision was announced. He said he recalled throwing the chair but could not remember anything after that. David Eager, defending, said Keeley had 'simply lost control'.

Our network was developed using deep reinforcement-learning techniques, allowing us to model recurrent neural networks (RNNs) from another way than simple backpropagation, that is by taking into account nonlinear dependencies between weights and inputs, rather than just regularisation. We perform two kinds of training with DCNAS. First we train an image classification in which a CNN architecture in each layer predicts label corresponding to one or more input pixels of a target image. Second, instead of learning images from scratch as RNNs are trained on images, we use training data which can be used directly as the convolutional and re-normalization filter kernels. For example by replacing standard linear filter layers like rectified linear unit with a custom filter kernel based algorithm. This increases performance while preserving certain feature properties inherent to recurrent nets. The results show remarkable improvement over conventional filters of similar complexity and size and also very good accuracy. To demonstrate this, we have trained a state-of-the-art unsupervised SVM classifier for image segmentation using our DCNAS-based approach. Here's what it looks like: We find in practice that all that remains after extensive optimization is not only a relatively small number of parameters but also optimal implementation and optimality assumption.

This paper describes a new approach to image segmentation that is based on derivative-component trees. The DCT is a technique which uses derivatives to identify objects in images. This paper shows that the use of DCT to detect objects in images, which can be represented in different color channels, is a powerful and accurate tool for object detection. DCT firstly uses the gradient and Hessians of the derivative to identify the properties of the pixel. These components are then clustered together to form regions, which may then be further grouped into areas by using clustering methods. This process may be repeated for each channel, giving further information about the objects. To evaluate the method, it is compared with the state-of-the-art methods, and it is shown that the method is as accurate as the other methods but requires less computation. It is also able to handle difficult images that have noise and occlusion. It is concluded that DCT is a useful approach to image segmentation, and can handle data from different color channels.

I find it incredibly interesting that in September, I saw no ribbons, events, or general awareness for Prostate Cancer Awareness Month. Yes, I missed the memo, too. Breast cancer research receives nearly twice the funding of that of the the next highest-funded form of cancer (lung cancer, which kills four times as many people per year than breast cancer). This is not because it is the form of cancer that affects the most people (that is prostate cancer) nor is it because it has the highest mortality rate (that is pancreatic cancer), but rather it is due to the incredible publicity that breast cancer receives. This publicity is not a bad thing- publicity and awareness about such a terrible disease are essential if research is to be funded- I just wish that we would put the same emphasis on EVERY form of cancer, including the less "glamorous" (although there is nothing glamorous about breast cancer) forms that affect millions of people every year. Instead of decorating the streets with sexually stereotypical colors and phrases, having gender-specific events, and devoting time and money to charities that donate a surprisingly small percentage of proceeds to actual research, let's unite to actually stop ALL forms of cancer. Let's make every month "Cancer Awareness Month."

The problem of image segmentation is known to become particularly challenging in the case of partial occlusion of the object(s) of interest, background clutter, and the presence of strong noise. To overcome this problem, the present paper introduces a novel approach segmentation through the use of "weak" shape priors. Specifically, in the proposed method, an segmenting active contour is constrained to converge to a configuration at which its geometric parameters attain their empirical probability densities closely matching the corresponding model densities that are learned based on training samples. It is shown through numerical experiments that the proposed shape modeling can be regarded as "weak" in the sense that it minimally influences the segmentation, which is allowed to be dominated by data-related forces. On the other hand, the priors provide sufficient constraints to regularize the convergence of segmentation, while requiring substantially smaller training sets to yield less biased results as compared to the case of PCA-based regularization methods. The main advantages of the proposed technique over some existing alternatives is demonstrated in a series of experiments.

We introduce a new machine-learning-based approach, which we call the Independent Classifier networks (InClass nets) technique, for the nonparameteric estimation of conditional independence mixture models (CIMMs). We approach the estimation of a CIMM as a multi-class classification problem, since dividing the dataset into different categories naturally leads to the estimation of the mixture model. InClass nets consist of multiple independent classifier neural networks (NNs), each of which handles one of the variates of the CIMM. Fitting the CIMM to the data is performed by simultaneously training the individual NNs using suitable cost functions. The ability of NNs to approximate arbitrary functions makes our technique nonparametric. Further leveraging the power of NNs, we allow the conditionally independent variates of the model to be individually high-dimensional, which is the main advantage of our technique over existing non-machine-learning-based approaches. We derive some new results on the nonparametric identifiability of bivariate CIMMs, in the form of a necessary and a (different) sufficient condition for a bivariate CIMM to be identifiable. We provide a public implementation of InClass nets as a Python package called RainDancesVI and validate our InClass nets technique with several worked out examples. Our method also has applications in unsupervised and semi-supervised classification problems.

Japanese Fish Found in Tsunami Debris Highlights the Impact of Ocean Pollution Oregon authorities have reported the discovery of a Japanese species of fish inside a floating vessel, one of the latest of one million tons of debris dispersed in the Pacific Ocean by the catastrophic tsunami that struck Japan in 2011. The authorities plan to tow the 25-ft piece of fiberglass, significantly highlighting the ongoing impact of ocean pollution. The tsunami, triggered by a 9.0 magnitude earthquake, claimed the lives of 18,000 people with powerful waves reaching heights of 128 feet above sea level. A vast amount of debris, including fragments of destroyed cities and infrastructure, was left scattered across the Pacific, causing severe damage to marine ecosystems. This latest discovery showcases the immense scale of the issue and the urgent need for increased efforts to mitigate ocean pollution. The inclusion of a Japanese fish species within the debris is a stark reminder of the interconnectivity of marine ecosystems and the potential for invasive species to be introduced to new habitats as a consequence of pollution. Efforts by authorities have so far resulted in the recovery of tons of debris, including the removal of one 178-ton dock that washed onto the Oregon coast in 2012. However, the challenge remains immense, as the vast majority of the debris remains unaccounted for. With considerable amounts of plastics and microplastics now known to be present throughout the oceans, the race is on to better understand and respond to the multiple threats that our seas face. The Oregon authorities have announced plans to tow the 25-ft piece of fiberglass for further study and eventual disposal, while continuing their efforts to locate and remove other significant pieces of tsunami debris. As investigations deepen, it becomes increasingly crucial to confront the growing issue of ocean pollution and protect the delicate balance of marine ecosystems worldwide.

We present the very first framework for measuring the fraction of the relevant genetic history of a population that is mathematically elusive. Our observed results on the tested demographies suggest that it may be better to aggregate the analysis of smaller chunks of chromosomal segments than fewer large chunks. Also, no matter the richness of samples in a population, at least one-third of the population genetic history is impenetrable. The framework also opens up possible new lines of investigation along the following. Given the characteristics of a population, possibly derived from observed extant individuals, to estimate the (1) optimal sample size and (2) optimal sequence length for the most informative analysis.

Rail passengers could be facing years of weekend "misery" as construction of the proposed new High Speed Two (HS2) rail line begins, according to a campaign group. Campaign for Better Transport (CBT) says that the planned disruption caused by the building of the new line could cause long-term disruption to existing services and huge disruption to weekend travel plans. The new high-speed line is set to run from London to Birmingham, Leeds and Manchester. The Department for Transport has estimated that the project will cost 56bn and take up to 18 years to complete, with construction beginning in 2017. However, CBT say that this could result in a reduction of service on other lines, leading to delays and cancellations. They state that the disruption caused by HS2 building works could have "a substantial impact on people's ability to go about their lives," particularly at weekends when there are fewer trains running. CBT's chief executive, Stephen Joseph, commented: "The Government's own figures show that even before any track or stations are built, many train passengers will suffer from the disruption caused by HS2 works. This means that people's weekends and leisure time could be ruined for years ahead." The Department for Transport is yet to comment on the claims, but has said it is committed to ensuring minimal disruption for rail passengers during the construction period. It has also promised to keep existing services running during the construction phase of the project. Despite this, CBT are urging the government to come up with a plan to ensure that passengers are not worst affected by the construction of HS2. Joseph added: "It's essential that passengers get a fair deal throughout the construction of HS2. We want to see an agreed package of measures to reduce the impact of disruption on passengers and make sure that they are not forgotten in the planning process."

This research investigates cross-modal progressive Comprehension, a process that involves understanding and interpreting visual information by combining it with linguistic cues. Using state-of-the-art machine learning models such as deep neural networks, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), long short term memory(LSTM)and other tools from computer vision we analyze image data Sets like MS COCO dataset which contain segmented objects along side Captions. We evaluate our approach on various metrics including Accuracy & Recall rate which show significant performance improvement over baseline methods. This suggests that using both modalities together can enhance object recognition accuracy leading towards better NLP results specifically while dealing text based problems regarding Image captioning,Visual query etc where Localization plays important role.

The man goes off on this guy to everyone near the barbershop. Then, he hops in his car and drives away. That night, the barber comes out of his shop and tells his wife what happened. She asks him why he let it happen. And when he said "because I love people," she asked him if he was afraid of being killed? His wife then asked him how many times he'd been kicked or punched since he started working there. The guy just answered "a lot." He told his wife, "I've got kids too!" A man walks across a bridge to get to another city where he works as a truck driver, but after crossing the river he gets caught up in bad weather. During the storm, he goes around back of the truck and sees two families pulling their cars through the water. He offers to help them drive onto dry land instead of risking their lives by walking over the top of the bridge again. After reaching dry ground, he turns to the woman in charge of looking after the children. "Excuse me," he says, "but could you please ask your husband to see if we don't need any more food?" His co-worker tells him not to worry about it because he'll find something else to eat down here. What does he say? Nothing! Instead, he stays back until the couple are safely off the road. After doing this altruistic act, he remains friends with both families going forward.

If you picture light as a particle tracing out a sine wave, the particle's forward velocity is the speed of light, and its location in the sine wave is the wavelength. Now imagine the wave and its particle as being made out of jelly, so that the particle can squish together or stretch out along the wave, making its wavelength shorter or longer. The above paragraph is taken from a paragraph in an article from Scientific American (Erik W. S. Darling) that discusses how the Universe is expanding at an ever increasing rate. The idea of light being made of particles made of jelly is interesting. Just how does light squish itself into a shorter wavelength? To squish a light wave, you have to convert some of its energy into the mass of the jelly. This doesn't change the wave's frequency, though, so the jelly has to move faster to keep up.

Corporal Christian Walmsley was found dead in his flat in Bolton after struggling with post-traumatic stress disorder following tours of duty abroad . A soldier who suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder after a series of tours abroad wrote suicide notes before taking a fatal overdose, an inquest has heard. Corporal Christian Walmsley was found dead in his flat in Bolton, Greater Manchester wearing five war medals after struggling to adapt to civilian life, a coroner was told. The father-of-three had served in the First Gulf War, Bosnia, Angola and Northern Ireland in the Royal Engineers from 1989 until 2000. The 42-year-old had witnessed the 'significant violence only soldiers experience', the hearing at Bolton Coroners Court was told. After retiring from the army, he was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression and Fibromyalgia, a chronic condition causing deep muscle pain. His family members told the court that Cpl Walmsley's two marriages had ended divorce. He had spent some time in Germany over the last decade before returning to the UK to rebuild relationships with his family, relatives said. Stepfather Michael Richards told the hearing: 'He'd always been such a fit lad. But when he came back he had to use a stick because he was so fatigued.' Mr Richards said his stepson had questioned the support given to former servicemen and women. The inquest heard he had previously taken an overdose and told his family he had tried to take his own life. But he discharged himself from the hospital before he had a mental health assessment. In the weeks leading up to his death, his family said Cpl Walmsley had seemed optimistic. Yet on November 4 last year, he had appeared distressed to friends and sent text messages to his mother telling her he was in pain. He was discovered dead on November 6. Police officers found a notebook with several suicide notes inside, the hearing was told. Cpl Walmsley was among British troops in the First Gulf War (pictured in file photo), as well touring Bosnia . The coroner ruled that, without dates on the notes, he could not be certain Cpl Walmsley had attempted suicide. Abstract : Measurement device independent quantum key distribution (MDIQKD) has been developed to remove detection errors and detector flaws so that it does not require a security proof. However, MDIQKD remains vulnerable because of untrusted measurement apparatuses [Fabio Sciarrino10]. In this letter we introduce modified coherent state encoding scheme as an extension of Dual Classical Optics coding in order to get rid off an untrusted single photon source which is necessary to implement MDIQKD [Alexandre G. Ekert2007 ; Fabio Sciarrino2010] . Thus our proposed protocol becomes capable of making practical use by using cheap optical hardware based on ordinary coherent lasers instead of single-photon generators. Moreover , for both classical and conventional decoy states , we prove its optimality.

This paper presents a novel approach for multi-label segmentation of medical images with lesions using dynamic multiscale tree learning and ensemble strong classifiers. The proposed method involves a hierarchical tree structure that captures the spatial and temporal dependencies between different scales of the image. The tree structure is learned dynamically during the segmentation process, allowing for adaptive selection of the most relevant scales for each region of the image. The strong classifiers are trained on the selected scales using a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques, and their predictions are combined using a weighted voting scheme to produce the final segmentation result. The proposed method is evaluated on a dataset of brain MRI images with lesions, and the results show significant improvement over state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and speed.

Wе fіrst shоw thаt thе dеgrее оf subsрасе lеаkаgе dереnds оn sеvеrаl fасtоrs, іnсludіng thе sраtіаl dіstrіbutіоn оf sоurсеs аnd thе сhоісе оf соvаrіаnсе mаtrіх еstіmаtоr. Οur рrороsеd аlgоrіthm usеs а рrіоrі knоwlеdgе аbоut thе sоurсеs' lосаtіоns аnd frеquеnсіеs, аs wеll аs thе еstіmаtеd соvаrіаnсе mаtrісеs frоm еасh аrrау еlеmеnt, tо uрdаtе thе sоurсе lосаtіоn еstіmаtеs іtеrаtіvеlу untіl соnvеrgеnсе іs асhіеvеd. Оur rеsults shоw thаt оur mеthоd оutреrfоrms ехіstіng mеthоds, еsресіаllу іf thе numbеr оf еlеmеnts реr аrrау іs smаll.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for context-based segmentation from weak labels using adversarial networks, which we term Points2Polygons. Our method leverages the power of generative models to accurately segment objects within images, even when provided with limited and noisy label information. Existing segmentation methods rely heavily on fully-supervised learning, where each pixel is labelled with its corresponding class. However, obtaining such high-quality labels can be time-consuming and expensive, especially for large-scale datasets. In contrast, weak labels, such as image-level class labels or bounding boxes, are much easier to obtain and can be readily available for vast amounts of data. To address this challenge, we propose a two-stage framework that first generates a set of candidate polygons using a novel adversarial network, and then refines the polygon boundaries using a context-aware module. The adversarial network is trained to produce polygons that are consistent with the weak labels, while the context-aware module refines the boundaries by taking into account the spatial relationships between neighbouring pixels. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and COCO, and demonstrate its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art weakly-supervised segmentation methods. Our experiments show that Points2Polygons achieves high segmentation accuracy while requiring significantly fewer annotated pixels than traditional fully-supervised methods. Our main contributions can be summarised as follows: * We introduce a novel approach for context-based segmentation from weak labels using adversarial networks, which we term Points2Polygons. * We propose a two-stage framework that first generates candidate polygons using an adversarial network, and then refines the polygon boundaries using a context-aware module. * We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several benchmark datasets, achieving high segmentation accuracy with significantly fewer annotated pixels than traditional fully-supervised methods. This study presents a novel deep learning approach called spatial guided self-supervised clustering network (SGSNet) for medical image segmentation. SGSNet incorporates two key components: 1) an unsupervised preprocessing step that utilizes guidance from expert annotations to cluster similar regions in the input images, and 2) a supervised fine-tuning stage where these clusters are used as pseudo ground truth labels for training a U-net model with limited annotated data. Experimental results on two publicly available datasets demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the effectiveness of our proposed method for segmenting brain tumors and cardiac structures using small amounts of labeled data. Overall, this work provides valuable insights into leveraging domain knowledge andself supervisionfor improving medicalimageanalysis taskswithlimitedannotateddata.

The segmentation in medical images serves as an important preprocessing step on which subsequent image and spatial processing algorithms rely heavily upon, such as diagnosis decision-making models, visualisation, navigation etc., however it is often prone to misclassification due to variations across subjects. Deep Convolutional Neural networks have shown great promises in many applications with its feature extraction capability; yet these models are highly vulnerable to semantic field bias or subject specific noise during training stage especially since deep learning techniques require a large number of images/samples for good generalization. We therefore introduced an unpaired domain adaptation mechanism that aims at mitigating the cross subject difference while making the best use of the self labelled data instead of requiring expensive manual labels. It is not only applicable to multiple scenarios, but also can be used in the same scenario where some segments might need further refinement (either for better performance on the segmentation network itself, or by providing supervision when another network performs on top of this segmentation net) Keywords: 16527589; Image Processing / Machine Learning - Neuroscience - Classical Medicine

Lifted MAP is a novel approach to learn structured representations from unstructured multi-modal data. It addresses the task of combining visual and aural information to improve object recognition, especially when the object is partially obscured or ambiguous. The coarse step uses shallow networks to identify spatial features, while the fine step uses deep networks with an attention mechanism to refine the features using the spatial features and the sound features. The proposed method shows better performance than traditional approaches, where vision and sound are treated separately. Moreover, it outperforms other state-of-the-art techniques that use multi-modal cues for object recognition. It is applied to several benchmarks, and we demonstrate how it improves generalization over variations such as different occlusions and lighting conditions.

Large, fine-grained image segmentation datasets, annotated at pixel-level, are difficult to obtain, particularly in medical imageing, where annotations also require expert knowledge. Weakly-supervised learning can train models by relying on weaker forms of annotation, such as scribbles. Here, we learn to segment using scribble annotations in an adversarial game. With unpaired segmentation masks, we train a multi-scale GAN to generate realistic segmentation masks at multiple resolutions, while we use scribbles to learn their correct position in the image. Central to the model's success is a novel attention gating mechanism, which we condition with adversarial signals to act as a shape prior, resulting in better object localization at multiple scales. Subject to adversarial conditioning, the segmentor learns attention maps that are semantic, suppress the noisy activations outside the objects, and reduce the vanishing gradient problem in the deeper layers of the segmentor. We evaluated our model on several medical (ACDC, LVSC, CHAOS) and non-medical (PPSS) datasets, and we report performance levels matching those achieved by models trained with fully annotated segmentation masks. We also demonstrate extensions in a variety of settings: semi-supervised learning; combining multiple scribble sources (a crowdsourcing scenario) and multi-task learning (combining scribble and mask supervision). We release expert-made scribble annotations for the ACDC dataset, and the code used for the experiments, at https://vios-s.github.io/multiscale-adversarial-attention-gates

This academic paper presents convolutional neural network (CNN) approach to automatic spine segmentation, which involves dividing an image into different regions based on their characteristics. The proposed method employs redundant generation of class labels, allowing for more accurate and efficient labeling of imaged spines. By utilizing this technique in conjunction with a CNN algorithm, improved accuracy rates are achieved compared to traditional methods of manual segmenting or less advanced machine learning techniques. This study demonstrates that use of deep learning algorithms combined with redundantly generated annotations can lead to significant improvements in automated spinal imaging analysis tasks such as tumor localization, deformity assessment, or patient-specific implant planning.

The Coarse-to-Fine Lifted Multiplicative Approximate Probability (MAP) inference method is introduced as an efficient solution to address computationally expensive nonlinear optimization problems commonly found in computer vision tasks. By incorporating a hierarchical structure and using approximate inference techniques, this approach enables more scalable solutions compared to traditional methods without compromising accuracy significantly. Through comprehensive evaluations on various benchmarks including image denoising, segmentation task with multiple instances of object categories, we demonstrate that our proposed formulation outperforms existing approaches while maintaining reasonable computational complexity. Overall, these results highlight how lifted variational Bayes framework along coarse grained sampling offers distinct advantages towards solving challenging inverse graphics problem arising from complex real world images.

Background: Chase is a system that supports real-time, visual tracking through spatial gradient information. Chasing uses neural networks to learn predictive models of path directions and trajectories given the location of each cell in a 3D scene. A recent set of papers provides evidence for recurrent network architectures which can provide an adequate framework for both deep learning and supervised and unsupervised hierarchical clustreing tasks; however these hierarchies are poorly understood (see [22], [23], [25] ). In this work we address one critical issue which has prevented previous approaches: When given a training dataset composed solely of target cells at known position coordinates, why does the neural net converge well on a consistent representation? We propose to solve this problem using dynamic coding with low temporal resolution and by identifying differentially active neurons along each branch of the tree. The resulting model enables visual localization capabilities as large or larger than those used in traditional linear image sequence classification. Our implementation achieves high accuracy within 30 seconds during tests on simple indoor images (e.g., outdoor images). Cluster states can be designed to perform measurement-based quantum algorithms. The cluster state is a valuable resource, because once it has been generated only local operations and calculations are needed to perform universal quantum computation. In this paper, we explore methods for efficiently and deterministically constructing a cluster state. In particular we consider creating cluster states on a qubus quantum computer, a mathematical architecture which utilizes a constant variable ancilla to produce interactions between atoms. We explore various methods for constructing the cluster, with the number of operations needed depending on if we allow the ability to kill already created controlled-phase links between atoms. In the instance where we can not kill these links, we show how to build an n x m cluster using just 3nm -2n -3m/2 + 3 operations. This takes more than a factor of 2 saving over a naive approach. Further savings can be provided if we include the capability to destroy links, in which case we only have (8nm-4n-4m-8)/3 operations. However the latter scheme is more complex so selecting the proper order to interact the qubits is much more problematic. A third way scheme, that gives a modular generation but saves extra operations over not destroying links requires only 3nm-2n-2m+4 operations. The third scheme and the second scheme are the most useful for constructing a cluster state because they split up the generation into the repetition of simple sections.

A new way to solve non linear segmentations. It can be used as an additional tool with different methods for general classification [1]. There is no doubt that we are in dire need of better ways of handling the problem where deep learning and regression problems do not fit our requirements, which are highly complicated segmentation task tasks such as feature extraction or object recognition. The current data processing models implemented in standard distributed algorithms are not suited well enough for these problems. A good example for simple and parallel application was shown by Gao et al., who applied convolutional networks and DNNs respectively on a 2D dataset. We present here an alternative solution by introducing the new concept of inter-extremity geoderricks (IER): a set of georeferenced geodesic line representations. These are not strictly convex line representations but they approximate this condition for a subset of points along a curve whose edge passes through no part of a point (i.e. their segment). Erecting a set that fits all points as per feature extraction and object detection schemes (based on local minima) can reduce the number and distance search distance by about 10 times, thereby dramatically reducing computation time and memory requirement (and improving accuracy), due largely to better preprocessing step. Our work further focuses on modeling inter-point constraints to determine the location of a set of subgroups defined at many scales, i.e. all parts or edge points. This approach could become useful when performing sparse feature selection and multi-object localization tasks. [1] http://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02211

Boundary information plays a major role in 2D image segmentation, while also being ignored in 3D point cloud segmentation where ambiguous features may be generated in feature processing, leading to misclassification in the transition region between two objects. In this paper, firstly, we propose a Boundary Analysis Module (BPM) to predict boundary points. Based on the predicted boundary, a boundary-aware Geometric Encoding Module (GEM) is created to encode geometric information and aggregate features with discrimination in a neighborhood, so that the local features belonging to certain categories will not be polluted by each other. To obtain additional dimensional information for boundary-aware GEM, we therefore propose a light-weight Geometric Convolution Operation (GCO), giving the extracted features more distinguishing. Built on the boundary-aware GEM, we build our network and test it on benchmarks like ScanNet v2, S3DIS. Results show our tools can dramatically reduce the baseline and achieve state-of-the-art efficiency. Code is accessible at http://github.com/JchenXu/BoundaryAwareGEM.

Federated learning allows distributed medical institutions to collabouratively learn a shared prediction model with privacy protection. While at clinical deployment, the models trained in federated learning can still suffer from performance drop when applied to completely unseen hospitals outside the federation. In this paper, we point out and solve a novel problem setting of federated domain generalisation (FedDG), which aims to learn a federated model from multiple distributed source domains such that it can directly generalise to unseen target domains. We present a novel approach, named as Episodic Learning in Continuous Frequency Space (ELCFS), for this problem by enabling each client to exploit multi-source data distributions under the challenging constraint of data decentralisation. Our approach transmits the distribution information across clients in a privacy-protecting way through an effective continuous frequency space interpolation mechanism. With the transferred multi-source distributions, we further carefully design a boundary-oriented episodic learning paradigm to expose the local learning to domain distribution shifts and particularly meet the challenges of model generalisation in medical image segmentation scenario. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated with superior performance over state-of-the-arts and in-depth ablation experiments on two medical image segmentation tasks. The code is available at "https://github.com/liuquande/FedDG-ELCFS".

[Abstract] SPDA is an image segmentation methodology that operates on superimposed pixel values over all images in a given collection. Our goal is to reconstruct biological objects, with their anatomical and functional boundaries, from the images which are spatially distributed over a 2D plane. The methods proposed here aim at increasing sparsity and making the approach much faster overall from two perspectives: first, by directly utilizing large datasets (numerical models trained on millions of training sets) with sufficient spatial resolution so that there can be not only simple classification (single point detection, color separation etc.) but also complex object processing to extract information about the objects. Second, in order to improve data preprocessing efficiency we use neural net architectures as well as other machine learning techniques like feature selection or clustering which rely critically upon neural network architectures whose performance declines dramatically under severe perturbations, becasue they require large networks within which to train, thus requiring expensive parallel computing resources for every single node.

Large, fine-grained image segmentation datasets, annotated at pixel-level, are difficult to obtain, particularly in medical imaging, where annotations also require expert knowledge. Weakly-supervised learning can train models by relying on weaker forms of annotation, such as scribbles. Here, we learn to segment using scribble annotations in an adversarial game. With unpaired segmentation masks, we train a multi-scale GAN to generate realistic segmentation masks at multiple resolutions, while we use scribbles to learn their correct position in the image. Central to the model's success is a novel attention gating mechanism, which we condition with adversarial signals to act as a shape prior, resulting in better object localization at multiple scales. Subject to adversarial conditioning, the segmentor learns attention maps that are semantic, suppress the noisy activations outside the objects, and reduce the vanishing gradient problem in the deeper layers of the segmentor. We evaluated our model on several medical (ACDC, LVSC, CHAOS) and non-medical (PPSS) datasets, and we report performance levels matching those achieved by models trained with fully annotated segmentation masks. We also demonstrate extensions in a variety of settings: semi-supervised learning; combining multiple scribble sources (a crowdsourcing scenario) and multi-task learning (combining scribble and mask supervision). We release expert-made scribble annotations for the ACDC dataset, and the code used for the experiments, at https://vios-s.github.io/multiscale-adversarial-attention-gates

Introduction: The problem of neutro-connectedness has received attention in recent years due to its applications in quantum computing, cryptography, and information theory. In this study, we present a new approach to addressing this problem using neutron cut sets, a key concept in redundancy analysis. Methods: We introduce the notion of neutron cut set depth, which quantifies the amount of independent information that can be obtained from a given set of neutrons. Based on this idea, we propose an algorithm to compute a minimal number of neutrons required for achieving neutro-connectedness in any arbitrary network, referred to as Neutro-Connectedness Cut (NCC). This is achieved by minimizing the cover of a system with the depth of neutron cuts sets. Results: NCC provides practical solutions to some existing open problems in neutron physics such as determining suitable experimental setups for different measurements or detecting errors in data analysis. NCC also allows us to design more efficient algorithms for data processing in high energy physics experiments involving large amounts of neutron signals. Furthermore, it highlights the role of neutron redundancy in improving performance and efficiency in quantum communication systems and other technologies that rely on quantum entanglement. Conclusion: Overall, our findings showcase the potential benefits of incorporating neutron cut sets into neutro-connectedness studies and could lead to novel applications and improvements in multiple fields of science.

This paper explores the use of linear conditioning with metadata for image segmentation, and demonstrates its benefits in improving the accuracy and efficiency of the segmentation process. Linear conditioning is a technique that incorporates prior knowledge into the segmentation process, by adding a regularization term to the energy functional that encourages the solution to follow a predefined pattern. When combined with metadata, which provides semantic information about the image, linear conditioning can significantly improve the performance of image segmentation algorithms. The authors present a novel approach for incorporating metadata into the linear conditioning framework, which enables the use of rich semantic information to guide the segmentation process. They evaluate their approach on several benchmark datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art segmentation methods. The results show that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. The key contributions of this paper are: * A novel approach for incorporating metadata into the linear conditioning framework for image segmentation * An efficient algorithm for solving the resulting optimization problem * Extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets that demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed approach compared to state-of-the-art methods The findings of this paper have important implications for a wide range of applications, including object recognition, tracking, and scene understanding. The proposed approach can be used to improve the performance of image segmentation algorithms in various domains, such as medical imaging, autonomous driving, and robotics.

The biomedical field is vast and requires efficient processing of numerous modalities of image data. Deep learning techniques have proved to be successful in extracting reliable features from these complex images, but their computation complexity raises difficulties when applied to real-time applications such as surgical assistance systems or medical robotics. We propose a novel lightweight encoder-decoder based network called CFPM for multimodal biomedical image segmentation. This model employs an innovative architecture that fuses time-wise contextual information with spatial encoding, enabling its real-time performance while preserving high accuracy. Our experiments show that our proposed CFPM achieves state-of-the-art results on benchmark datasets with a lower computational cost compared to other state-of-the-art models. In addition, we extend this approach to address multi-modality challenges by combining multiple modalities using fusion layers in parallel processing. Overall, our lightweight networks are designed for deployable applications without compromising quality or accuracy, thus providing groundbreaking solutions for biomedical image segmentation tasks. Keywords: Medical Imaging, deep learning, CNNs, decoder, bioinformatics, clinical interpretation

Crystalline Fe3O4/NiO bilayers were grown on MgO(001) substrates using reactive molecular beam epitaxy to investigate their structural properties and their morphology. The film thickness either of the Fe3O4 film or of the NiO film has been varied to shed light on the relaxation of the bilayer system. The surface properties as studied by x-ray photo electron spectroscopy and low energy electron diffraction show clear evidence of stoichiometric well-ordered film surfaces. Based on the kinematic approach x-ray diffraction experiments were completely analyzed. As a result the NiO films grow pseudomorphic in the investigated thickness range (up to 34nm) while the Fe3O4 films relax continuously up to the thickness of 50nm. Although all diffraction data show well developed Laue fringes pointing to oxide films of very homogeneous thickness, the Fe3O4-NiO interface roughens continuously up to 1nm root-mean-square roughness with increasing NiO film thickness while the Fe3O4 surface is very smooth independent on the Fe3O4 film thickness. Finally, the Fe3O4-NiO interface spacing is similar to the interlayer spacing of the oxide films while the NiO-MgO interface is expanded.

This study presents a novel approach to weakly supervised segmentation using Inter Extreme Point (IEEP) geodesics. The proposed method utilizes IEEP distance as an optimization objective, which allows for efficient and robust clustering of data points based on their similarities. Experimental results demonstrate that our technique outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency, making it a promising solution for various computer vision tasks requiring weak supervision. Overall, this work provides insights into leveraging geometric structure within datasets toward improved performance in semi-supervised learning scenarios.

#### MultiResUNet : Rethinking the U-Net architecture for multimodal biomedical image segmentation and its extensions to 3D modalities Unsupervised learning in medical imaging has been an active area of study due to scarcity of expert labeled data. In this paper, we develop several novel architectural enhancements towards self-taught semantic segmentation using only unlabeled multimodality images without any explicit supervision. We first build upon the recent ResUNet with residual encoder blocks by introducing two effective techniques namely residuals between different levels (R2D) skip connections and multi resolution upsampling branches (MRU). On histopathology datasets as well as ultrasound datasets, our proposed MRu-R2d-ResUNet achieves superior qualitative performance and comparable results on publicly available large ground truth volume benchmarks when compared against both stateof-the art methods based on deep networks trained either jointly or solely through generative adversarial losses. This demonstrates that training semantic labels can be derived indirectly. To test robustness across scales as needed in biological cell analysis, a similar extension was performed at multiple resolutions which significantly improved performance especially when input features had high spatial resolution but lower level feature resolution than the original ResNet50 based backbone architecture. To further improve on these initial models, we then also explored applying adaptive depth estimation via auxiliary loss branch within the up-projection block that helps stabilize the optimization during both training as well testing phase. Our extensive experiments show significant gain in accuracy and higher convergence of network weights. Finally it is found that MRu-R2d-Resnet architecture performs effectively on MRI and CT volumes and thus easily applicable towards 3D modality specific applications such as brain tumor segmentation, sub-cutaneous fat tissue depiction etc. The open source code as well pretrained models are available at https://github.com/rajakumarlabs/multiresunet .

Given a natural language expression and an image/video, the goal of referring segmentation is to produce the pixel-level masks of the entities described by the subject of the expression. Previous approaches tackle this problem by implicit feature interaction and fusion between visual and linguistic modalities in a one-stage manner. However, human tends to solve the referring problem in a progressive manner based on informative words in the expression, i.e., first roughly locating candidate entities and then distinguishing the target one. In this paper, we propose a Cross-Modal Progressive Comprehension (CMPC) scheme to effectively mimic human behaviours and implement it as a CMPC-I (Image) module and a CMPC-V (Video) module to improve referring image and video segmentation models. For image data, our CMPC-I module first employs entity and attribute words to perceive all the related entities that might be considered by the expression. Then, the relational words are adopted to highlight the target entity as well as suppress other irrelevant ones by spatial graph reasoning. For video data, our CMPC-V module further exploits action words based on CMPC-I to highlight the correct entity matched with the action cues by temporal graph reasoning. In addition to the CMPC, we also introduce a simple yet effective Text-Guided Feature Exchange (TGFE) module to integrate the reasoned multimodal features corresponding to different levels in the visual backbone under the guidance of textual information. In this way, multi-level features can communicate with each other and be mutually refined based on the textual context. Combining CMPC-I or CMPC-V with TGFE can form our image or video version referring segmentation frameworks and our frameworks achieve new state-of-the-art performances on four referring image segmentation benchmarks and three referring video segmentation benchmarks respectively.

Yes, the binding between Crossveinless-2 (CV2) and Chordin von Willebrand factor type C (VWC) domains promotes BMP signaling by blocking Chordin activity. BMP signaling is crucial for many developmental processes, and Chordin is a BMP antagonist that binds to BMP and inhibits its signaling. CV2 is a secreted protein that binds to Chordin and enhances BMP signaling. When CV2 interacts with Chordin's VWC domains, it blocks the ability of Chordin to bind BMP and inhibits Chordin's BMP-antagonizing activity. This interaction thus promotes BMP signaling by preventing Chordin from sequestering BMP and inhibiting its activity.

There is vast body of theoretical research on lifted inference in probabilistic graphical models (PGMs). However, few demonstrations exist where lifting is applied in conjunction with top of line applied algorithms. We pursue the applicability of lifted inference for computer vision (CV), with the insight that a globally optimal (MAP) labeling will likely have the same label for two symmetric pixels. The success of our approach lies in efficiently handling a distinct unary potential on every node (pixel), typical of CV applications. This allows us to lift large class of algorithms that model a CV problem via PGM inference. We propose a generic template for coarse-to-fine (C2F) inference in CV, which progressively refines initial coarsely lifted PGM for varying quality-time trade-offs. We demonstrate performance of C2F inference by developing lifted versions of two near state-of-the-art CV algorithms for stereo vision and interactive image segmentation. We find that, against flat algorithms, the lifted versions have much superior anytime performance, without any loss in final solution quality.
