Ιmаgе аnаlуsіs usіng mоrе thаn оnе mоdаlіtу (і.е. multі-mоdаl) hаs bееn іnсrеаsіnglу аррlіеd іn thе fіеld оf bіоmеdісаl іmаgіng. Оnе оf thе сhаllеngеs іn реrfоrmіng thе multіmоdаl аnаlуsіs іs thаt thеrе ехіst multірlе sсhеmеs fоr fusіng thе іnfоrmаtіоn frоm dіffеrеnt mоdаlіtіеs, whеrе suсh sсhеmеs аrе аррlісаtіоn-dереndеnt аnd lасk а unіfіеd frаmеwоrk tо guіdе thеіr dеsіgns. Іn thіs wоrk wе fіrstlу рrороsе а соnсерtuаl аrсhіtесturе fоr thе іmаgе fusіоn sсhеmеs іn suреrvіsеd bіоmеdісаl іmаgе аnаlуsіs: fusіng аt thе fеаturе lеvеl, fusіng аt thе сlаssіfіеr lеvеl, аnd fusіng аt thе dесіsіоn-mаkіng lеvеl. Furthеr, mоtіvаtеd bу thе rесеnt suссеss іn аррlуіng dеер lеаrnіng fоr nаturаl іmаgе аnаlуsіs, wе іmрlеmеnt thе thrее іmаgе fusіоn sсhеmеs аbоvе bаsеd оn thе Соnvоlutіоnаl Νеurаl Νеtwоrk (СΝΝ) wіth vаrіеd struсturеs, аnd соmbіnеd іntо а sіnglе frаmеwоrk. Τhе рrороsеd іmаgе sеgmеntаtіоn frаmеwоrk іs сараblе оf аnаlуzіng thе multі-mоdаlіtу іmаgеs usіng dіffеrеnt fusіng sсhеmеs sіmultаnеоuslу. Τhе frаmеwоrk іs аррlіеd tо dеtесt thе рrеsеnсе оf sоft tіssuе sаrсоmа frоm thе соmbіnаtіоn оf Μаgnеtіс Rеsоnаnсе Іmаgіng (МRІ), Соmрutеd Тоmоgrарhу (СΤ) аnd Ρоsіtrоn Еmіssіоn Τоmоgrарhу (РЕΤ) іmаgеs. Іt іs fоund frоm thе rеsults thаt whіlе аll thе fusіоn sсhеmеs оutреrfоrm thе sіnglе-mоdаlіtу sсhеmеs, fusіng аt thе fеаturе lеvеl саn gеnеrаllу асhіеvе thе bеst реrfоrmаnсе іn tеrms оf bоth ассurасу аnd соmрutаtіоnаl соst, but аlsо suffеrs frоm thе dесrеаsеd rоbustnеss іn thе рrеsеnсе оf lаrgе еrrоrs іn аnу іmаgе mоdаlіtіеs.

This paper maps the national UK web presence on the basis of an analysis of the .uk domain from 1996 to 2010. It reviews previous attempts to use web archives to understand national web domains and describes the dataset. Next, it presents an analysis of the .uk domain, including the overall number of links in the archive and changes in the link density of different second-level domains over time. We then explore changes over time within a particular second-level domain, the academic subdomain .ac.uk, and compare linking practices with variables, including institutional affiliation, league table ranking, and geographic location. We do not detect institutional affiliation affecting linking practices and find only partial evidence of league table ranking affecting network centrality, but find a clear inverse relationship between the density of links and the geographical distance between universities. This echoes prior findings regarding offline academic activity, which allows us to argue that real-world factors like geography continue to shape academic relationships even in the Internet age. We conclude with directions for future uses of web archive resources in this emerging area of research.

Performing inference in graphs is a common task within several machine learning problems, e.g., image segmentation, community detection, among others. For a given undirected connected graph, we tackle the statistical problem of exactly recovering an unknown ground-truth binary labeling of the nodes from a single corrupted observation of each edge. Such problem can be formulated as a quadratic combinatorial optimization problem over the boolean hypercube, where it has been shown before that one can (with high probability and in polynomial time) exactly recover the ground-truth labeling of graphs that have an isoperimetric number that grows with respect to the number of nodes (e.g., complete graphs, regular expanders). In this work, we apply a powerful hierarchy of relaxations, known as the sum-of-squares (SoS) hierarchy, to the combinatorial problem. Motivated by empirical evidence on the improvement in exact recoverability, we center our attention on the degree-4 SoS relaxation and set out to understand the origin of such improvement from a graph theoretical perspective. We show that the solution of the dual of the relaxed problem is related to finding edge weights of the Johnson and Kneser graphs, where the weights fulfill the SoS constraints and intuitively allow the input graph to increase its algebraic connectivity. Finally, as byproduct of our analysis, we derive a novel Cheeger-type lower bound for the algebraic connectivity of graphs with signed edge weights.

RLCorrector: Reinforced Proofreading for Connectomics Image Segmentation. In a recent study on cerebral networks, it was found that an effective method for obtaining accurate and efficient brain network representations is to use both manual and automatic methods. RLCorrector combines the strengths of both by using a reinforcement learning technique to correct the errors made by an initial automatic method. The experimental results obtained on a standard dataset show that the accuracy and efficiency of connectomic images are improved using RLCorrector. It can also reduce the need for manual verification, thereby making it an important tool for future research in cerebral networks.

The increasing prevalence of visual and auditory data in today's digital world has given rise to new challenges in information processing. This is particularly true when it comes to tasks such as referring segmentation, which requires the ability to identify objects based on both visual and audio cues. In this study, we propose a novel approach called cross-modal progressive comprehension (CMP) that leverages multiple modalities to improve performance. Specifically, our proposed method uses a multi-task learning framework that jointly trains two sets of models: one that predicts semantic labels from the text modality, another that performs object detection within an image. To further enhance the capacity for understanding complex referral expressions, we introduce a progressively refining module that iteratively incorporates predictions made by previous models into updated outputs at each step. Our experiments demonstrate significant improvements over baselines using both synthetic and real-world data, indicating promising results for CMP as a tool for accurate and efficient referring segmentation across multiple modalities.

In this paper, we present RLCorrector, a novel approach to connectomics image segmentation that leverages reinforcement learning to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the proofreading process. Connectomics is emerging field that aims to map the neural connections within brain, and image segmentation is crucial step in this process. However, current methods often suffer from errors and inconsistencies in produced masks, which can significantly impact the subsequent analysis and interpretation of the data. To address these limitations, we propose RLCorrector, which combines reinforcement learning with a proofreading framework to optimize correction of errors in the masks. Our approach uses deep neural network to learn a policy that accurately identifies and corrects errors in the masks, while also adapting to various types of mistakes and anomalies. We evaluate RLCorrector on several datasets and compare it to existing methods, demonstrating its superior performance and ability to produce high-quality masks with reduced manual effort. We also perform series of ablation studies to analyze the effects of different components of our method and provide insights into reinforcement learning process. The results show that RLCorrector achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks, outperforming traditional proofreading methods and other baselines. Additionally, we demonstrate versatility of our approach by applying it to various connectomics imaging modalities, including electron microscopy and fluorescence microscopy. Our work has significant implications for the future of connectomics research, as it provides reliable and efficient means of producing accurate masks for neural connection tracing. By improving quality and consistency of data, RLCorrector has potential to accelerate discoveries in neuroscience and enhance our understanding of the brain's complex neural networks.

The academic paper titled "CHASE: Robust Visual Tracking via Cell-Level Differentiable Neural Architecture Search" presents a novel approach to visual tracking using cell-level differentiable neural architecture search. The proposed method, called CHASE, utilizes a hierarchical cell structure to learn robust feature representations for tracking tasks. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the CHASE approach through extensive experiments and comparisons with state-of-the-art tracking algorithms. Overall, CHASE provides a promising solution for robust visual tracking and showcases the potential of cell-level differentiable neural architecture search in computer vision applications.

Abstract: This paper discusses the Height Theorem, which provides a relation between the semantic structure (or 'height') of regular expressions defining piecewise testable languages, and their linguistic properties. Additionally, it explains how this theory can be employed to determine computational difficulties associated with checking if substrings ('subwords') occur within strings belonging to such languages. Using logical reasoning supplemented by mathematical statements, we show that many natural subsets cannot belong to these classes without substantially altering overall language membership decisions or accepting probabilities; thereby establishing some tight limits on heights while not shedding light on underlying mathematical intricacies involved when manipulating partial data regarding linguistic tokens in practical scenarios relevant linguistics applications among people.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for quantifying segmentation uncertainty in dense multi-label CRFs, titled Perturb-and-MPM. Dense multi-label CRFs are widely used in image segmentation tasks, as they can model complex relationships between image pixels and multiple labels. However, the uncertainty in the segmentation process has been largely overlooked, which is crucial for building trustworthy models and improving their performance. Existing methods for quantifying segmentation uncertainty in CRFs are limited, and they often rely on approximations or heuristics. In contrast, our approach uses a principled method to compute the uncertainty in the segmentation process. We introduce a perturbation-based framework that generates a set of possible segmentations, and then use a Monte Carlo dropout technique to estimate the uncertainty of each segmentation. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and compare it with state-of-the-art methods. Our results show that Perturb-and-MPM outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in providing meaningful uncertainty estimates, which can be used for tasks such as active learning and anomaly detection. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: * We propose a novel approach for quantifying segmentation uncertainty in dense multi-label CRFs, which is based on a perturbation-based framework and Monte Carlo dropout. * We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. * We show that our approach provides meaningful uncertainty estimates, which can be used for tasks such as active learning and anomaly detection. Overall, our work fills a significant gap in the field of image segmentation, and provides a new tool for building trustworthy models that can handle complex relationships between image pixels and multiple labels.

Abstract Selection of an appropriate labeled drawing to fit into deep learning architectures has been problematic in recent years, since many trained examples exhibit unexpected features when viewed as images. This study provides simple guidelines for identifying such unlabelled examples through image recognition training on a large, open source system, called ImageNet. A classification accuracy of 62% was achieved with 1 hour and 12 supervised tests, which includes all features classified by the network, while an example validation set contained just 88 classes. Our method can identify some types of unlabeled images efficiently enough to be useful in some kinds of applications. Furthermore, its approach enables significant reduction of data collection time relative to prior methods that require several hours for labeling (e.g., manually examining hundreds or thousands of labeled images), and it does so despite providing an almost uniform distribution of labels across the entire dataset even though not every image on the ground belongs to any of those classes. We believe our results show how quickly image segmentation techniques can improve in the face of increasing parallelism in deep-learning architectures; furthermore, their fast response to changing the number of categories during training also suggests the utility of incorporating more than one category into our architecture at the same time. These preliminary results provide important directions for future work on these problems.

Single Image Super Resolution (SISR) techniques based on Super Resolution Convolutional Neural Networks (SRCNN) are applied to micro-computed tomography ({\mu}CT) images of sandstone and carbonate rocks. Digital rock imaging is limited by the capability of the scanning device resulting in trade-offs between resolution and field of view, and super resolution methods tested in this study aim to compensate for these limits. SRCNN models SR-Resnet, Enhanced Deep SR (EDSR), and Wide-Activation Deep SR (WDSR) are used on the Digital Rock Super Resolution 1 (DRSRD1) Dataset of 4x downsampled images, comprising of 2000 high resolution (800x800) raw micro-CT images of Bentheimer sandstone and Estaillades carbonate. The trained models are applied to the validation and test data within the dataset and show a 3-5 dB rise in image quality compared to bicubic interpolation, with all tested models performing within a 0.1 dB range. Difference maps indicate that edge sharpness is completely recovered in images within the scope of the trained model, with only high frequency noise related detail loss. We find that aside from generation of high-resolution images, a beneficial side effect of super resolution methods applied to synthetically downgraded images is the removal of image noise while recovering edgewise sharpness which is beneficial for the segmentation process. The model is also tested against real low-resolution images of Bentheimer rock with image augmentation to account for natural noise and blur. The SRCNN method is shown to act as a preconditioner for image segmentation under these circumstances which naturally leads to further future development and training of models that segment an image directly. Image restoration by SRCNN on the rock images is of significantly higher quality than traditional methods and suggests SRCNN methods are a viable processing step in a digital rock workflow.

Inter Extreme Points (IEPs) provide a promising approach to weakly supervised image segmentation. IEPs are points in images that can be computed from a small region around them using geometric properties such as distance and angles, without requiring explicit object detection or pixel-level labeling. In our work, we explore their potential in weakly supervised automatic segmentation by analyzing their structural relationships with local neighbors and other regions within an image. We show that IEPs possess rich information about object boundaries, shape, texture, and contextual hierarchy, which makes them well suited for weak supervision. However, direct use of IEPs is limited by their low resolution compared with pixels, leading to spatial ambiguity. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework that constructs intermediate representations between spatial neighborhoods and pixels based on smooth 3-D geodetic paths connecting extreme points across regions with similar geometric structures. Our scheme explicitly exploits spatial continuity, while preserving local geometric relationships among elements in these regions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of intermediate levels of supervisory information using IEPs to improve accuracy for both unsupervised and semi-supervised image segmentation tasks. It also enables visualization of underlying image structure through analysis of IEP cluster connectivity patterns. Overall, our proposed method offers new insights into interpreting spatial hierarchy and integrating nonlocal features at various scales and resolutions for weakly supervised image processing in computer vision applications.

Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitors are a class of drugs commonly used for the treatment of erectile dysfunction (ED). Since the introduction of the first PDE5 inhibitor, sildenafil (Viagra), in 1998, several other drugs have been developed and approved for use in treating ED. These include vardenafil (Levitra), tadalafil (Cialis), and avanafil (Stendra). Mechanism of Action: PDE5 inhibitors work by promoting relaxation of the smooth muscle tissues of the corpus cavernosum, resulting in increased blood flow to the penile shaft and erection. They achieve this by selectively inhibiting the phosphodiesterase enzyme type 5, which is responsible for the degradation of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) in the penile smooth muscle cells. With PDE5 inhibition, cGMP levels increase, leading to smooth muscle relaxation and enhanced blood flow. Efficacy and Safety: Numerous clinical trials and analyses have demonstrated the efficacy of PDE5 inhibitors in improving erectile function in men with ED of varying etiologies, including organic, psychogenic, and mixed causes. PDE5 inhibitors have been found to be effective in treating ED in men with comorbid conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease. In general, PDE5 inhibitors are well-tolerated by most patients. Common side effects include headache, facial flushing, nasal congestion, dyspepsia, and back pain. These side effects are typically mild and transient. However, more severe side effects such as the risk of priapism, sudden hearing loss, and vision disturbances have been reported, although they are rare. Contraindications to the use of PDE5 inhibitors include concurrent use of nitrates and hypersensitivity to the drug or any of its components. We show that problem of computing cost of a winning strategy is NP-hard, and we present polynomial-time algorithm for computing the cost of winning strategy in parity games with costs. We also show that the problem of computing the cost of a winning strategy is NP-hard, and we present a polynomial-time algorithm for computing cost of a winning strategy in parity games with costs.

Incorporating shape information is essential for the delineation of many organs and anatomical structures in medical images. While previous work has mainly focused on parametric spatial transformations applied on reference template shapes, in this paper, we address the Bayesian inference of parametric shape models for segmenting medical images with the objective to provide interpretable results. The proposed framework defines a likelihood appearance probability and a prior label probability based on a generic shape function through a logistic function. A reference length parameter defined in the sigmoid controls the trade-off between shape and appearance information. The inference of shape parameters is performed within an Expectation-Maximisation approach where a Gauss-Newton optimization stage allows to provide an approximation of the posterior probability of shape parameters. This framework is applied to the segmentation of cochlea structures from clinical CT images constrained by a 28 parameter shape model. It is evaluated on three different datasets, one of which includes more than 200 patient images. The results show performances comparable to supervised methods and better than previously proposed unsupervised ones. It also enables an analysis of parameter distributions and the quantification of segmentation uncertainty including the effect of the shape model.

We provide closed form expressions and inequalities between some stochastically dominated complex random variables, that have applications to statistical physics. In particular we show how these results can used when dealing with relaxations in quantum spin models on trees and Cayley graphs such as the Potts model or the Ising model. Using these we derive bounds and exact quantities for correlation functions, order parameters and free energies of systems exhibiting phase transitions, such as Potts spins located at vertices connected by an array of triangles within a mean field approximation, which has recently found application with QUBO algorithms. Finally, our exact solutions enable us to revisit known approximations related to high-temperature expansions of partition sums and obtain further improved estimates along similar lines.

Importance of visual context in scene understanding tasks is well recognized in the computer vision community. However, to what extent the computer vision models for image classification and semantic segmentation are dependent on the context to make their predictions is unclear. A model overly relying on context will fail when encountering objects in context distributions different from training data and hence it is important to identify these dependencies before we can deploy the models in the real-world. We propose a method to quantify the sensitivity of black-box vision models to visual context by editing images to remove selected objects and measuring the response of the target models. We apply this methodology on two tasks, image classification and semantic segmentation, and discover undesirable dependency between objects and context, for example that "sidewalk" segmentation relies heavily on "cars" being present in the image. We propose an object removal based data augmentation solution to mitigate this dependency and increase the robustness of classification and segmentation models to contextual variations. Our experiments show that the proposed data augmentation helps these models improve the performance in out-of-context scenarios, while preserving the performance on regular data.

> Object proposal generation is a fundamental step in many computer vision tasks, such as object detection and image retrieval. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to generate discriminative object proposals. The key idea is to rank the object proposals by a submodular function, which is defined by the discriminative power of the proposals. We show that the submodular function can be efficiently optimised by a greedy algorithm. We also propose a novel method to learn the submodular function from the training data. Experimental results on the PASCAL VOC 2007 and 2012 datasets show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. The paper is available here.

The paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation using adversarial networks. The proposed method, called Points2Polygon, utilizes weak labels and contextual information to produce more accurate segmentations than traditional pixel classification methods. The model is trained in an end-to-end fashion with an adversary network that encourages the generation of coherent and realistic polygonal segments. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches while requiring less annotated data. Overall, this study provides a promising technique for efficient and effective semantic segmentation utilizing limited supervision.

If you picture light as a particle tracing out a sine wave, the particle's forward velocity is the speed of light, and its location in the sine wave is the phase (if it's at the top, middle or bottom). For a single photon, there isn't much difference. The interesting effects start happening when you have a bunch of photons traveling together. Every photon in the group travels at c, if they are all the same wavelength (if the sine waves they trace are equal) then the phase velocity will just be c, because they all trace the same wave over and over (lasers use this property. They set the photons up so they are all tracing the EXACT same sine wave). Photons with different wavelengths (different length sine waves, stretched or compressed like a spring) then it is possible to line the photons up so the at the peaks of the sine waves line up for a moment, but then they diverge into random squiggling. The moment they line up and draw a single peak, they are "in phase" It is also possible to set them up so that the single sine wave appears to "move" in the direction the photons are moving. It's really just an illusion, nothing is actually moving, other than the point where all of the wavelengths line up. So the phase velocity is how fast the point where all the photons are in is moving. The actual velocity is how fast the individual photons in the stream are moving (c).

Annotated datasets with fine-grained image annotations are difficult to obtain, especially in medical images, where expert knowledge is needed for annotations. Weakly supervised learning can build a model from weak annotations, such as scribbles. In this paper we use scribbles to learn to segment an image in an adversarial game. With unpaired masks, we train a multi-scale GAN to learn realistic masks at multiple resolutions, while using scribbles to learn their true position in the image. An important feature of our model is an attention mechanism that is conditioned by the adversarial information and works as a shape prior, leading to improved object localization at multiple scales. The attention mechanism can also suppress the noise and the vanishing gradient of the deep layer in the region-based deep network. Our model has been tested on medical images (ACDC, LVSC, CHAOS) and non-medical images (PPSS), and its performance is comparable to that of the models with full-annotated masks. We have also explored semi-supervised learning, scribbles combined with other crowds, and mixed-in tasks. We share the ACDC scribbles, as well as the code for the experiments, at https: // github.com/vios-s/Multi-Scale-Adversarial-Attention-GAN/.

This paper provides a novel Spatial Guided Self-supervised Clustering System (SGS-Net) for medical image segmentation. The proposed method uses a self-supervised cluster approach to find meaningful representations from unlabeled data, which are then used to guide the segmentation network. The SGS-Net provides a visual guidance component that maintains continuity between the learned clusters and the temporal structure of the image, increasing the reliability of the segmentation results. Clinical findings on two medical image datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach compared to state-of-the-art methods.

This paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation using multi-scale adversarial attention gates. The proposed method utilizes scribbles, which are simple and easy-to-provide annotations, to train a deep neural network that can accurately segment objects in images. The network is designed to learn from scribbles at multiple scales, allowing it to capture both local and global context. Additionally, attention gates are employed to focus on relevant regions of image, further improving segmentation accuracy. The effectiveness of proposed method is demonstrated through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods for image segmentation from scribbles.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "ISNet: Integrate image-Level and Semantic-Level Context for Semantic Segmentation" is as follows: Semantic Segmentation is A critical task in computer vision that involves assigning a label to each pixel in an image. While recent Deep learning-based methods have achieved remarkable performance, they often suffer from overfitting and lack Of contextual understanding. In this paper, we propose ISNet, a novel approach that integrates both image-level and semantic-level context for semantic segmentation. Specifically, we leverage image-level context to provide global information about the image and semantic-level context to provide local information about the objects in the image. We achieve this by Combining a pre-trained image-level classifier with a semantic segmentation network. Our experiments show that ISNet outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

Such a large number of audio-visual data has become increasingly ubiquitous in the digital world, posing new challenges to information processing. For example, tasks such as phrase segmentation require the ability to recognize objects using both visual and auditory features. We propose a new method called multi-modal progressive learning, which combines the two features to improve performance. The proposed method uses a multi-task learning framework, and jointly trains two types of models: one predicts semantic labels from text, and the other detects objects in images. To better understand complex referring expressions, we introduce an iterative model-progressing process, which progressively refines the results of the previous models. The result is an improved performance in both synthetic and real data.

> We propose a new method for learning tree potentials in Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) for image segmentation. The method is based on a structured learning framework that uses a tree-structured graphical model to represent the potentials. The tree structure is learned from the data using a greedy algorithm that iteratively adds edges to the tree. The method is evaluated on the task of image segmentation using the PASCAL VOC 2011 dataset. The results show that the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods for learning tree potentials in CRFs. The paper is available here.

This paper is a critical survey of recent developments in quantum field theory, with particular emphasis on experimental observations relating to the braiding of quarks. The authors review the experimental apparatus used to study the phenomenon, including the Large Hadron Collider experiment Beauty, the ALICE experiment, and the ATLAS experiment at CERN, and the CDF II detector at the Alp-Alfa facility. They also compare the theoretical predictions made by the lattice gauge theorists with the data obtained by the various experiments, and they bring out the discrepancies and the points where the experimentalists are deficient. As a result of this comprehensive overview, readers will gain a better understanding of the braiding phenomenon, both theoretically and in terms of experimental observations. This will help prepare the way for further research into the more basic questions and aspects of braiding, such as phenomenological implications, etc.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for semantic segmentation that leverages the power of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to learn a high-level prior for segmentation. Traditional segmentation methods rely on hand-crafted features and low-level cues, which can be limited in their ability to capture complex contextual relationships between image regions. In contrast, our approach uses CNNs to learn a high-level prior that captures the underlying structure of the image, enabling more accurate and robust segmentation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several challenging benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes. Our experiments show that incorporating the learned high-level prior into a segmentation framework leads to significant improvements in segmentation accuracy, outperforming state-of-the-art methods that rely solely on low-level features. We also perform ablation studies to analyse the contributions of different components of our approach, providing insights into the role of the high-level prior in improving segmentation performance. Our main contributions can be summarised as follows: * We propose a novel approach for semantic segmentation that learns a high-level prior using CNNs, capturing complex contextual relationships between image regions. * We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several challenging benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance. * We perform ablation studies to analyse the contributions of different components of our approach, providing insights into the role of the high-level prior in improving segmentation performance. Overall, our work has important implications for the development of robust and accurate semantic segmentation methods, and highlights the potential of using high-level priors learned from deep neural networks for improving computer vision tasks.

In this paper, we propose novel approach to weakly supervised segmentation, called Inter Extreme Points Geodesics (IEPG), which leverages concept of geodesics in the space of probability distributions to segment objects in images. Unlike traditional segmentation methods that rely on strongly supervised learning or fully convolutional networks, IEPG only requires weak supervision in form of bounding boxes around objects of interest. The key insight behind IEPG is that the geodesic distance between probability distributions of pixels in image and bounding box can be used to identify the pixels that belong to object. We propose an efficient algorithm to compute the geodesic distance and use it to optimize a segmentation mask that separates the object from the background. We evaluate performance of IEPG on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes, and show that it achieves competitive segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods, while requiring significantly less annotated data. We also demonstrate the versatility of IEPG by applying it to various segmentation tasks, such as instance segmentation, semantic segmentation, and video segmentation. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: * We introduce a novel approach to weakly supervised segmentation based on inter extreme points geodesics, which only requires weak supervision in the form of bounding boxes. * We propose efficient algorithm to compute geodesic distance between probability distributions and use it to optimize a segmentation mask. * We demonstrate the effectiveness of IEPG on several benchmark datasets and show that it achieves competitive segmentation accuracy with significantly less annotated data. * We highlight versatility of IEPG by applying it to various segmentation tasks, including instance segmentation, semantic segmentation, and video segmentation. Overall, this paper provides new perspective on weakly supervised segmentation and offers a promising solution for segmenting objects in images with minimal annotation effort.

This research presents a deep learning object detection method to initiate clusters effectively. The proposed approach utilizes advanced computer vision techniques and machine learning algorithms to identify objects in images or videos, detect patterns of interest, and categorize them into different groups based on their visual features. By implementing this technique, it becomes possible to automatically initialize cluster formations without human intervention, thereby increasing overall efficiency while reducing workloads associated with manual clustering tasks. Results demonstrate that our innovative solution achieves superior accuracy rates when compared to traditional methods used for initiating clustered environments within various industries such as agriculture or manufacturing. Overall, we believe these advancements represent significant steps forward towards automating critical decision-making processes through cutting-edge technology solutions like artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics.

Boundary information plays a significant role in 2D image segmentation, while usually being ignored in 3D point cloud segmentation where ambiguous features might be generated in feature extraction, leading to misclassification in the transition area between two objects. In this paper, firstly, we propose a Boundary Prediction Module (BPM) to predict boundary points. Based on the predicted boundary, a boundary-aware Geometric Encoding Module (GEM) is designed to encode geometric information and aggregate features with discrimination in a neighbourhood, so that the local features belonging to different categories will not be polluted by each other. To provide extra geometric information for boundary-aware GEM, we also propose a light-weight Geometric Convolution Operation (GCO), making the extracted features more distinguishing. Built upon the boundary-aware GEM, we build our network and test it on benchmarks like ScanNet v2, S3DIS. Results show our methods can significantly improve the baseline and achieve state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/JchenXu/BoundaryAwareGEM.

This academic paper presents a novel divide-and-conquer approach to understanding deep neural networks. The proposed method allows researchers to break down complex networks into smaller and more manageable sub-networks, enabling them to analyze each part individually while still maintaining a holistic view of the entire network's behavior. The paper demonstrates how this technique can be used to identify key features in image recognition tasks as well as uncover hidden dependencies between nodes, leading to improved understanding and optimization of deep learning systems. Overall, this work provides significant insights into the inner workings of deep neural networks and contributes valuable tools for researchers working with these powerful models.

In this paper, we investigate the sample complexity of auctions with side information. We consider a setting in which bidders have private information about their valuations for the item being auctioned, and they can also observe public information that is correlated with the valuations. We study the sample complexity of various auction mechanisms, including the widely used second-price auction and the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) auction. Our results show that the sample complexity of these auctions can be significantly affected by the presence of side information. In particular, we show that the second-price auction has a higher sample complexity than the VCG auction when bidders have side information. This is because the second-price auction relies on the bidders' reported bids to determine the winner, whereas the VCG auction uses a mechanism that takes into account the bidders' private information. We also consider the impact of different types of side information on the sample complexity of the auctions. We show that when the side information is highly correlated with the valuations, the sample complexity of the second-price auction can be significantly higher than that of the VCG auction. On the other hand, when the side information is weakly correlated with the valuations, the sample complexity of the second-price auction can be lower than that of the VCG auction. Our results have important implications for the design of auctions in the presence of side information. They suggest that the VCG auction may be a better choice than the second-price auction when bidders have private information, as it can achieve a lower sample complexity and lead to better efficiency. However, the choice of auction mechanism also depends on other factors, such as the distribution of valuations and the level of competition among bidders. Overall, our paper provides new insights into the sample complexity of auctions with side information and highlights the importance of considering the interplay between private and public information in the design of auctions.

> Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision, which aims to assign a semantic label to each pixel in an image. Recent advances in deep learning have led to significant improvements in semantic segmentation. However, most existing methods rely on the image itself as the only source of information, ignoring the contextual information that can be extracted from the surrounding environment. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to semantic segmentation that leverages contextual information beyond the image. Our method uses a transformer-based model to extract contextual information from the surrounding environment and incorporates it into the segmentation process. We evaluate our method on the Cityscapes and ADE20K datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both datasets. Our method is also more robust to changes in the environment, such as weather conditions and lighting. We believe that our approach can be applied to other computer vision tasks that require contextual information, such as object detection and image captioning. The paper is available here.

After commenting that retiring the A-10 Warthog aircraft was equivalent to 'treason,' Major General James Post III was dismissed from his position. The controversial viewpoint he expressed has further stoked the already existing dispute regarding the move to retire the highly esteemed low-flying plane known for its effectiveness in destroying tanks, and favored by ground troops. Post argued that he used the word "treason" in a theatrical manner, instead of as a legal declaration, as a way of justifying himself. It has been reported that Post denied saying, "If someone accuses me of making that statement, I will deny it ... whoever is providing information to Congress regarding the capabilities of A-10 is committing an act of treason." Post has clarified that the meaning behind his words was misinterpreted. According to him, even though the Air Force had no intention of retiring the A-10 Warthog, they had to do it because of the financial limitations that currently exist. Although Post's remarks had other meanings, his use of the word "treason" resulted in his dismissal, marking the conclusion of his 32-year-long profession. He showed remorse for his actions and stated that he made the comment with the intention of directing the audience's attention towards working within the limitations of the command. For the past 40 years, the A-10 Warthog has been actively serving the US military and has been utilized in ground-attack missions in various places such as Iraq, Afghanistan, and most recently, against ISIS.

> > Abstract: Path tracing and label propagation both suffer from incomplete recovery in complex images often occurring around boundary objects whose appearance highly deviates from other structures, such as fiber termini or neuropil regions. In this work, we introduce Reinforce Proofreader (RLcor): an interactive proofreader that enables crowdworkers to review image segmentations by learning reinforcements with only few human corrections on well-known connectome. By design, our algorithm learns what partitions are difficult to recover accurately while iteratively reinforcing workers' correction at the corresponding locations. We show how RLcor’s self-learning mechanism can effectively alleviate tedious labor input during ground truth validation through two major phases: 1) refining unground-truth labels based on its own prediction; and 2) identifying uncertain pixels requiring expert attention so as to accelerate path tracer's processing over complicated structures via an active masking strategy; thus enabling significantly better performance than previous approaches. As illustrating application, we apply three state-of-the-art methods on D. melanogaster brain datasets including Path Tracker, DeepPath and Interactive deepPath.

RANKL is involved in osteoclast differentiation, and it is considered to promote cell cycle arrest and differentiation by upregulation of these two cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors. Studies have reported that RANKL can induce the expression of p21CIP1 and p27KIP1 in bone marrow-derived macrophages and preosteoclast cell lines, leading to cell cycle arrest in the G1 phase. This cell cycle arrest is essential for proper differentiation of osteoclasts, as it prevents undesirable proliferation of the cells. The upregulation of p21CIP1 and p27KIP1 by RANKL is thought to play a critical role in this process, providing a link between cell cycle regulation and osteoclast differentiation. Nevertheless, the exact molecular mechanisms of how RANKL regulates these cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors are not yet fully understood, and further studies are necessary to elucidate the complexity of this process within the bone microenvironment.

This paper presents the development and evaluation of a serious game designed to enhance human environmental consciousness education in residents' daily life. The game, called "Eco-Life," is aimed at raising awareness about sustainable practices and promoting environmentally responsible behaviors among adults. It was developed based on the theory of planned behavior and incorporates various game mechanics, such as points, badges, and leaderboards, to engage players and encourage behavior change. A randomized controlled trial was conducted with a sample of 102 participants to evaluate the effectiveness of the game. Results show that participants who played Eco-Life demonstrated significant improvements in environmental knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors compared to those in the control group. In addition, feedback from player surveys indicated high levels of user satisfaction and motivation to continue playing the game. The study contributes to the growing body of research on gamification and serious games, providing insights into how game design elements can be used to promote pro-environmental behaviors in everyday life.

The field of medical image segmentation has seen significant advancements in recent years, as researchers strive to extract meaningful insights from complex imaging data. While promising results have been achieved through various algorithms, there is still a need for more accurate and efficient methods to improve the overall quality of clinical outcomes in this area. In this study, we present an innovative technique called data-swapping method (DSM) that aims to rapidly improve the accuracy of 3D medical image segmentation using transfer learning approaches. Our approach involves leveraging pre-trained models on large datasets for medical image analysis while simultaneously swapping key features during training, enabling the model to learn multiple modalities simultaneously. Additionally, we propose novel optimization techniques that facilitate seamless transfer learning between different image modalities. We evaluate our proposed method extensively on five publicly available 3D medical imaging datasets, including brain MRI, liver CT, lung CT, pancreas MRI, and kidney MRIs. Results demonstrate that our DSM outperforms state-of-the-art methods by achieving faster convergence rates, higher accuracy, and better generalization capabilities. These findings provide useful implications for improving patient care and advancements in biomedical research based on high-quality medical images.

> Dental implants are considered gold-standard solution to restore teeth functionalities when they have been lost due to different reasons including caries, root fractures or periapical lesions that cannot be treated by conventional endodontic therapy . Mandibular morphology plays an essential role in successful prosthetically planned dental implantations. Therefore; a comprehensive plan prior to any reconstruction or surgery requires detailed examination of bones’ conditions and shapes via three dimensional (3D) virtual rendering techniques such as cone beam computed tomography (CBCT). However accurate delineation of bone structures manually using available commercial tools or even semi automatically can take long time. We propose efficient yet effective methodologies with high level of automation while having flexible user controls. Fuzzy C means clustering technique and watershed algorithm were used during two successive steps to perform required automatic or manual contouring based on radiological densitometry information embedded into data sets which was then applied upon the entire set voxels belonging to the same structure. Our algorithms outperformed current technologies while preserving users friendliness.

Unlike traditional methods that rely on hand-designed architectures, CAS leverages reinforcement learning to automatically discover and optimize task-specific neural network architectures. By explicitly incorporating domain knowledge into search process, CAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets while also providing valuable insights into the design principles of effective semantic segmentation models. Experiments conducted using CAS show that it can efficiently explore a large space of possible architectures and identify high-performing models that are tailored to specific problem domains. notably, our results demonstrate that CAS outperforms traditional architecture designs in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, we find that the discovered architectures exhibit interpretable patterns and structures, allowing us to gain deeper understanding of what makes a good semantic segmentation model. The key contribution of this work is development and application of a customizable architecture search framework for semantic segmentation tasks. BiSeNet has been proved to be a popular two-stream network for real-time segmentation. However, its principle of adding an extra path to encode spatial information is time-consuming, and the backbones borrowed from pretrained tasks, e.g., image classification, may be inefficient for image segmentation due to the deficiency of task-specific design. To handle these problems, we propose a novel and efficient structure named Short-Term Dense Concatenate network (STDC network) by removing structure redundancy. Specifically, we gradually reduce the dimension of feature maps and use the aggregation of them for image representation, which forms the basic module of STDC network. In the decoder, we propose a Detail Aggregation module by integrating the learning of spatial information into low-level layers in single-stream manner. Finally, the low-level features and deep features are fused to predict the final segmentation results. Extensive experiments on Cityscapes and CamVid dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by achieving promising trade-off between segmentation accuracy and inference speed. On Cityscapes, we achieve 71.9% mIoU on the test set with a speed of 250.4 FPS on NVIDIA GTX 1080Ti, which is 45.2% faster than the latest methods, and achieve 76.8% mIoU with 97.0 FPS while inferring on higher resolution images.

The segmentation of medical images is a fundamental step in automated clinical decision support systems. Existing medical image segmentation methods based on supervised deep learning, however, remain problematic because of their reliance on large amounts of labelled training data. Although medical imaging data repositories continue to expand, there has not been a commensurate increase in the amount of annotated data. Hence, we propose a new spatial guided self-supervised clustering network (SGSCN) for medical image segmentation, where we introduce multiple loss functions designed to aid in grouping image pixels that are spatially connected and have similar feature representations. It iteratively learns feature representations and clustering assignment of each pixel in an end-to-end fashion from a single image. We also propose a context-based consistency loss that better delineates the shape and boundaries of image regions. It enforces all the pixels belonging to a cluster to be spatially close to the cluster centre. We evaluated our method on 2 public medical image datasets and compared it to existing conventional and self-supervised clustering methods. Experimental results show that our method was most accurate for medical image segmentation.

Image segmentation is a crucial task in computer vision and machine learning. In this paper, we propose an unsupervised image segmentation method based on global and local criteria optimization using Bayesian networks. Our approach utilizes a Bayesian network to model the dependencies between pixels in an image and optimizes the segmentation based on both global and local criteria. The global criteria optimize the segmentation based on the overall structure of the image, while the local criteria optimize the segmentation based on the local context of each pixel. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in segmenting images with complex structures and varying levels of noise. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance and provides a flexible framework for customizing the segmentation based on different criteria.

The composites we use are cured with blue light. NOT UV LIGHT. It is a polymerizing reaction that is initiated by (usually) camphorquinone. The polymerization is best at 470nm which is blue light. The yelloworange filter you see us using filters out the blue light from white light so it doesn't cure the composite as we're shaping the tooth. Source: Dentist Edit: Reddit - Where facts don't matter and all that does is hurt Fee Fees," "Short answer: Light particles trigger a chain reaction in the glue causing it to make long chains and harden. If the particles have too less energy, they fail. If they have too much, they are less likely to interact with the glue. The most commonly used type of dental glue has this perfect energy to harden at the wavelength we consider blue. The glue is set up in such a way that it can be made to harden through a chain reaction. This chain reaction happens when bonds in one chemical in the glue get broken. If the particles of light are too'slow' (long and of lower frequency), such as infrared light, they cannot break the bonds of this chemical. As uQuadrupol said, the best wavelength for the most common one is 470 nm, and at this point the particles of light are fast enough that they perfectly break the bonds and start the chain reaction. Why not go fasterstronger then? You could move on to more energetic quicker UV rays. The problem with them is that as the particles of light go faster, they are often less likely to interact with the chemical (lower absorption cross-section). Also, even if they interact, their wavelengths are too small to cause chain reactions (low quantum yield)

"So what's your power?" Kevin, my older brother, asked for the twentieth time after I've cooled down a bit. I had been pacing about since my superpower had awakened and, unlike many of the other kids in our town, I hadn't been scared at all when it first happened. I looked around at what seemed like hundreds of people who'd gathered to watch me. The school was packed with curious kids looking on as superheroes and villains fought each other onstage while the world-famous superhero Spiderman took the stage. For some reason that night, however, no one was concerned with Spiderman or any of his latest battles. Everyone was more interested in this new kid with green hair and glowing eyes - me! Since I didn't have any real idea how to describe myself, I told them nothing but this: "My powers are really strange." In this paper, we adress a fundamental problem in natural language processing: entity segmentation. Traditional approaches to entity segmentation rely on hand-crafted rules or machine learning models that are limited by their ability to handle out-of-vocabulary (OoV) entities, leading to poor performance in real-world applications. We propose an open-world approach to entity segmentation that enables the recognition of both known and unknown entities, improving upon traditional closed-world methods. We introduce an unsupervised, Graph-based Open-world Entity Segmentation (GOES) algorithm that leverages knowledge graphs to identify entities in text data without relying on predefined lexicons or training data. Our novel approach combines subword modeling, graph-based clustering, and reinforcement learning to accurately segregate entities in an open-world setting. Evaluated on several benchmark datasets, GOES exhibits competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art entity segmentation systems while demonstrating improved capability in identifying OoV entities. Additionally, we analyze the effectiveness of different components within our framework, providing insights into the importance of each module in achieving robust entity segmentation. The main contributions of our work can be summarized as follows: 1. We introduce an open-world entity segmentation approach that is not limited by the vocabulary size of the training data. 2. We develop a novel, unsupervised GOES algorithm that integrates subword modeling, graph-based clustering, and reinforcement learning. 3. Our proposed method shows superior performance in identifying OoV entities compared to traditional closed-world entity segmentation systems. 4. We provide a comprehensive evaluation of the component parts of our framework, shedding light on their individual contributions to overall system performance. This paper lays the foundation for further research in developing more advanced open-world entity segmentation techniques, ultimately enabling better Natural Language Understanding (NLU) systems that can handle unexpected or previously unknown entities.

My friend, Brian, was ill so I drove him to an emergency room. When we entered the emergency room there were only twelve people in it. A man who was waiting spoke to me, "I'm having a heart attack." I said, "Call 911." He did. I looked at the emergency room desk, there was no one there. I waited for two minutes then I said to Brian, "I'm going to go get help." I walked down the hallway to the other end of the hospital. I was walking fast and kept looking around for someone who might be a nurse or doctor. As I was walking I noticed a sign that said, "Cardiac." I looked up, on the wall there was an Emergency Call button. I pressed the button and heard a voice say, "You have been connected to the Emergency Room." I said, "I'm in the emergency room and there are twelve people in the room and no one is here." The voice said, "What number is on the sign above your head?" I looked up and saw a number 11. The voice said, "You are in the trauma center. Emergency room one is at the other end of the hospital." I said, "Okay." I walked back to the emergency room. I went inside and said to Brian, "Get up and let's leave." We left the hospital and went to another hospital. Brian's health was fine. I wondered why the man who was having a heart attack did not press the emergency button. I wondered why there was no one at the desk. I wondered why the nurse or doctor did not answer the emergency button. I wondered why there was no one around to help the man having a heart attack. I wondered why I had to go out of the emergency room to get help. I wondered why the nurse did not come in to help the man having a heart attack. I wondered why I had to wait two minutes to find help. I prayed, "You know all things, Father. You know all the answers to these questions. I don't know the answers. I give my questions to you." Later, I had another conversation with Brian. He said, "I want to learn how to do everything that Jesus did." I thought to myself, "I don't want to be like Jesus, I want to be like Brian."

> Fast semantic segmentation methods usually leverage low-level image features such as color and texture, which lead to suboptimal results in challenging conditions in various scenarios. In addition, current state-of-the-art techniques require deep networks or multi-scale convolutions during testing which make real time applications impractical due to heavy computations involved. To alleviate these limitations, we propose an efficient approach that leverages spatial context to propagate semantics among neighbor regions instead of learning complex representations based on large amounts of training images. Our method also adopts multiple layers via skip connections (or guided filters) between different feature levels, leading to high quality final results. In contrast to fully data driven approaches which learn pixel level information for every single class at once, our proposed algorithm focuses initially on two classes using only boundary pixels within small neighborhood patches followed by iteratively expanding segments until all the objects are identified accordingly without resorting to any post processing step. Such fast local refinement steps result in improved performance over baseline models while maintaining similar run times using only simple off-the shelf operators to handle both RGB and depth inputs. Experiments comparing our work against several state-of-the art algorithms showcase significant accuracy improvements with much faster runtime compared to other methods despite simpler implementation on most popular datasets including Oxford105K PascalVOC2007 and 2012, MS COCO, SUN397 and CamVid.

This paper proposes a novel approach for texture-based image segmentation of chili pepper X-ray images using Gabor filter. Chili peppers are an important crop that requires accurate segmentation for automated sorting and quality control. X-ray imaging is a non-destructive technique that can reveal internal defects and texture information of chili peppers. However, the X-ray images often have low contrast and noisy texture, making it challenging to segment the peppers accurately. In this paper, we propose a texture-based image segmentation approach that utilizes the Gabor filter to extract relevant texture features from the X-ray images. The Gabor filter is a type of texture filter that models the response of the human visual system to different spatial frequencies and orientations. By applying the Gabor filter to the X-ray images, we can extract a set of texture features that are useful for distinguishing between the chili peppers and the background. We evaluate the performance of our approach using a dataset of chili pepper X-ray images. The results show that our method achieves an accuracy of 96.5% in segmenting the peppers, outperforming traditional image segmentation methods such as thresholding and edge detection. We also analyze the effects of different parameters of the Gabor filter on the segmentation performance and provide insights into the optimal choice of parameters for this application. The main contributions of this paper are: * A novel approach for texture-based image segmentation of chili pepper X-ray images using Gabor filter * An extensive evaluation of the proposed method using a dataset of chili pepper X-ray images * Analysis of the effects of different parameters of the Gabor filter on the segmentation performance The proposed approach has important implications for the automation of chili pepper sorting and quality control processes, and can potentially be applied to other agricultural products with similar texture features.

Uber is having a very public fight right now with NYC Mayor Bill de Blasio, basically arguing that they should be allowed to compete with yellow cabs in a free market, and that they're being unfairly targeted by the city. De Blasio, who has made himself into a darling of the liberal left, is using the public outcry to his advantage, saying that the Uber fight is "pitting working people against working people," or as a local reporter put it, "the poor against the rich." On one side are the company's many New York supporters, who say Uber is an innovative service that makes it easier for people to get around the city; on the other are de Blasio's supporters, who say the company's operations are unfairly taking business away from yellow cabs. "I think Uber is just exploiting the public's desire to get around the city, and it's not being held accountable," de Blasio told reporters on Saturday. "We want to put the city's needs first, and the only way to do that is to make sure that those who are providing transportation are paying the city and doing it fairly." The fight, of course, will likely be a tempest in a teapot, with Uber continuing to operate, as it has been doing in New York since August, despite de Blasio's protestations. But it's a high-profile issue for a mayor who is running for president, and it will probably make de Blasio's brand as a liberal firebrand even more popular.

Advances in deep neural networks (DNN) greatly bolster real-time detection of anomalous IoT data. However, IoT devices can barely afford complex DNN models due to limited computational power and energy supply. While one can offload anomaly detection tasks to the cloud, it incurs long delay and requires large bandwidth when thousands of IoT devices stream data to the cloud concurrently. In this paper, we propose an adaptive anomaly detection approach for hierarchical edge computing (HEC) systems to solve this problem. Specifically, we first construct three anomaly detection DNN models of increasing complexity, and associate them with the three layers of HEC from bottom to top, i.e., IoT devices, edge servers, and cloud. Then, we design an adaptive scheme to select one of the models based on the contextual information extracted from input data, to perform anomaly detection. The selection is formulated as a contextual bandit problem and is characterized by a single-step Markov decision process, with an objective of achieving high detection accuracy and low detection delay simultaneously. We evaluate our proposed approach using a real IoT dataset, and demonstrate that it reduces detection delay by 84 while maintaining almost the same accuracy as compared to offloading detection tasks to the cloud. In addition, our evaluation also shows that it outperforms other baseline schemes.

This paper presents comprehensive modeling and control study of active constrained layer (ACL) beam subject to two voltage sources, with and without consideration of magnetic effects. The ACL beam is a type of smart structure that utilizes piezoelectric materials to introduce intelligence and adaptability in structural systems. It consists of constraint layer sandwiched between two piezoelectric layers, which are excited by voltage sources. By modeling the electromechanical behavior of ACL beam using combination of theoretical and numerical methods, we investigate effectiveness of different control strategies in regulating its vibration response. We also examine the influence of magnetic effects on behavior of the system, particularly when operating in high-frequency regime. Our results demonstrate the ability to accurately predict and manipulate the behavior of ACL beam under various conditions, including the presence of magnetic fields, and highlight the potential advantages of incorporating magnetic effects into the control strategy. These findings hold significant implications for the design and operation of intelligent structures, such as those used in vibrations isolation, energy harvesting, and nanopositioning applications.

Boundary information plays a significant role in 2D image segmentation, while usually being ignored in 3D point cloud segmentation where ambiguous features might be generated in feature extraction, leading to misclassification in the transition area between two objects. In this paper, firstly, we propose a Boundary Prediction Module (BPM) to predict boundary points. Based on the predicted boundary, a boundary-aware Geometric Encoding Module (GEM) is designed to encode geometric information and aggregate features with discrimination in a neighborhood, so that the local features belonging to different categories will not be polluted by each other. To provide extra geometric information for boundary-aware GEM, we also propose a light-weight Geometric Convolution Operation (GCO), making the extracted features more distinguishing. Built upon the boundary-aware GEM, we build our network and test it on benchmarks like ScanNet v2, S3DIS. Results show our methods can significantly improve the baseline and acheive state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/JchenXu/BoundaryAwareGEM.

BiSeNet has been proved to be a popular two-stream network for real-time segmentation. However, its principle of adding an extra path to encode spatial information is time-consuming, and the backbones borrowed from pretrained tasks, e.g., image classification, may be inefficient for image segmentation due to the deficiency of task-specific design. To handle these problems, we propose a novel and efficient structure named Short-Term Dense Concatenate network (STDC network) by removing structure redundancy. Specifically, we gradually reduce the dimension of feature maps and use the aggregation of them for image representation, which forms the basic module of STDC network. In the decoder, we propose a Detail Aggregation module by integrating the learning of spatial information into low-level layers in single-stream manner. Finally, the low-level features and deep features are fused to predict the final segmentation results. Extensive experiments on Cityscapes and CamVid dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by achieving promising trade-off between segmentation accuracy and inference speed. On Cityscapes, we achieve 12.2% mIoU on the test set with a speed of 250.4 FPS on NVIDIA GTX 1080Ti, which is 69.1% faster than the latest methods, and achieve 66.9% mIoU with 97.0 FPS while inferring on higher resolution images.

This paper studies the context aggregation problem in semantic image segmentation. Most existing methods improve the receptive field of the pixel representation by aggregating the local context information in an image. Besides, these methods ignore the significance of the receptive field of the corresponding class in other images. This paper first constructs a dynamic feature memory that can learn the feature of the class. Then, using the supervision of ground truth, it learns the class probability distribution of each pixel representation. Then, according to the distribution of the class, it aggregates the dataset-level feature. Moreover, based on the accumulated data, it introduces the learning method of data-level feature consistency to enhance the consistency of the classifier. The above method can be easily integrated into the existing frameworks, such as FCN, PSPNet, OCRNet, and DeepLabV3, and the performance can be improved by a large margin. On the four datasets of ADE20K, LIP, CityScapes, and COCO-Stuff, this method achieves the best performance in terms of the number of objects recognized.

This academic paper investigates the thermalisation process for small random perturbations of dynamical systems. The study focuses on understanding how these perturbations affect the long-term behavior of the system and whether they lead to thermal equilibrium. Through a series of mathematical analyses and numerical simulations, the paper provides insights into the underlying mechanisms of thermalisation and the conditions under which it occurs. The results of this research have implications for a wide range of fields, including physics, engineering, and computer science, and contribute to the broader understanding of complex systems and their behavior.

Breidt, Thomas Mikkelsen, and Sune Kaae Larsen, dated December 3, 2009 (submitted to ISBA Spring Meeting (Econometrics), Brussels, March 6 -4 , 4502). ## Abstract: This paper investigates two novel techniques called `relabeling' and `summarization' that can be used to reduce the computational burden associated with signal decomposition problems where it is unknown or uncertain how many components are present. These signal structure detection issues have recently been highlighted as major obstacles standing between users of nonparametric modeling technologies and solutions. It turns out that if we consider prior distributions over signals where all components within signals have the same functional form but differ according to a parameter which controls location, variation levels, smoothness etc., then relabelings and summarizations can be accomplished analytically after Gibbs sampler iterations via deterministic mappings of random quantities. In this way both model uncertainty and data richness can be handled efficiently at least on a theoretical level. This work extends earlier findings concerning finite state space Markov chains and Gaussian processes found in Bayesian hierarchical models using Dirichlet process priors.

This is a first step in the development of medically related clinical decision support systems. Existing methods based on supervised learning, however, have a problem of excessive dependence on the availability of large amounts of labeled training data. Although the size of medical image data bases increases, an increase in annotated data has not followed. Thus, we propose a novel self-supervised clustering method based on a spatially guided self-supervised clustering network (SGSCN), which is able to learn both the feature representation and the clustering assignment of each pixel in a single image. We also propose a context-dependent consistency loss that enables the learning of more precise shapes and boundaries. Our loss function ensures that all the pixels in a cluster are spatially close to the cluster center. We tested our method on two publicly available medical image data sets and compared it with existing conventional and self-supervised clustering methods. In this paper, we present a comprehensive analysis of exact inference in graphs from the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy. We explore the capabilities and limitations of this powerful inference technique, which has been widely used in various fields, including computer vision, machine learning, and social network analysis. Our work provides a thorough understanding of the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy, including its theoretical foundations, computational complexity, and applications to graphical models. We demonstrate the versatility of this approach by applying it to a variety of graphical models, including Bayesian networks, Markov random fields, and Gaussian graphical models. Our main contributions include the development of novel inference algorithms that leverage the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy to perform exact inference in graphs. We also derive tight computational complexity bounds for these algorithms, providing insights into their scalability and performance. Our experimental evaluation on several real-world datasets demonstrates the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed methods. We show that they can accurately perform exact inference in large-scale graphs, outperforming existing methods in terms of computational speed and scalability. Our work has important implications for a wide range of applications, including image segmentation, natural language processing, and recommendation systems. It also provides a foundation for future research in graphical models and exact inference, opening up new avenues for developing more powerful and efficient inference techniques. In summary, our paper offers a comprehensive view of exact inference in graphs from the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy, providing novel algorithms, computational complexity analysis, and experimental evaluation. Our work has significant implications for both theoretical and practical applications, advancing the state-of-the-art in graphical models and exact inference.

We generalize Ebert's Hat Problem for two persons and four colours. All teams guess simultaneously the colour of their own hat observing only the hat colors of the other teams. It is not required for each team to pass: no colour is guessed. The player loses if at least one team guesses his or her hat color correct and none of the teams has an incorrect clue. This paper studies Ebert's hat problem, where the probabilities of the colors can be different (asymmetric case). Our objective is to minimize the probability of losing the tournament and to identify winning strategies. In this paper we use the concept of an appropriate set. The construction of sufficient sets is independent of underlying probabilities and we can use this notion in the study of the asymmetric case. A point of concern is the fact that numerical simplicity using adequate sets is significantly higher than using standard methods.

Uniform determinantal representations (UDRs) are a powerful tool for studying the structure of random matrices. In this paper, we explore the properties and applications of UDRs, with a focus on their use in statistical physics and machine learning. We begin by introducing the concept of UDRs and their connection to random matrix theory. We then discuss their use in the study of random graphs and networks, and their application to the study of phase transitions in statistical physics. Finally, we explore the use of UDRs in machine learning, specifically in the study of deep learning algorithms and their relationship to random matrices. Throughout the paper, we provide examples and illustrations to illustrate the power and versatility of UDRs.

The impact of Bi implantation on the conductivity and the thermopower of GeTe, Ge-Sb-Te, and Ga- La-S films is investigated. The enhanced conductivity appears to be notably sensitive to a dose of an implant. Incorporation of Bi in amorphous chalcogenide films at doses up to 1x1015 cm-2 is seen not to change the majority carrier type and activation energy for the conduction process. Higher implantation doses may reverse the majority carrier type in the studied films. Electron conductivity was observed in GeTe films implanted with Bi at a dose of 2x1016 cm-2. These studies indicate that native coordination defects present in amorphous chalcogenide semiconductors can be deactivated by means of ion implantation. A substantial density of implantation-induced traps in the studied films and their interfaces with silicon is inferred from analysis of the space-charge limited current and capacitance-voltage characteristics taken on Au/amorphous chalcogenide/Si structures.
