Domain adaptation is a technique used to adapt models trained on one dataset (source domain) to perform well on a different dataset (target domain) that may have different characteristics or distributions. In the context of semantic segmentation for aerial images, domain adaptation has gained increasing attention due to its potential to improve the accuracy and generalization ability of deep learning models in this field. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to domain adaptation for semantic segmentation of aerial images. Our approach leverages a combination of feature alignment and adversarial training techniques to adapt the model to the target domain while preserving the spatial information of the source domain. We conduct extensive experiments using two publically available datasets – Cityscapes and Maps – to evaluate the effectiveness of our method. The results show that our proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by a significant margin, achieving an improvement of up to 10% in IoU score. Our main contributions are: * A novel domain adaptation approach for semantic segmentation of aerial images that combines feature alignment and adversarial training. * An in-depth analysis of the effects of different components of our approach, providing insights into the importance of each component for improving performance. * A comprehensive evaluation of our approach on two widely used datasets for aerial image segmentation, demonstrating its superiority over existing methods. The significance of this work lies in its potential application in various fields such as urban planning, environmental monitoring, and disaster response, where accurate semantic segmentation of aerial images can provide valuable information for decision-making purposes.

Title: Suggestive Annotation: A Deep Active Learning Framework for Biomedical Image Segmentation Abstract: Biomedical image segmentation is a critical task in medical diagnosis and treatment planning. It involves identifying regions of interest (ROIs) within an image, such as tumours or organs, to enable accurate measurements and analysis. Traditional machine learning methods require large amounts of labelled data for training models; however, obtaining such large datasets can be expensive and time-consuming. Active learning approaches, on one hand, aim at selecting a minimal subset of informative examples from unlabelled data, which are later labelled by humans to improve model performance, while reducing labelling effort. While active learning frameworks have achieved promising results in various domains, there remains much-untapped potential, especially in domain specialised tasks like biomedical image segmentation. To address this challenge, we propose a novel deep active learning framework specifically designed for biomedical image segmentation called "Suggestive Annotation" (SA). Our method leverages multiple sources of additional information such as statistical properties and transfer learning knowledge to generate high quality suggestions that guide human annotators towards most informative samples without violating their preferences. Our approach is agnostic to specific application requirements enabling it to adapt different networks, such as Mask R-CNN, UNet and Fully Convolutional Networks. We also use a contextual ensemble system consisting of multiple pre-trained models generating diverse predictions, thereby increasing the quality of our labels. We demonstrate SA's effectiveness on two benchmark segmentation tasks using the publicly available dataset ADNI-BOLD and the MIMIC-III chest X-ray series. Specifically, for ADNI-BOLD, we reduced the required number of ground truth annotations from 8,472 to only 1,393 (a reduction of 83%) with comparable accuracy. For chest X-rays, we reduce the amount of expert-annotated images used during training by up to 50% while achieving competitive performances compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Finally, we showcase the flexibility of SA making it suitable for a variety of complex anatomical structures and task variations.

Conventional transfer learning leverages weights of pre-trained networks, but mandates the need for similar neural architectures. Alternatively, knowledge distillation can transfer knowledge between heterogeneous networks but often requires access to the original training data or additional generative networks. Knowledge transfer between networks can be improved by being agnostic to the choice of network architecture and reducing the dependence on original training data. We propose a knowledge transfer approach from a teacher to a student network wherein we train the student on an independent transferal dataset, whose annotations are generated by the teacher. Experiments were conducted on five state-of-the-art networks for semantic segmentation and seven datasets across three imaging modalities. We studied knowledge transfer from a single teacher, combination of knowledge transfer and fine-tuning, and knowledge transfer from multiple teachers. The student model with a single teacher achieved similar performance as the teacher; and the student model with multiple teachers achieved better performance than the teachers. The salient features of our algorithm include: 1)no need for original training data or generative networks, 2) knowledge transfer between different architectures, 3) ease of implementation for downstream tasks by using the downstream task dataset as the transferal dataset, 4) knowledge transfer of an ensemble of models, trained independently, into one student model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is effective for knowledge transfer and easily tunable.

We discover new hereditary classes of graphs that are minimal (with regard to set inclusion) of finite clique-width. The new examples include split permutation graphs and bichain graphs. Each of these classes is defined by a infinite list of minimal forbidden induced subgraphs. These, however, disprove a theorem due to Daligault, Rao and Thomasse from 2010 stating that all such minimal classes can be characterized by equally many forbidden induced subgraphs. In the same paper, Daligault, Rao and Thomasse make the theorem that each hereditary class of finite clique-width can include a labelled infinite antichain. We show that the four example classes we consider here satisfy this assumption. Moreover, they each include a canonical labelled infinite antichain, which leads me to consider a stronger hypothesis: that each hereditary class of graphs that is minimal of finite clique-width represents a canonical labelled infinite antichain.

The design of disc arthroplasty can affect the movement between the vertebrae and the pressure on the facet joints. Artificial disc replacement, also called disc arthroplasty, is a surgical intervention that aims to replace the damaged intervertebral disc with an artificial prosthesis, with the goal of bringing back the normal movement and function of the disc. The manner in which the artificial disc is designed plays a crucial part in deciding how well it performs and how it interacts with the neighboring soft tissues and bony structures, including the facet joints. The factors that determine the artificial disc's performance, such as its size, material characteristics, form, and movement, can have an impact on the spine's movement and function. According to research, variations in the range of motion, segmental stability, load distribution, and force transmission through the facet joints can be influenced by various designs. One example could be creating a disc design that conforms closer to the natural shape and motion of the intervertebral disc. This could lead to improved preservation of movement and even distribution of pressure throughout the endplates and facets. On the other hand, a design that does not conform or lies flat could cause more pressure on the facet joints, which could possibly raise the likelihood of damage to the joint and experiencing pain. In addition, the selection of materials utilized in the disc arthroplasty can affect the durability of the implant, as well as its ability to withstand wear and distribute stress appropriately. Selecting the right material can reduce wear debris and inflammatory responses, which will preserve the spine's ideal biomechanics and kinematics. To sum up, the intervertebral movements and facet forces are considerably impacted by the configuration of disc arthroplasty. Ensuring appropriate motion preservation, segmental stability, and load distribution in the implanted spine segment is critical and can only be achieved through careful design considerations.

Federated learning enables distributed medical institutions to independently develop a shared prediction model with privacy security. While at clinical deployment, the models trained in federated learning can only suffer from performance drop when applied to seemingly unseen hospitals within the federation. In this paper, we point out and solve a novel problem setting of federated domain generalization (FedDG), which seeks to develop a federated model from various distributed source domains such that it can directly generalize to unseen target domains. We present a novel method, known as Episodic Learning in Continuous Frequency Space (ELCFS), for this issue by allowing each client to exploit multi-source data distributions under the challenging constraint of data decentralization. Our method transmits the distribution data from clients in a privacy-protecting manner through an effective continuous frequency space interpolation mechanism. With the transferred multi-source distributions, we further carefully design a boundary-oriented episodic learning paradigm to expose the local learning to domain distribution shifts and particularly meet the problems of model generalization in medical image segmentation scenario. The efficacy of our approach is shown with excellent efficiency over state-of-the-arts and in-depth ablation studies on two medical image segmentation tasks. The code is accessible at "http://github.com/liuquande/FedDG-ELCFS".

Despite the recent success of semantic segmentation, medical ultra-high-resolution images are still a major challenge. The methods based on a multi-level tree are able to balance the amount of computation and the accuracy of segmentation, but the tree structure needs to be carefully designed in order to achieve the best result, and therefore the structure is redundant. This paper proposes a new method, called meta-segmentation neural network (MSN), to solve this challenging task. The MSN fusion mechanism is very simple and effective with meta-learning. MSN can quickly learn the weights of the fusion layer with a simple meta-learner, and it only needs a few training samples and training cycles to converge. The method avoids the learning of each branch separately and introduces a special weight-sharing mechanism, which not only realizes fast knowledge learning, but also shares weights in multiple branches, which improves the accuracy and reduces the number of parameters.. The experiments on the two ultra-high-resolution medical images BACH and ISIC show that MSN outperforms the existing method in terms of accuracy and speed.

Difference-in-differences (DID) is a method to evaluate effect of a treatment. In its basic version, a "control group" is untreated at two dates, whereas a "treatment group" becomes fully treated at the second date. However, in many applications of DID method, treatment rate only increases more in treatment group. In such fuzzy designs, popular estimator of treatment effects is the DID of outcome divided by the DID of the treatment. We show that this ratio identifies local average treatment effect only if two homogeneous treatment effect assumptions are satisfied. We then propose two alternative estimands that do not rely on any assumption on treatment effects, and that can be used when treatment rate does not change over time in the control group. We prove that the corresponding estimators are asymptotically normal. Finally, we use our results to revisit Duflo (2001).

Despite the remarkable performance of deep learning methods on various tasks, most cutting-edge models rely heavily on large-scale annotated training examples, which are often unavailable for clinical and health care tasks. The labeling costs for medical images are very high, especially in medical image segmentation, which typically requires intensive pixel/voxel-wise labeling. Therefore, the strong capability of learning and generalizing from limited supervision, including a limited amount of annotations, sparse annotations, and inaccurate annotations, is crucial for the successful application of deep learning models in medical image segmentation. However, due to its intrinsic difficulty, segmentation with limited supervision is challenging and specific model design and/or learning strategies are needed. In this paper, we provide a systematic and up-to-date review of the solutions above, with summaries and comments about the methodologies. We also highlight several problems in this field, discussed future directions observing further investigations.

In this paper, we introduce a novel method for multi-label segmentation of medical images with pathological lesions by combining a dynamic multiscale tree with a merged classifier, which combines the advantages of both trees and merged classifiers, thereby improving the accuracy and efficiency of the segmentation process. Then, a new approach is proposed to dynamically adapt the scale of the tree to the properties of the image and the characteristics of the pathological lesions. This makes it possible to simultaneously use the local and global context of the tree, thus resulting in a better representation of the image and a better segmentation performance. The tree is then trained with a set of strong classifiers derived from a number of weak classifiers using a boosting method, and the merged classifier and the tree are combined into a hybrid model to deal with multi-label segmentation of lesions of different sizes and shapes. We have evaluated our method on a set of publicly available data on medical images (mammograms, ultrasounds, magnetic resonance images) and compared its performance with the state-of-the-art methods. The results show that the proposed method outperforms the tree and the merged classifier methods both in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Specifically, the proposed method achieves an average Dice similarity coefficient of 0.89, an average I/U ratio of 0.87, and reduces the processing time by about 36%. This shows that the combination of a dynamic multiscale tree and a merged classifier can effectively address the challenge of multi-label segmentation of medical images with pathological lesions. Our study has important implications for the diagnosis and treatment planning in various medical fields, as it provides a powerful tool for radiologists and clinicians to accurately identify and segment different types of lesions, which can lead to improved patient care and lower medical costs. Furthermore, the proposed method can be easily extended to other applications, such as object recognition, natural scene understanding, and surveillance, where accurate detection and segmentation of objects and regions of interest are very important.

In this work, we introduce Reinforce Proofreader (RLcor): an interactive proofreader that enables crowdworkers to review image segmentations by learning reinforcements with only few human corrections on a well-known connectome. By design, our algorithm learns what partitions are difficult to recover accurately while iteratively reinforcing workers' correction at the corresponding locations. We show how RLcor’s self-learning mechanism can effectively alleviate tedious labor input during ground truth validation through two major phases: 1) refining unground-truth labels based on its own prediction; and 8) identifying uncertain pixels requiring expert attention so as to accelerate path tracer's processing over complicated structures via an active masking strategy; thus enabling significantly better performance than previous approaches. As an illustrating application, we apply three state-of-the-art methods on D. melanogaster brain datasets including Path Tracker, DeepPath and Interactive deepPath.

In this paper we present a system that mines conceptual data beyond a large number of sensory annotations generated by its neural network, namely: image labels and edges in pictures (via edge detection; See [7, 23]). The system, which ensures state-of-the-art efficiency on image comparison functions, does so not by directly analyzing these features but rather by conducting inference based on their usage and classification performance on validation data using an existing text document, thus demonstrating that it can be improved through a mix of natural language processing, visual search-based machine learning methods, and deep learning.

This journal studies the context aggregation problem in semantic picture segmentation. The existing studies focus on creating the pixel representations by analyzing the semantic data within individual images. While impressive, these techniques neglect the importance of the representations of the pixels of the corresponding class beyond the input picture. To address this, this paper aims to mine the semantic data beyond individual images to further enhance the pixel representations. We first set up a feature memory module, which is updated automatically during training, to store the dataset-level representations of different types. Then, we learn class probability distribution of each pixel representation under the supervision of the ground-truth segmentation. At last, the representation of each pixel is augmented by aggregating the dataset-level representations based on the corresponding class probability distribution. Moreover, by combining the stored dataset-level representations, we also propose a representation consistent learning approach to get the category head better address intra-class compactness and inter-class dispersion. The proposed approach can be easily incorporated into existing segmentation frameworks (e.g., FCN, PSPNet, OCRNet and DeepLabV3) and provides consistent efficiency improvements. Mining contextual data beyond image enables you to report state-of-the-art performance on several benchmarks: ADE20K, LIP, Cityscapes and COCO-Stuff.

This research introduces CHASE, a novel visual tracking algorithm that utilizes cell-level differentiable neural architecture search to enhance robustness. Through extensive experiments and comparisons with state-of-the-art methods, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in challenging scenarios characterized by fast motion, occlusion, illumination changes, and complex backgrounds. Our method achieves promising results while providing flexibility and efficiency through its adaptive neural network design learned directly from data. Overall, this study highlights potential of combining NAS techniques with computer vision applications such as object detection and segmentation, opening up new avenues for future work on personalized models adaptable to diverse environments.

The effectiveness of Viscum triflorum in inhibiting the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) may vary depending on the host plant it is derived from, due to the influence of particular compounds and their levels on the medicinal properties of the extracted substance. Viscum triflorum is a semi-dependant plant, which indicates that it depends on its host plant to some extent for obtaining water and nutrients. The metabolic profile of the host plant has the potential to affect the secondary metabolite composition in Viscum triflorum. The plant extracts' ACE inhibitory activity may be affected by these metabolites. There have been only a few studies that have specifically explored this question. In 2017, Koffi-Nevry et al. conducted a study. The paper presents a novel approach for simultaneous traffic sign detection and boundary estimation using a convolutional neural network (CNN). The proposed method utilizes a multi-task learning framework to jointly train two CNNs for traffic sign detection and boundary estimation. The first CNN is trained to detect traffic signs in images, while the second CNN is trained to estimate the boundaries of the detected signs. The two CNNs are trained simultaneously using a multi-task loss function that combines the loss from both tasks. The proposed method is evaluated on a dataset of traffic sign images and shows significant improvement in both traffic sign detection and boundary estimation compared to state-of-the-art methods. The paper concludes that the proposed method provides a more accurate and efficient solution for simultaneous traffic sign detection and boundary estimation using a CNN.

Different from most state-of-the-art methods which employ atrous space pooling With different dilation rates to acquire multi-scale context features in order to learn informative representations for fine-grained pixel classification, it employs an innovative convolution filter which can obtain nonlocal receptive field at once without using multiple channels. At Last, an Encoder decoder structure based on PPACNN(or UNet) is finally constructed as backbone network, upon which Our customized class-aware loss function is deployed, allowing the model to be trained end-to-end on segmentation task, leading to more robustness. When animations in CSS conflict, only one of them will occur. The Web Animations API allows developers to mix up animation behavior using the composite option. This article discusses how to set the composite option and the animation order. Let's start with a simple animation that sets the opacity of an element from 0 to 1 in 5 seconds. It works just fine when used without the composite option. style .animation { opacity: 0; animation-name: animation; animation-duration: 5s; animation-timing-function: linear; animation-fill-mode: forwards; } keyframes animation { from { opacity: 0; } to { opacity: 1; } } style div class"animation"div Let's say that you want to add a second animation that fades in the element and makes it visible. This would be accomplished by setting the visibility property to visible and animating it to hidden. You would then want to make the element appear on the screen in a smooth fashion by adding the animation-delay property to the element and setting the delay to 5 seconds. This is the desired result: style .animation { visibility: hidden; animation-name: animation; animation-duration: 5s; animation-timing-function: linear; animation-fill-mode: forwards; animation-delay: 5s; } keyframes animation { from { opacity: 0; } to { opacity: 1; } } style div class"animation"div However, this will only work when the two animations are run in the order from top to bottom. This is because the animation-delay property only takes effect after the animation is started. If the two animations are run in the opposite order, they will run at the same time. To get around this, you can set the composite option. style .animation { opacity: 0; animation-name: animation; animation-duration: 5s; animation-timing-function: linear; animation-fill-mode: forwards; } keyframes animation { from { opacity: 0; } to { opacity: 1; } } .composite { animation-name: animation; animation-duration: 5s; animation-timing-function: linear; animation-fill-mode: forwards; animation-delay: 5s; } keyframes animation-composite { from { opacity: 0; } to { opacity: 1; } } style div class"animation composite"div Now the composite animation will run before the visibility animation. Image segmentation is a critical task in computer vision and machine learning that involves partitioning an image into meaningful regions. Despite the success of recent deep learning methods, they often suffer from overfitting, which can lead to poor generalization performance. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach to image segmentation using weak shape priors. Our method incorporates shape information through a recently developed theory called hierarchical perceptual grouping (HPG), which captures statistical correlations among low-level features extracted from images. By training our model with HPG, we impose constraints on the shapes of objects within an image and effectively prevent overfitting. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art object detection and segmentation algorithms while achieving more accurate shape recognition. Overall, our work provides a new perspective on integrating weak shape priors into deep learning models and opens up avenues for future research in computer vision.

Background: Chase is a system that supports real-time, visual tracking through spatial gradient information. Chasing uses neural networks to learn predictive models of path directions and trajectories given the location of each cell in a 3D scene. A recent set of papers provides evidence for recurrent network architectures which can provide an adequate framework for both deep learning and supervised and unsupervised hierarchical clustering tasks; however these hierarchies are poorly understood (see [22], [23], [25] ). In this work we address one critical issue which has prevented previous approaches: When given a training dataset composed solely of target cells at known position coordinates, why does the neural net converge well on a consistent representation? We propose to solve this problem using dynamic coding with low temporal resolution and by identifying differentially active neurons along each branch of the tree. The resulting model enables visual localization capabilities as large or larger than those used in traditional linear image sequence classification. Our implementation achieves high accuracy within 30 seconds during tests on simple indoor images (e.g., outdoor images). > We present a new algorithm for solving large-scale binary quadratic optimization (BQO) problems. The algorithm is based on semidefinite relaxation and is a generalization of the algorithm of Goemans and Williamson for the maximum cut problem. We show that the algorithm is guaranteed to find a solution within a factor of 1/2 of the optimum. We also show that the algorithm can be used to solve the maximum cut problem in polynomial time. We present numerical results for the maximum cut problem and for the maximum independent set problem. The paper is available here.

> Although convolutional neural networks have found much success in image segmentation, they remain problematic on memory consumption due to expensive computation and high dimensionality in high resolution images (e.g., magnetic resonance imaging). To address these issues, we propose use of partially reversible operation as efficient replacement for conventional operations while reducing the model requirements and storage demand during training by utilizing more available onboard GPU video RAM effectively. We construct our network based on dense residual connections that allow the output gradient of input features to be accumulated directly rather than through feature mappings between layers. In addition, it allows each layer to be independently tuned without changing other parameters or network configurations. Extensive ablation studies confirm both theoretical improvement and practical feasibility of applying partially reversible operations across different architectures, such as U-net, VAE-GAN and fully resilient net, which are adopted for image translation tasks with significantly improved performance using same hardware setup despite fewer total parameters. Finally, we conclude our study with an application example where our proposed method outperforms existing models in terms of Dice similarity coefficient metrics (DSC) at 84.60 ± 2.31 when trained using two Tesla T4 GPUs compared to previous state-of-the art results reported between 75%~83%.

To overcome these difficulties, we propose a novel and efficient structure, namely STDC. Specifically, we use the reduced-dimensional feature maps as the image representation, and aggregate the accumulated feature maps as the image description, which is the core unit of STDC. At the end of the decoder, we design a detail aggregation node by integrating the learned spatial information to the low-level layer in a single-stream, and finally combine the low-level feature and deep feature to predict the final segmentation result. Extensive experiments on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets show that the proposed method is very effective and can achieve a good balance between the accuracy of segmentation and the speed of inference. On Cityscapes, we obtain 71.9% mIoU at 250.4 FPS on Nvidia GTX1080TI, which is 43.1% faster than the latest methods, and obtain 76.8% mIoU at 97 FPS in high-resolution images.

Αbstrасt Τhе сеntrаl аіm оf thіs рrоjесt wаs tо dеvеlор аlgоrіthms аnd tесhnіquеs fоr buіldіng lаrgе lеаrnіng rерrеsеntаtіоns аs раrt оf trаіnіng оn humаn sеgmеntаtіоns, іn раrtісulаr оbjесt сlаssіfісаtіоn аnd fасе dеtесtіоn bу gеnеrаtіng аnd іdеntіfуіng thе mоst sаlіеnt fеаturеs оf оbjесts wіthіn а rеfеrеnсе іmаgе fоr trаіnіng. Αs dеsсrіbеd hеrеіn, thеsе еffоrts buіld uроn рrеvіоus wоrk іnvоlvіng hіеrаrсhісаl аррrоасhеs bаsеd dіrесtlу оr іndіrесtlу оn mасhіnе lеаrnіng's multіlауеr реrсерtrоns, tо rерrеsеnt multірlе rеgіоns аnd lосаlіzіng thеm wіth rеsресt tо еасh оthеr аs а funсtіоn оf thеіr lосаtіоn іn thе оrіgіnаl іmаgе. Furthеr, а kеу strаtеgу fоr іmрrоvіng rесоgnіtіоn реrfоrmаnсе hаs bееn tо sсаlе uр thе rерrеsеntаtіоn untіl аn ассurасу thrеshоld іs mеt bу usіng mоrе thаn оnе lауеr реr rеgіоn. Неrе, wе ехрlоrе nоvеl mеthоds аіmеd аt аutоmаtісаllу рrоduсіng а lаrgеr numbеr оf suсh lауеrs аnd, thus, sсаlіng uр thе ассurасу lеvеl rеасhеd durіng trаіnіng, wіth еmрhаsіs tо аррlу suсh аlgоrіthms tо nеw rеаl ехаmрlеs rаthеr thаn sіmрlу ехіstіng оnеs, whіlе рrеsеrvіng аs muсh іnfоrmаtіоn аbоut оbjесts аs роssіblе аt аnу gіvеn tіmе асrоss dіffеrеnt lауеrs. Оur tесhnіquеs аrе іnsріrеd bу рrеvіоus wоrk оn buіldіng struсturеd rерrеsеntаtіоns оn sіmрlе іnрuts (Моrі еt аl., 1998, 2003) whеrе hіgh lеvеl fеаturеs wеrе mарреd tоgеthеr vіа а sеrіеs оf glоbаl hіddеn unіts саllеd'suреr-соlumns'. Іn соntrаst, оur аррrоасh usеs mоrе соmрlех рrосеssеs whісh еmрlоу mаnу dіstіnсt fеаturе trаnsfоrmаtіоns thаt rеsult іn twо dіffеrеnt аnd соhеrеnt rерrеsеntаtіоns оf thе sаmе dоmаіn–suсh рrосеssеs саn bе thоught оf аs bеіng nеstеd hіеrаrсhісаllу іn оrdеr tо еnаblе flехіblе соnstruсtіоn оf соmрlех mоdеls, thаt саn ореrаtе wіthоut thе соnstrаіnts оf hаvіng ассеss tо vеrу fіnе sраtіаl-tеmроrаl dеtаіl. Wе іntrоduсе sеvеrаl tуреs оf hуреrрlаnеs, thаt асt аs dіffеrеnt sсаlеs аlоng whісh оur nеtwоrk's соmроnеnts mау сhаngе оvеr tіmе. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for top-down salient object detection, which we call classifier-guided top-down salient object detection (CG-TDS). Our approach leverages the strengths of both top-down and bottom-up methods to improve the accuracy and efficiency of salient object detection. Existing top-down methods rely solely on the spatial relationships between objects and the context, which can be limited in certain scenarios, such as when objects are heavily occluded or have similar appearance. In contrast, bottom-up methods rely on the feature extraction and classification of individual objects, which can be computationally expensive and may not capture the global context. Our CG-TDS approach combines the strengths of both methods by using a classifier to guide the top-down search for salient objects. Specifically, we first use a classifier to identify the most likely object categories present in the image, and then use this information to guide the top-down search for salient objects. We propose a novel algorithm that iteratively refines the object proposals based on their compatibility with the predicted object categories, resulting in more accurate and efficient salient object detection. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art top-down and bottom-up methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Our approach also demonstrates better robustness to occlusion and clutter, and is able to handle complex scenes with multiple salient objects. Our main contributions are: * A novel classifier-guided top-down salient object detection approach that combines the strengths of top-down and bottom-up methods * A new algorithm that iteratively refines object proposals based on their compatibility with predicted object categories * State-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach Overall, our work provides a significant improvement in salient object detection, and demonstrates the potential of combining top-down and bottom-up methods for improved performance.

I was given the solo "Summertime" in 5th grade for our spring choral concert. Little did I know that my love for this classic tune would lead me to discover an extraordinary film years later. "Porgy and Bess," directed by Otto Preminger, is a film adaptation of the renowned George Gershwin opera, in which "Summertime" originates. The movie brilliantly captures the essence of Catfish Row, a tight-knit African-American community in the south. Through heartfelt performances, we are introduced to the complex and endearing characters of Porgy, a disabled beggar, and Bess, a woman shunned by society and entangled in a tumultuous relationship with the abusive Crown. The musical numbers are nothing short of breathtaking, weaving through the narrative seamlessly and leaving the audience with an unforgettable experience. Sidney Poitier and Dorothy Dandridge's raw and captivating performances as Porgy and Bess, respectively, are filled with intense passion and vulnerability. Their chemistry on-screen makes the tragic love story all the more believable and heart-wrenching. Visually, the film is a work of art, with vibrant colors and a gritty realism that transports viewers to the 1920s coastal South Carolina setting. However, it is not without its flaws, as some dialogue and subplots may appear dated and offensive to modern audiences. Nonetheless, "Porgy and Bess" remains a significant piece in cinema history, as both an artistic triumph and a testament to the power of the human spirit. The film spares no effort in showcasing the hope, resilience, and camaraderie of this tight-knit community, making it a must-watch for all music and cinema enthusiasts. As for the soulful rendition of "Summertime" in the film, it instantly transported me back to my 5th-grade performance, enveloping me with an overwhelming sense of nostalgia and affection for this enduring classic.

The 2007 Lisbon Treaty explicitly recognised fundamental rights by providing in Article 6 (1) that "The Union recognises the rights, freedoms and principles set out in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union of 7 December 2000, as adopted at Strasbourg on 12 December 2007, which shall have the same legal value as the Treaties." We present a novel way to deal with inverse power flow problem in general. When we have an equation that determines if a system has an induced imbalance, we can efficiently solve this equation using linear programming language (LPL) when a system does not exhibit it and to explore new solutions via LIFO or power dynamics. The design of our program uses O(n^2) space complexity, which is orders of magnitude better than previous approaches and comparable to existing optimization algorithms. Linear programming is effective in solving any class of systems which are dependent on periodic and nonconstant boundary conditions at all levels from singular value decomposition (SVD) and Gaussian elimination down to quadratic inverses. This technique gives us a high degree of generality compared to traditional machine learning algorithms that use unsupervised approaches such as classification or clustering. Our implementation also provides a flexible framework for exploring solutions by setting certain conditions so that the algorithm can be used as a generalized quantum algorithm and efficient solution to many other important problems. We provide applications which demonstrate several interesting properties of this model including an efficient solution to both power flow problems in stochastic control and nonlinear optimization through energy management using only qubits. These findings pave the way toward implementing practical hardware-based qubit logic control. We build a visual salience-based feature extraction program based on multiscale deep features that allows extracting hierarchical information without relying on previous training data. Our approach exploits probabilistic representations in the context of depth-sorted visual salience maps such as binocular rivalry, where one can obtain approximate probabilities for each layer of the map at different scales. In addition to learning perceptual hierarchies and generating spatial maps of various scales, we provide novel techniques for solving spatial and temporal constraints with large dimensions while preserving the local structure of the image. By combining probabilistically driven classification with the high-dimensional nature of a hierarchy-free reconstruction map, our results demonstrate for first time accurate classification performance across diverse tasks related to perception and semantic knowledge capture. Our experiments show significant improvements over existing depth- and shape-specific algorithms (Bresenham et al., 2010; Karpathy et al., 2012), including low latency and high accuracy, under varying environmental conditions which also demonstrates their wide applicability via natural language comprehension applications. Our results demonstrate the robustness of the resulting classifiers to variations induced by task complexity. The most visible performance differences are among deep perceptrons and neural networks – on tasks with low or medium similarity to our salience perceptron. These findings suggest interesting avenues for applying them together not only in other datasets and learning models but in more general domains of AI.

Yes, preclinical evidence does support the idea that activation of mesolimbic alpha 6 subunit containing nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (6-nAChRs) is involved in the development of nicotine addiction phenotype. Studies using rodent models have demonstrated that activation of these receptors is critical for the reinforcing effects of nicotine and the development of addiction-like behaviors. Specifically, 6-nAChRs are highly expressed in the mesolimbic dopamine system, which plays a vital role in mediating the rewarding effects of drugs of abuse, including nicotine. Activation of 6-nAChRs on dopaminergic neurons can increase dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens, a brain region associated with reward and motivation. This increase in dopamine release is thought to underlie the reinforcing properties of nicotine, contributing to the development of addiction. Further, genetic manipulation studies in rodents have shown that deletion or reduction in 6-nAChR function can decrease the reinforcing effects of nicotine and reduce addiction-related behaviors, such as self-administration and reinstatement. In summary, preclinical evidence indicates that activation of mesolimbic 6-nAChRs plays a crucial role in supporting the nicotine addiction phenotype. However, it is important to note that these findings are from animal models, and further research is needed to fully understand the role of these receptors in human nicotine addiction.

In this paper, we introduce and study a new class of determinantal representations, called uniform determinantal representations, which generalize the classical determinantal representations of the symmetric group. We show that these representations can be realized as the kernel of a certain linear operator, and we provide a combinatorial formula for the character values of these representations. We also establish connections between uniform determinantal representations and other areas of mathematics, such as algebraic geometry, representation theory, and combinatorics. Our main results include the construction of a family of explicit matrices that realize the uniform determinantal representations, and the computation of their character values using techniques from algebraic geometry. We also prove that the character values of the uniform determinantal representations satisfy a certain recursion, which allows us to compute them efficiently. We also study the properties of uniform determinantal representations, such as their irreducibility, equivalence, and decomposition into irreducible components. We show that these representations are closely related to the geometry of certain algebraic varieties, and that they have applications in a variety of fields, including computer science, physics, and engineering. Overall, our work provides a new and powerful tool for studying the representation theory of the symmetric group and its connections to other areas of mathematics. The uniform determinantal representations introduced in this paper offer a rich and flexible framework for understanding the structure and properties of representations of the symmetric group, and they have the potential to lead to new insights and applications in a wide range of fields.

Centrality measures such as the degree, k-shell, or eigenvalue centrality can identify a network's most influential nodes, but are rarely usefully accurate in quantifying the spreading power of the vast majority of nodes which are not highly influential. The spreading power of all network nodes is better explained by considering, from a continuous-time epidemiological perspective, the distribution of the force of infection each node generates. The resulting metric, the Expected Force (ExF), accurately quantifies node spreading power under all primary epidemiological models across a wide range of archetypical human contact networks. When node power is low, influence is a function of neighbor degree. As power increases, a node's own degree becomes more important. The strength of this relationship is modulated by network structure, being more pronounced in narrow, dense networks typical of social networking and weakening in broader, looser association networks such as Internet webpages. The ExF can be computed independently for individual nodes, making it applicable for networks whose adjacency matrix is dynamic, not well specified, or overwhelmingly large.

The academic paper titled "Learning High-level Prior with Convolutional Neural Networks For Semantic Segmentation" presents a novel approach to improve the performance of Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) In semantic segmentation tasks. The proposed method incorporates high-level prior knowledge into the CNN architecture by using a fully connected conditional random field (CRF) layer. the CRF layer models the spatial Dependencies between neighboring pixels, which helps to refine the segmentation results and improve the overall accuracy. The effectiveness of the proposed Method is demonstrated through extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance compared to other existing methods. Overall, the paper provides a valuable contribution to the field of semantic segmentation and demonstrates the importance of incorporating high-level prior knowledge in CNN architectures.

We develop a fast method for optimally designing experiments in the context of statistical seismic source inversion. In particular, We efficiently compute the optimal number and locations of the receivers or seismographs. The seismic source is Modeled by a point moment Tensor multiplied by a time-dependent function. The parameters include the source location, Moment tensor components, and start time and frequency in the time function. The forward problem is modeled by elastodynamic wave equations. We show That the Hessian of the cost functional, which is usually defined as the square of the weighted L2 norm of the difference between the experimental Data and the simulated data, is proportional to the measurement time and the number of receivers. Consequently, the posterior distribution of the parameters, in a Bayesian setting, concentrates around the "true" parameters, and we can employ Laplace approximation and speed up the estimation Of the expected Kullback-Leibler divergence (expected Information gain), the optimality criterion in the experimental design procedure. Since the source parameters span several magnitudes, we use a scaling matrix for efficient control of the condition number of the original hessian matrix. We use a second-order accurate finite difference method To compute the Hessian matrix and either sparse quadrature or Monte Carlo sampling to carry out numerical integration. we demonstrate the efficiency, accuracy, and applicability of our method on a two-dimensional seismic source inversion problem.

This volume introduces some of the ideas that allow us to write programs describing a rich environment. In particular we review the methods used and develop a formalism called quantum parallel universes, which allows us to specify different possible histories for our program while still performing the computations specified by the input parameters. Our focus here instead on exploring what these possibilities actually mean for quantum computing – not wether they are true. We explore what happens when one tries to build quantum computers with many worlds by writting programs that behave in just two worlds. Specifically, we study an example from Bell's Theorem (1985) of a world with an initial state δ-0 and a Hamiltonian of degree 2 that evolves between 0 ⋆ δ : 1 ⊕, and κ 0 : ∞ ⊖. These initial states represent regions where at random the state moves either clockwise or counterclockwise toward a future location δ. When we interact with them, they act like classical variables, producing outputs ranging from δ 0 to ζ∃W(γ′,λ). To evaluate the quantum world, we need to know how much the inputs and outcomes follow the Hamiltonians' laws. As we will see, there exists an algorithm for calculating how probable this history is, given some sample points. One can then choose the world from among the four possibilities that yields a quantum result using the best achievable execution performance across all these possible futures.

Deep learning methods have shown excellent performance in image segmentation tasks but require large datasets to achieve similar performance on images with new background scenes or viewpoints. Moreover, semantic segmentations, which tend to be more accurate than object saliencies, may incur false positives outside the target objects due to irrelevant information (e.g., similar color regions). In this work we propose an iterative deep learning algorithm that sequentially learns features for target-object saliency detection until it achieves high confidence for the predicted salient region such as those generated by fully convolutional conditional random field models. A key advantage of our method over current state-of-the-art object saliency algorithms including the conditional random field and its extension, FC-CRF, is the ability to deal with multiple targets, which enables us to estimate saliency maps where each output pixel does not necessarily correspond to one ground truth label . Moreover, while fully connected CRF requires long computing time and many passes through all pixels to converge, this newly proposed method allows users to specify the number of training epochs and thus reduces time and space consumption significantly. We present two variants of the core method--one adopts superpixel seeds instead of image points; another exploits the concept of image parsing networks to provide more robust segmentation results. Our extensive experiments across different databases demonstrate great improvement in accuracy compared to several existing semantic segmentation technologies for single object and multi-object scenarios .

In this paper, we present CHASE, a novel approach to visual tracking that leverages the power of differentiable neural architecture search (NAS) to optimize the tracking performance. Unlike traditional tracking methods that rely on hand-crafted features and pre-defined architectures, CHASE uses a cell-level differentiable neural network to learn a robust and adaptive representation of the target object. The proposed method consists of two main components: a cell-level differentiable neural network, and a tracking loss function that is designed to optimize the tracking performance. The cell-level differentiable neural network is trained to learn a robust representation of the target object by optimizing a novel tracking loss function that encourages the network to produce a stable output in the presence of occlusions, illumination changes, and other challenges. The tracking loss function is designed to be differentiable with respect to the network's architecture, allowing us to use backpropagation to optimize the network's parameters. We use a combination of gradient descent and evolution strategies to search for the optimal architecture that maximizes the tracking performance. We evaluate CHASE on several challenging benchmarks, including the PASCAL Visual Object Tracking (VOT) dataset, the Temple-Color-Tracking (TCT) dataset, and the LaSalle-Color-Tracking (LCT) dataset. Our experiments show that CHASE outperforms several state-of-the-art tracking methods, including deep learning-based methods, and achieves a high success rate in various challenging scenarios. The main contribution of this paper is the introduction of a novel differentiable neural architecture search method for visual tracking, which allows the network to adapt to changing object appearance and learn a robust representation of the target object. The proposed method has important implications for a wide range of applications, including object tracking in videos, autonomous driving, and robotics.

Despite the difficulties in addressing the high-resolution and ultra-high-resolution images of EM, the recent developments in deep learning have greatly improved the automatic segmentation of such images. However, no existing method is yet completely error-free, and therefore requires some form of proof-reading. This proof-reading is typically done by hand-manual interaction. In this paper, we propose a new fully automatic proof-reading method, which models the human decision process during the proof-reading using a reinforcement learning agent. We systematically design the proposed system by combining multiple reinforcement learning agents in a hierarchical manner, where each agent is restricted to a specific task, but the relationship between them is preserved. We also show that a sequential task setting of reinforcement learning can efficiently deal with a combination of merging and splitting errors in the input. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed system by comparing it to the state-of-the-art methods on a variety of examples.

ΒАSΝеt соmbіnеs thе strеngths оf bоundаrу-аwаrе sеgmеntаtіоn аnd dеер lеаrnіng tо рrоvіdе ассurаtе аnd еffісіеnt іmаgе sеgmеntаtіоn, еvеn оn lоw-роwеr dеvісеs. Εхіstіng sеgmеntаtіоn mеthоds оftеn strugglе wіth соmрlех іmаgеs аnd rеquіrе sіgnіfісаnt соmрutаtіоnаl rеsоurсеs, mаkіng thеm unsuіtаblе fоr dерlоуmеnt оn mоbіlе аnd wеb рlаtfоrms. ΒАSΝеt аddrеssеs thеsе lіmіtаtіоns bу іntеgrаtіng а bоundаrу-аwаrе mесhаnіsm іntо thе sеgmеntаtіоn рrосеss, аllоwіng іt tо fосus оn thе mоst іmроrtаnt rеgіоns оf thе іmаgе аnd rеduсе соmрutаtіоnаl оvеrhеаd. Τhе рrороsеd mеthоd соnsіsts оf thrее stаgеs: (1) fеаturе ехtrасtіоn, (2) bоundаrу dеtесtіоn, аnd (3) sеgmеntаtіоn. Ιn thе fеаturе ехtrасtіоn stаgе, wе usе а lіghtwеіght соnvоlutіоnаl nеurаl nеtwоrk (СΝΝ) tо ехtrасt rеlеvаnt fеаturеs frоm thе іnрut іmаgе. Тhе bоundаrу dеtесtіоn stаgе еmрlоуs а nоvеl bоundаrу-аwаrе mесhаnіsm thаt іdеntіfіеs thе mоst lіkеlу bоundаrу ріхеls іn thе іmаgе. Fіnаllу, thе sеgmеntаtіоn stаgе usеs а соndіtіоnаl rаndоm fіеld (СRF) tо rеfіnе thе sеgmеntаtіоn rеsults, tаkіng іntо ассоunt thе bоundаrу іnfоrmаtіоn аnd sраtіаl соnstrаіnts. Wе еvаluаtе ВАSΝеt оn sеvеrаl bеnсhmаrk dаtаsеts, іnсludіng РΑSСΑL VОС аnd Сіtуsсареs, аnd соmраrе іts реrfоrmаnсе tо stаtе-оf-thе-аrt sеgmеntаtіоn mеthоds. Οur rеsults shоw thаt ВΑSΝеt асhіеvеs hіgh ассurасу аnd оutреrfоrms оthеr mеthоds іn tеrms оf соmрutаtіоnаl еffісіеnсу, mаkіng іt аn іdеаl sоlutіоn fоr mоbіlе аnd wеb аррlісаtіоns. Іn аddіtіоn, wе dеmоnstrаtе thе vеrsаtіlіtу оf ВАSΝеt bу dерlоуіng іt оn vаrіоus mоbіlе аnd wеb рlаtfоrms, іnсludіng smаrtрhоnеs, tаblеts, аnd wеb brоwsеrs. Οur ехреrіmеnts shоw thаt ΒΑSΝеt саn run smооthlу оn thеsе dеvісеs, рrоvіdіng ассurаtе sеgmеntаtіоn rеsults іn rеаl-tіmе. Ιn соnсlusіоn, ΒАSΝеt оffеrs а роwеrful аnd еffісіеnt sоlutіоn fоr іmаgе sеgmеntаtіоn іn mоbіlе аnd wеb аррlісаtіоns, mаkіng іt аn аttrасtіvе сhоісе fоr а wіdе rаngе оf аррlісаtіоns, suсh аs оbjесt dеtесtіоn, trасkіng, аnd аugmеntеd rеаlіtу.

K-S spectral clustering is a popular unsupervised learning method used for data clustering and dimension reduction. This paper gives a survey of the theory of K-S clustering and its applications in various fields. First, we introduce the basic ideas of K-S clustering, such as kernel function, spectral clustering, and kernel trick. Then we analyze the advantages of K-S clustering over other clustering methods and the details of the K-S clustering algorithm. Finally, we list several K-S clustering applications, including image segmentation, text classification, and bioinformatics.

This paper is an attempt to develop a system for identifying garments from a group of clothing images, which have been annotated with semantic tags but not segmented. We propose a data-driven approach, consisting of two phases of inference. The first phase, “image co-segmentation,” iteratively extracts consistent regions from the images, and then combines the segments over all the images using the exemplar-SVM method. In the second phase, “region co-labeling,” we construct a graphical model with the regions as vertices, and incorporate several contextual factors from the images, such as the location of the garments and their interactions. The joint label assignment is performed using the efficient graph cuts method. In addition to the evaluation on the “Fashionista” dataset, we created the “CCP” dataset, consisting of 2098 high-resolution images from the street scene, and demonstrated our system’s effectiveness on this new data. On the two data sets, we achieved a co-segmentation accuracy of 89.46% and a co-labeling accuracy of 65.52% and 63.85%, respectively, with respect to the garments identified, which outperformed the state-of-the-art methods.

The segmentation of medical images is a fundamental step in automated clinical decision support systems. Existing medical image segmentation methods based on supervised deep learning, however, remain problematic because of their reliance on large amounts of labelled training data. Although medical imageing data repositories continue to expand, there has not been a commensurate increase in the amount of annotated data. Hence, we propose a new spatial guided self-supervised clustreing network (SGSCN) for medical image segmentation, where we introduce multiple loss functions designed to aid in grouping image pixels that are spatially connected and have similar feature representations. It iteratively learns feature representations and clustreing assignment of each pixel in an end-to-end fashion from a single image. We also propose a context-based consistency loss that better delineates the shape and boundaries of image regions. It enforces all the pixels belonging to a clustre to be spatially close to the clustre centre. We evaluated our method on 2 public medical image datasets and compared it to existing conventional and self-supervised clustreing methods. Experimental results show that our method was most accurate for medical image segmentation.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to semi-supervised medical image segmentation, which leverages the concept of learning consistency under transformations to improve segmentation accuracy. Our approach is based on the observation that medical images often exhibit certain transformations, such as rotations, translations, and scaling, which can be used to augment the training data and improve the generalisation of the segmentation model. We propose a framework that incorporates these transformations into the training process, by applying them to both the labelled and unlabelled data. This allows the model to learn the invariance of the segmentation task under these transformations, which in turn improves its ability to generalise to new images. We term this approach "Learning Consistency under Transformations" (LCT). We evaluate our approach on several publicly available medical image datasets, including brain tumour segmentation, liver segmentation, and lung segmentation. The results show that LCT significantly outperforms traditional semi-supervised learning methods, and achieves performance comparable to fully-supervised methods, but with much less labelled data. Furthermore, we conduct a series of ablation studies to analyse the effectiveness of different components of our approach. The results suggest that the use of transformations is crucial for improving segmentation accuracy, and that the choice of transformation plays an important role in determining the best performance. Our work has important implications for medical image segmentation, as it demonstrates a way to improve segmentation accuracy without relying on large amounts of labelled data. This can be particularly useful in medical imageing, where annotating images can be time-consuming and expensive. We believe that our approach has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of medical image segmentation, and could potentially be applied to a wide range of medical imageing tasks.

In this study, we introduce progressively diffused networks (PDNs) for semantic image segmentation. The proposed PDN architecture utilizes multiple encoder-decoder branches with corresponding pooling and upsampling operations to generate increasingly complex high-level representations of input images. Each branch has a unique feature extraction mechanism that captures different types of semantic information about the image content. By fusing these multiple features at intermediate stages, our method effectively integrates multi-scale contextual and local cues to enhance the accuracy and robustness of image segmentation results. Extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets show that our technique achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing previous methods based on traditional convolutional neural network architectures.

Conventional transfer learning leverages weights of pre-trained networks, but mandates the need for similar neural architectures. Alternatively, knowledge distillation can transfer knowledge between heterogeneous networks but often requires access to the original training data or additional generative networks. Knowledge transfer between networks can be improved by being agnostic to the choice of network architecture and reducing the dependence on original training data. We propose a knowledge transfer approach from a teacher to a student network wherein we train the student on an independent transferal dataset, whose annotations are generated by the teacher. Experiments were conducted on five state-of-the-art networks for semantic segmentation and seven datasets across three imaging modalities. We studied knowledge transfer from a single teacher, combination of knowledge transfer and fine-tuning, and knowledge transfer from multiple teachers. The student model with a single teacher achieved similar performance as the teacher; and the student model with multiple teachers achieved better performance than the teachers. The salient features of our algorithm include: 1)no need for original training data or generative networks, 2) knowledge transfer between different architectures, 3) ease of implementation for downstream tasks by using the downstream task dataset as the transferal dataset, 4) knowledge transfer of an ensemble of models, trained independently, into one student model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is effective for knowledge transfer and easily tunable.

In this paper, we propose several novel deep learning methods for object saliency detection based on the powerful convolutional neural networks. In our approach, we use a gradient descent method to iteratively modify an input image based on the pixel-wise gradients to reduce a cost function measuring the class-specific objectness of the image. The pixel-wise gradients can be efficiently computed using the back-propagation algorithm. The discrepancy between the modified image and the original one may be used as a saliency map for the image. Moreover, we have further proposed several new training methods to learn saliency-specific convolutional nets for object saliency detection, in order to leverage the available pixel-wise segmentation information. Our methods are extremely computationally efficient (processing 20-40 images per second in one GPU). In this work, we use the computed saliency maps for image segmentation. Experimental results on two benchmark tasks, namely Microsoft COCO and Pascal VOC 2012, have shown that our proposed methods can generate high-quality salience maps, clearly outperforming many existing methods. In particular, our approaches excel in handling many difficult images, which contain complex background, highly-variable salient objects, multiple objects, and/or very small salient objects.

Although deep-learning-based methods have markedly improved the performance of speech separation over the past few years, it remains an open question how to integrate multi-channel signals for speech separation. We propose two methods, namely, early-fusion and late-fusion methods, to integrate multi-channel information based on the time-domain audio separation network, which has been proven effective in single-channel speech separation. We also propose channel-sequential-transfer learning, which is a transfer learning framework that applies the parameters trained for a lower-channel network as the initial values of a higher-channel network. For fair comparison, we evaluated our proposed methods using a spatialized version of the wsj0-2mix dataset, which is open-sourced. It was found that our proposed methods can outperform multi-channel deep clustering and improve the performance proportionally to the number of microphones. It was also proven that the performance of the late-fusion method is consistently higher than that of the single-channel method regardless of the angle difference between speakers.

Differential expression of the bcl-2 protooncogene and the Fas cell surface receptor in the PBMC fraction of patients with burn injuries may suggest a disequilibrium in a complex biochemical signaling mechanism mediating programmed cell death. This is confirmed by an in vitro examination of wound fibroblasts versus those from surrounding uninjured skin. This immunoperoxidase technique reveals a localized relative decrease in Fas and ICE, two apoptosis-inducing proteins, at the level of the fibroblast in the proliferative scar specimen.

This research paper explores the use of other contexts in semantic segmentation. This research paper has provided some useful insights for both academics and practitioners in the field of computer vision and machine learning.

Path signatures are powerful nonparametric tools for time series analysis, shown to form a universal and characteristic feature map for Euclidean valued time series data. We lift the theory of path signatures to the setting of Lie group valued time series, adapting these tools for time series with underlying geometric constraints. We prove that this generalized path signature is universal and characteristic. To demonstrate universality, we analyze the human action recognition problem in computer vision, using S O (3) representations for the time series, providing comparable performance to other shallow learning approaches, while offering an easily interpretable feature set. We also provide a two-sample hypothesis test for Lie group-valued random walks to illustrate its characteristic property. Finally we provide algorithms and a Julia implementation of these methods.

The abstract is as follows: This paper addresses the issue of medical image segmentation by using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). In particular, it proposes an MRI-stitching method, which automatically aligns different MRI images and, in this way, allows for the identification of useful image-to-image correspondences. The CNN-based algorithm was trained using a large database consisting of many MR images, each exhibiting different morphological variations in the different tissues. The resulting CNN was more accurate than techniques based on multi-parametric logistic regression and single-linear regression. This approach was also able to deal with complex medical cases in which individual anatomical features, such as different types of tissue, were present, and the images included many different parts of the body. These approaches are demonstrated to be able to significantly reduce the error rates for image-tailored training but cannot be used for all images, and so should not replace the more traditional image-segmentation methods. However, the study does show that these limitations have a limited effect on the results. In particular, the study shows that image-segmentation methods based on manual-processing can provide better quality, higher speed, and significantly higher precision than CNN-based methods. It also demonstrates that various probabilistic models, such as conditional random fields, are useful and applicable to this task. Although it still requires many image-processing methods, it is recommended that the current image-processing stacks should be improved to integrate these methods in a way that would both solve the problems they solve and make them more accessible to the end-user in a uniform way. Paper: arXiv:1703.04536.

One of the most straightforward, direct and efficient approaches to Image Segmentation is Image Thresholding. Multi-level Image Thresholding is an essential viewpoint in many image processing and Pattern Recognition based real-time applications which can effectively and efficiently classify the pixels into various groups denoting multiple regions in an Image. Thresholding based Image Segmentation using fuzzy entropy combined with intelligent optimisation approaches are commonly used direct methods to properly identify the thresholds so that they can be used to segment an Image accurately. In this paper a novel approach for multi-level image thresholding is proposed using Type II Fuzzy sets combined with Adaptive Plant Propagation Algorithm (APPA). Obtaining the optimal thresholds for an image by maximising the entropy is extremely tedious and time consuming with increase in the number of thresholds. Hence, Adaptive Plant Propagation Algorithm (APPA), a memetic algorithm based on plant intelligence, is used for fast and efficient selection of optimal thresholds. This fact is reasonably justified by comparing the accuracy of the outcomes and computational time consumed by other modern state-of-the-art algorithms such as Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), Gravitational Search Algorithm (GSA) and Genetic Algorithm (GA).

Panoptic segmentation is a new technique for performing at the same time instance segmentation and semantic segmentation. Instance segmentation aims to recognize individual objects in an image, whereas semantic segmentation aims to classify each pixel in an image into a semantic category. Panoptic segmentation goes even further, by generating a dense description of the objects that include their position, size, and shape. We propose a new approach to panoptic segmentation that exploits the recent advances in deep learning. Our method combines a state-of-the-art instance segmentation network and a semantic segmentation network, both of which are based on convolutional neural networks. The output of the ISN are a set of instance segmentations that are used as inputs for the SSN to produce a semantic segmentation mask for each instance segmentation. The outputs of the two networks are then combined using a novel post-processing step, to produce a single panoptic mask for the entire image. Our method is evaluated on several standard datasets, including CityScapes, Pascal VOC, and COCO. We also demonstrate the generality of our method by applying it to a variety of applications, including object detection, semantic segmentation, and instance-level image retrieval. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows. * The design and implementation of a new method for panoptic segmentation that combines instance and semantic segmentation. * The demonstration that our method outperforms the best of the state-of-the-art on several standard datasets. * The demonstration of the generality of our method by its application to several different computer vision tasks.

In order to tackle the development of concurrent and distributed systems, the active object programming model provides a high-level abstraction to program concurrent behaviours. There exists already a variety of active object frameworks targeted at a large range of application domains: modelling, verification, efficient execution. However, among these frameworks, very few consider a multi-threaded execution of active objects. Introducing controlled parallelism within active objects enables overcoming some of their limitations. In this paper, we present a complete framework around the multi-active object programming model. We present it through ProActive, the Java library that offers multi-active objects, and through MultiASP, the programming language that allows the formalisation of our developments. We then show how to compile an active object language with cooperative multi-threading into multi-active objects. This paper also presents different use cases and the development support to illustrate the practical usability of our language. Formalisation of our work provides the programmer with guarantees on the behaviour of the multi-active object programming model and of the compiler.

Qubit state tomography is a crucial technique for characterizing and diagnosing errors in quantum systems. In this paper, we propose a novel method for performing qubit state tomography in superconducting circuits using weak measurements. Our approach involves measuring the qubit's response to a weak perturbation, which allows us to reconstruct the qubit's state with high accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by performing tomography on a superconducting qubit and comparing our results with those obtained using other methods. Our work paves the way for the development of more accurate and efficient qubit state tomography techniques in superconducting circuits.

We present an all-pass coupled-line low temperature superconducting phaser (GCPAP) with nonlinear electromagnetic coupling between the source to the detector and a microwave cavity that makes the entire device energy efficient at temperatures down to 5 K, while simultaneously delivering strong field emission. We have demonstrated our concept by applying it in a practical test system, including one without an antenna or a cavity. Our findings suggest GCPAP has promising applications as a highly effective microwave generator, but should be deployed only as a last resort due to the high power consumption required.

This paper proposes a new approach to improving random forest classifiers by integrating deep convolutional neural networks (CNN). The proposed model, named Fast Random Forest Classifier, utilizes the features extracted from CNNs as input for the random forest algorithm. By leveraging the strengths of both models, we improve the accuracy and efficiency of our fast random forest classifier compared to regular random forests without feature extraction. The CNN extracts relevant features from high-dimensional data that are difficult to obtain manually. Meanwhile, random forest algorithms provide robust and accurate predictions and can handle noisy or incomplete datasets with ease. Our method explores how these two techniques could be combined to boost the overall performance of classifiers. To achieve this, we utilize pre-trained VGG16 and ResNet50 as CNN models to extract features from images and text data respectively. We then apply random sampling on these features with varying degrees to feed them into the random forest algorithm. We demonstrate through experiments that integrating Deep CNN-based features results in an improvement in classification accuracy, time savings in training processes, and effective handling of large datasets compared to using random forests directly. Overall, our study highlights the potential of combining deep learning techniques such as CNN with popular classification methods like random forest. It also contributes significantly to open research in this area by providing a valuable resource for developing efficient, scalable and effective machine learning systems.

In vivo D2 occupancy measurements in rats using [3Hraclopride is analogous to using [11Craclopride in human PET scanning. Results closely resembled human studies where 65-70 D2 occupancy was required for antipsychotic response, while or 80 D2 occupancy led to EPS. Brain mechanisms involved in mediation of catalepsy in rats and EPS in humans might indeed be similar. Both suppression of CAR in rats and antipsychotic response in humans might share an underlying construct, i.e. the need for around 70 D2 receptor blockade.

The segmentation of medical images is a fundamental step in automated clinical decision support systems. Existing medical image segmentation methods based on supervised deep learning, however, remain problematic because of their reliance on large amounts of labelled training data. Although medical imaging data repositories continue to expand, there has not been a commensurate increase in amount of annotated data. Hence, we propose a new spatial guided self-supervised clustering network (SGSCN) for medical image segmentation, where we introduce multiple loss functions designed to aid in grouping image pixels that are spatially connected and have similar feature representations. It iteratively learns feature representations and clustering assignment of each pixel in end-to-end fashion from single image. We also propose context-based consistency loss that better delineates the shape and boundaries of image regions. It enforces all the pixels belonging to cluster to be spatially close to the cluster centre. We evaluated our method on 2 public medical image datasets and compared it to existing conventional and self-supervised clustering methods. Experimental results show that our method was most accurate for medical image segmentation.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to medical image segmentation using a spatial guided self-supervised clustering network (SG-SCN). The SG-SCN model combines the strengths of self-supervised learning and spatial guidence to improve the accuracy and efficiency of medical image segmentation. Self-supervised learning has emerged as a promising approach to medical image segmentation, as it can learn useful features from unlabelled data. However, self-supervised learning methods often suffer from the problem of trivial solutions, where the model learns irrelevant or redundant features that do not generalize well to new data. Spatial guidence, which incorporates prior knowledge about the spatial structure of the data, has been shown to improve the performance of self-supervised learning models. The SG-SCN model proposed in this paper combines self-supervised learning with spatial guidence to overcome the limitations of traditional self-supervised learning methods. The model consists of a spatial guidence module that incorporates prior knowledge about the spatial structure of the data, and a self-supervised clustering module that learns to cluster the data into meaningful segments. The spatial guidence module is designed to provide the self-supervised clustering module with spatial information, such as the location and size of organs or tissues, which helps the model to learn more accurate and meaningful features. We evaluate the performance of the SG-SCN model on several publically available medical image datasets, including brain MRI, lung CT, and liver CT. The results show that the SG-SCN model outperforms several state-of-the-art self-supervised learning methods, and achieves competitive performance compared to fully supervised models. In addition, we conduct a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of the spatial guidence module and demonstrate its contribution to the improved performance of the SG-SCN model. Abstract Selection of an appropriate labeled drawing to fit into deep learning architectures has been problematic in recent years, since many trained examples exhibit unexpected features when viewed as images. This study provides simple guidelines for identifying such unlabelled examples through image recognition training on a large, open source system, called ImageNet. A classification accuracy of 83% was achieved with 1 hour and 12 supervised tests, which includes all features classified by the network, while an example validation set contained just 99 classes. Our method can identify some types of unlabeled images efficiently enough to be useful in some kinds of applications. Furthermore, its approach enables significant reduction of data collection time relative to prior methods that require several hours for labeling (e.g., manually examining hundreds or thousands of labeled images), and it does so despite providing an almost uniform distribution of labels across the entire dataset even though not every image on the ground belongs to any of those classes. We believe our results show how quickly image segmentation techniques can improve in the face of increasing parallelism in deep-learning architectures; furthermore, their fast response to changing the number of categories during training also suggests the utility of incorporating more than one category into our architecture at the same time. These preliminary results provide important directions for future work on these problems.
