In this paper, we present novel approach to segmenting images based on weak labels, called Points2Polygons. Our method uses adversarial networks to learn a context-based segmentation model that can accurately separate objects from their surroundings, even in cases where object boundaries are not well-defined or there is significant background noise. Traditional image segmentation methods rely on hand-crafted features and heuristics, which often lead to suboptimal performance when dealing with complex scenes or low-quality data. Moreover, obtaining high-quality labels for training these models can be time-consuming and expensive. In contrast, our approach leverages recent advances in deep learning to learn a segments representation directly from input data, without relying on manual feature engineering. The key insight behind Points2Polygons is to use adversarial training to learn a polygon-based representation of image, where each polygon corresponds to a coherent region of scene. This allows us to effectively capture object boundaries and handle irregularly shaped objects, while also propagating information across neighboring regions to produce more accurate segmentations. We evaluate Points2Polygons on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes, comparing it against state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms. Our results show that our approach significantly outperforms traditional segmentation methods, especially in situations where the label quality is poor or there is significant contextual variation between training and test data. Overall, this work represents an important step towards developing robust and efficient image segmentation techniques that can operate effectively in real-world scenarios. The proposed method has broad applications in computer vision, robotics, medical imaging, and other domains where image understanding is critical.

TransFuse is an innovative technique that utilizes the strengths of Transformers and Convolutional Neural Systems (CNN) for medical image segmentation. By combining the robust feature processing capabilities of CNNs and the long-range dependencies captured by Transformers, TransFuse produces state-of-the-art performance on many clinical imaging tasks, including segmentation of brain cells, tumor tumors, and liver tumors. The fusion of these three technologies allows TransFuse to efficiently handle complex clinical image data and improve the reliability of segmentation results. Overall, TransFuse demonstrates a major innovation in clinical imagery research and has the potential to revolutionize the field.

In this paper, we explore the use of information theoretic inequalities as bounds in superconformal field theory. Specifically, we consider the concept of mutual information, which measures the amount of information that can be extracted from one system about another. We show that mutual information can be used to bound the entropy of a system in superconformal field theory, providing a new way to understand the behavior of these systems. In this paper, we propose A novel approach to semantic segmentation that leverages contextual information beyond the image itself. Traditional methods of semantic segmentation rely solely on the visual content Of the Image, neglecting valuable contextual information That can improve Accuracy and robustness. We introduce a framework that incorporates external knowledge and priorities to enhance the feature representation and overcome the limitations of standard CNN-based segmentation models. Our approach consists of two main components: (1) a knowledge injection module that incorporates external knowledge from various sources, such as textual descriptions, object categories, and scene understanding, into the feature extraction process; and (2) a priority-aware module that adapts the feature representations based on the importance of each pixel in the image. We evaluate our method on Several benchmark datasets, including Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and COCO, and demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art segmentation methods. The key contributions of this paper Are: * A novel framework that effectively incorporates Contextual information beyond the image into the semantic segmentation process. * An Efficient knowledge injection module that Integrates external knowledge from diverse sources without requiring manual annotation. * A priority-aware module that Adapts the feature representations according to the importance of each pixel, enhancing the overall performance and robustness of the model. Our experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation approaches, demonstrating the effectiveness of mining Contextual information beyond the image for semantic segmentation tasks. This work has important implications for applications where accurate segmentation is critical,such as autonomous driving, robotics, and medical imaging.

(CNN) The underwater search area for missing Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 looks set to double in size. Teams are scouring the depths of a remote part of the southern Indian Ocean for the remains of the passenger jet that disappeared more than a year ago with 239 people on board. So far, they've covered about 60 of the priority search zone without reporting any trace of the airliner. Families of passengers and crew members still have no answers about what happened to their loved ones. If the searchers haven't found anything by the time they've covered the entire 60,000-square-kilometer priority zone, the search will stretch into a new equally vast area, government officials from Malaysia, Australia and China announced Thursday. "Ministers remain committed to bring closure and some peace to the families and loved ones of those on board Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370," the three countries said in a joint statement. The search of the current priority zone is expected to be completed in May. Covering the new zone could take as long as a year. At that point, "all high probability search areas would have been covered," the governments said Thursday. The size of the doubled search area, the equivalent of more than 46,000 square miles, would be bigger than the U.S. state of Pennsylvania. Flight 370 vanished after taking off from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, on March 8, 2014, bound for Beijing. Officials are still trying to figure out why it veered dramatically off course over the sea between Malaysia and Vietnam and where exactly it ended up. An international team of experts used satellite data to calculate that the plane eventually went down in the southern Indian Ocean, far off the coast of Western Australia. The people on board the Boeing 777 came from various nations, but the majority were Chinese. CNN's Elizabeth Joseph contributed to this report.

This study investigates the convergence of two thermal boundary condition approaches, namely fixing the heat flux at a surface versus keeping that surface'stemperature constant. By analyzing these methods in conjunction with rapid rotation effects on convective flow patterns, we demonstrate their asymptotically equivalent behavior under certain limiting conditions. This result has important implications for modeling and simulation efforts involving rotational dynamics and thermally driven fluid motions. Our analysis provides insights into when one approach may be more advantageous than the other based upon computational considerations and desired accuracy levels.

The goal of this study is to develop an unsupervised approach for joint segmentation and deconvolution in ultrasonic tissue images using a hierarchical Bayesian model based on generalized Gaussian priors. We begin by performing the initial denoising step followed by image registration. Then, we utilize hierarchical Bayes methods with a generalized additive prior to provide robust spatial regularization while preserving edge information. To overcome challenges associated with noise, partial information masked regions, and inter-slice variability, the model employs a Bayesian inference mechanism that updates priors iteratively as more data become available during segmentation and provides higher accuracy results compared to state-of-the-art algorithms. Our method offers flexible control over trade-off between model interpretability and performance, making it suitable for multiple applications such as cardiac or liver analysis. In summary, our proposed method utilizes a hierarchical Bayesian approach combining generalized Gaussian priors to provide improved joint segmentation and deconvolution in noisy ultrasound images with superior convergence characteristics than typical approaches used previously.

Title: Automatic segmenting teeth in X-ray images: Trends, A novel data set, benchmarking and future perspectives. Abstract: Dental X-rays are essential tools used by dental professionals to diagnose various oral health Conditions. However, accurate interpretation of these X-rays requires skilled radiographers Or dentists to manually segment out individual teeth from the image. This process can be time Consuming, error prone, And is limited to highly trained personnel. In recent years, advances in computer vision And machine learning have led to developments in automatic tooth segmentation methods that aim to automate this task. This paper reviews current trends and techniques in the automatic segmentation of teeth in X-ray images. We also discuss a novel data set developed specifically for this purpose, which provides an extensive range of variations to enable thorough testing and evaluation Of algorithms. Finally, we present benchmarks against existing state-of-the-art methods and discuss potential future directions for research and applications.

In this paper, we provide a comprehensive review of multi-fidelity modeling techniques and their applications in various fields. Multi-fidelity modeling is a approach that combines multiple models with different levels of fidelity to solve complex engineering problems. The idea behind this method is to use low-fidelity models for most instances and high-fidelity models only when necessary, thus reducing computational costs while maintaining accuracy. We start by introducing the concept of multi-fidelity modeling and its benefits, followed by a detailed discussion of the different methods used to couple multiple models. We then examine the various approaches to selecting the appropriate level of fidelity for a given problem, including adaptive and hierarchical methods. The next section of the paper reviews several case studies from diverse fields such as aerospace, automotive, and mechanical engineering, where multi-fidelity models have been successfully applied. These examples demonstrate how multi-fidelity models can significantly reduce computation time and increase accuracy compared to traditional single-fidelity models. Finally, we discuss some challenges associated with implementing multi-fidelity models, such as managing data transfer between models and ensuring the reliability of the results. We also highlight some future research directions, including the integration of machine learning algorithms and uncertainty quantification techniques into multi-fidelity frameworks. Overall, this review provides a thorough overview of multi-fidelity modeling techniques and their potential to revolutionize the field of engineering design and optimization. It serves as a valuable resource for both practitioners and researchers interested in exploring the power of multi-fidelity models for solving complex engineering problems.

In this work, we explain the working mechanism of MixUp in terms of adversarial training. We introduce a new class of adversarial training schemes, which we refer to as directional adversarial training, or DAT. In a nutshell, a DAT scheme perturbs a training example in the direction of another example but keeps its original label as the training target. We prove that MixUp is equivalent to a special subclass of DAT, in that it has the same expected loss function and corresponds to the same optimization problem asymptotically. This understanding not only serves to explain the effectiveness of MixUp, but also reveals a more general family of MixUp schemes, which we call Untied MixUp. We prove that the family of Untied MixUp schemes is equivalent to the entire class of DAT schemes. We establish empirically the existence of Untied Mixup schemes which improve upon MixUp.

The academic paper titled "Path Integral Representation of Lorentzian Spinfoam Model, Asymptotics, and Simplicial Geometries" presents a study on the path integral representation of Lorentzian spinfoam models. The paper explores the asymptotics of these models and their relationship to simplicial geometries. The authors demonstrate that the path integral representation provides a useful tool for understanding the behavior of Lorentzian spinfoam models and their connection to simplicial geometries. The problem of expressing a specific polynomial as the determinant of a square matrix of affine-linear forms arises from algebraic geometry, optimisation, complexity theory, and scientific computing. Motivated by recent developments in this last area, we introduce the notion of a uniform determinantal representation, not of a single polynomial but rather of all polynomials in a given number of variables and of a given maximal degree. We derive a lower bound on the size of the matrix, and present a construction achieving that lower bound up to a constant factor as the number of variables is fixed and the degree grows. This construction marks an improvement upon a recent construction due to Plestenjak-Hochstenbach, and we investigate the performance of new representations in their root-finding technique for bivariate systems. Furthermore, we relate uniform determinantal representations to vector spaces of singular matrices, and we conclude with a number of future research directions.

This paper presents a design methodology for optimal transmission energy allocation at a sensor equipped with energy harvesting technology for remote state estimation of linear stochastic dynamical systems. In this framework, the sensor measurements as noisy versions of the system states are sent to the receiver over a packet dropping communication channel. The packet dropout probabilities of the channel depend on both the sensor's transmission energies and time varying wireless fading channel gains. The sensor has access to an energy harvesting source which is an everlasting but unreliable energy source compared to conventional batteries with fixed energy storages. The receiver performs optimal state estimation with random packet dropouts to minimize the estimation error covariances based on received measurements. The receiver also sends packet receipt acknowledgments to the sensor via an erroneous feedback communication channel which is itself packet dropping. The objective is to design optimal transmission energy allocation at the energy harvesting sensor to minimize either a finite-time horizon sum or a long term average (infinite-time horizon) of the trace of the expected estimation error covariance of the receiver's Kalman filter. These problems are formulated as Markov decision processes with imperfect state information. The optimal transmission energy allocation policies are obtained by the use of dynamic programming techniques. Using the concept of submodularity, the structure of the optimal transmission energy policies are studied. Suboptimal solutions are also discussed which are far less computationally intensive than optimal solutions. Numerical simulation results are presented illustrating the performance of the energy allocation algorithms.

Distributed machine learning is becoming a popular model-training method due to privacy, computational scalability, and bandwidth capacities. In this work, we explore scalable distributed-training versions of two algorithms commonly used in object detection. A novel distributed training algorithm using Mean Weight Matrix Aggregation (MWMA) is proposed for Linear Support Vector Machine (L-SVM) object detection based in Histogram of Orientated Gradients (HOG). In addition, a novel Weighted Bin Aggregation (WBA) algorithm is proposed for distributed training of Ensemble of Regression Trees (ERT) landmark localization. Both algorithms do not restrict the location of model aggregation and allow custom architectures for model distribution. For this work, a Pool-Based Local Training and Aggregation (PBLTA) architecture for both algorithms is explored. The application of both algorithms in the medical field is examined using a paradigm from the fields of psychology and neuroscience - eyeblink conditioning with infants - where models need to be trained on facial images while protecting participant privacy. Using distributed learning, models can be trained without sending image data to other nodes. The custom software has been made available for public use on GitHub: Results show that the aggregation of models for the HOG algorithm using MWMA not only preserves the accuracy of the model but also allows for distributed learning with an accuracy increase of 0.9 compared with traditional learning. Furthermore, WBA allows for ERT model aggregation with an accuracy increase of 8 when compared to single-node models.

I had driven past the decrepit, shitty building at least a thousand times since moving into the apartment complex it sat next to, constantly polluting the space in which I lived. I had seen what little looked like a staircase, a few floors up. The weirdest part of it all was that I had never seen anyone go inside. I had also heard that a rich hipster, who was also a realtor, had tried to buy the building, but the owner wouldn't let him. "They wanted it knocked down, but I just couldn't do it," the owner would say, repeatedly. "I have such fond memories of that place." When I saw my new roommate walking towards me, I asked him if he knew anything about the building. "It's this big empty thing on the corner that has 'For Rent' signs posted on it," he said. "Do you know anything about it?" "I don't know anything, but I've heard some wild rumors. People say it's haunted and that you can get locked in there if you go in and don't come back out." "Really? Well, the way I see it, whoever owns the building is going to let me in there to take a look around. I'll tell them that I'll be out in a half hour or so. I'll probably be back out in ten minutes." "You're a crazy man. If you're locked in there, you're going to be in a lot of trouble." "Yeah, but I'm just going to be looking around. I'm not going to touch anything or get locked in." "Alright. Just be careful. If I don't see you back here, I'm calling the cops and having them break in the front door. No offense, but you're kind of a fucking idiot." "I'll be fine. I'll only be in there for a few minutes." A few minutes turned into an hour. The roommate saw me walking out of the building and panicked. "I'm going to call the cops," he said, and took off running down the street. By the time I made it back to the apartment, my roommate had called the cops, the cops had arrived, and the cops had taken me away. I didn't know what was going on, and when I asked the cop, he told me that I was being charged with trespassing and that the property owner had filed a police report.

A strong visual object tracker nowadays relies on its well-crafted modules, which typically consist of manually-designed network architectures to deliver high-quality tracking results. Not surprisingly, the manual design process becomes a particularly challenging barrier, as it demands sufficient prior experience, enormous effort, intuition and perhaps some good luck. Meanwhile, neural architecture search has gaining grounds in practical applications such as image segmentation, as a promising method in tackling the issue of automated search of feasible network structures. In this work, we propose a novel cell-level differentiable architecture search mechanism to automate the network design of the tracking module, aiming to adapt backbone features to the objective of a tracking network during offline training. The proposed approach is simple, efficient, and with no need to stack a series of modules to construct a network. Our approach is easy to be incorporated into existing trackers, which is empirically validated using different differentiable architecture search-based methods and tracking objectives. Extensive experimental evaluations demonstrate the superior performance of our approach over five commonly-used benchmarks. Meanwhile, our automated searching process takes 41 (18) hours for the second (first) order DARTS method on the TrackingNet dataset.

The usage of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for unsupervised image segmentation was investigated in this study. In the proposed approach, label prediction and network parameter learning are alternately iterated to meet the following criteria: (a) pixels of similar features should be assigned the same label, (b) spatially continuous pixels should be assigned the same label, and (c) the number of unique labels should be large. Although these criteria are incompatible, the proposed approach minimizes the combination of similarity loss and spatial continuity loss to find a plausible solution of label assignment that balances the aforementioned criteria well. The contributions of this study are four-fold. First, we propose a novel end-to-end network of unsupervised image segmentation that consists of normalization and an argmax function for differentiable clustering. Second, we introduce a spatial continuity loss function that mitigates the limitations of fixed segment boundaries possessed by previous work. Third, we present an extension of the proposed method for segmentation with scribbles as user input, which showed better accuracy than existing methods while maintaining efficiency. Finally, we introduce another extension of the proposed method: unseen image segmentation by using networks pre-trained with a few reference images without re-training the networks. The effectiveness of the proposed approach was examined on several benchmark datasets of image segmentation.

Semantic segmentation is a critical task in computer vision that involves assigning a label to each pixel in an image based on its semantic meaning. While recent advances in deep learning have led to significant Improvements in image-based semantic segmentation, there Are still challenges in accurately segmenting objects in complex scenes with Ambiguous or occluded regions. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to mining contextual information beyond image for semantic Segmentation. Our approach leverages additional contextual information such as textual Descriptions, 3D models, and user feedback to enhance the accuracy of semantic segmentation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our Approach on several benchmark datasets and show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art image-based semantic segmentation methods. Our work paves the way for more accurate and robust semantic segmentation in complex scenes.

The graph theory litreature has seen tremendous growth, and exact inference techniques have been a major focus. However, recent research shows that previous approaches suffer from significant limitations when applied to graphs with degree 4 or more vertices as their number increases rapidly while still maintaining a feasible graph structure. To address this issue, we propose an efficient approach based on the degree-4 sum of squares hierarchy (DSSH), which efficiently generates lower bounds for exact solutions to problems over these graphs. Our proposed method involves representing each vertex node using its degree vector, so that a solution can be considered a valid assignment if it satisfies the DSSH constraints. We then develop algorithms based on dynamic programmeming to generate such assignments systematically, starting with small subproblems containing fewer nodes and iterating towards larger ones. Our results show improvements in efficiency of order O(N log N) compared to previous methods with the same level of accuracy. Furthermore, our work contributes significantly towards understanding the structure of degree-4 graphs using mathematical analysis and theoretical insights, paving the way for future development of efficient exact inference techniques specifically tailored to meet these needs. Overall, our findings offer new avenues for research and the potential for significant advancements in applying combinatorial optimisation techniques to real-world scenarios involving complex networks. In summary, this paper presents an innovative approach to exact inference in graphs using the degree-4 sum of squares hierarchy, resulting in improved efficiency and better understanding of the underlying graph structures.

Also Known as Pack Hardening, Blister Steel, Shear Steel From what I understand from reading old texts, traditionally, case hardening was a technique were a blacksmith would infuse a piece of wrought iron, which is low in carbon, with additional carbon in the outer layers of the metal. This would allow the smith to harden those layers infused with carbon, while the core of the metal remained ductile. This was typically done by packing the wrought iron in a mixture of ground bone and charcoal (or some other strange recipe) in a tightly sealed box. This box was then heated until the metal was near welding temperature, at which point the outer layers would be near melting, and the added carbon would be able to mix in. One this process was completed, the smith could then reheat and quench the metal, hardening the layers with increased carbon content. This process formed what has been called blister steel or shear steel. It was used mainly before the the ability to produce steel, when wrought iron was still too soft for the application. In later times, a piece of steel might be case hardened by a process of carefully heating the outer layers of a thicker piece of steel and quenching it. This again leaves the inner portion ductile, reducing the brittleness of the steel. The carbon content of the steel was not affected by this process. In this paper, we present a novel approach to lifted MAP inference in computer vision, which we call coarse-to-fine lifted MAP inference. This approach combines the strengths of coarse-to-fine search and lifted MAP inference, leading to improved performance in various computer vision Tasks. lifted MAP inference is A powerful framework for solving inference problems in computer vision, as it allows for efficient and effective inference in complex Models. However, traditional lifted MAP inference algorithms suffer from the problem of local optima, where the search process may get stuck in a suboptimal solution. Coarse-to-fine search, on the other Hand, is a technique that has been shown to be effective in avoiding local Optima By starting with a coarse search and gradually refining it. Our proposed approach combines these two techniques, using a coarse-to-fine search to guide the lifted MAP inference process. We first perform a coarse search To identify a set of promising regions In the image, and then use lifted MAP inference to refine the search and identify the final solution. we repeat this process multiple times, with each iteration refining the search region and improving the accuracy of the solution. We demonstrate the Effectiveness of our approach on several challenging computer vision tasks, including image segmentation, object recognition, and image reconstruction. Our results show that coarse-to-fine Lifted MAP inference significantly outperforms traditional lifted MAP inference algorithms, and achieves state-of-the-art performance in these tasks. In addition, we analyze the computational complexity of our approach and show that it is significantly faster than traditional lifted MAP Inference algorithms, making It a more practical solution for real-world applications. We also discuss the limitations of our approach and identify areas for future research. Overall, Our paper presents a novel approach to lifted MAP inference in computer vision that combines the strengths of coarse-to-fine search and lifted MAP inference. Our proposed approach significantly improves the performance of lifted MAP inference in various Computer vision tasks and has important implications for the development of efficient and effective inference algorithms in computer vision.

We introduce $\textit{InExtremIS}$, a weakly supervised 3D approach to train a deep image segmentation network using particularly weak train-time annotations: only 6 extreem clicks at the boundary of the objects of interest. Our fully-automatic method is trained end-to-end and does not require any test-time annotations. From the extreem points, 3D bounding boxes are extracted around objects of interest. Then, deep geodesics connecting extreem points are generated to increase the amount of "annotated" voxels within the bounding boxes. Finally, a weakly supervised regularised loss derived from a Conditional Random Field formulation is used to encourage prediction consistency over homogeneous regions. Extensive experiments are performed on a large open dataset for Vestibular Schwannoma segmentation. $\textit{InExtremIS}$ obtained competitive performance, approaching full supervision and outperforming significantly other weakly supervised techniques based on bounding boxes. Moreover, given a fixed annotation time budget, $\textit{InExtremIS}$ outperforms full supervision. Our code and data are available online.

Exact inference in graphs is crucial problem in many areas of computer science and statistics. In this paper, we present thorough view of exact inference in graphs from the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy. We first introduce the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy, which is powerful tool for exact inference in graphs. We then show how to use this hierarchy to solve a wide range of exact inference problems in graphs, including clique detection, minimum cut, and maximum flow. We also discuss some of the limitations of the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy and propose some possible extensions. Overall, our paper provides comprehensive overview of exact inference in graphs from degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy and demonstrates its effectiveness in solving a variety of problems.

Laura couldn't afford to buy a dress for the school dance. She made one out of a pretty floral fabric. She was afraid the other girls would make fun of her, but she went anyway and had a good time. The next fall when Laura and her friends went back to school, they had new math teacher, Mr. Johnson. He taught them about fractions. How could you divide something into two parts? But math teachers are always smarter than everybody else, so by this time it wasn't hard for everyone to understand what fractions meant. The boys didn't like fractions as much though. They said it was too complicated and girls don't need to know that kind of stuff. So most of the male students got C's in their division tests. That was fair enough I guess - they'd been at least trying. But some guys who hadn't tried still passed and claimed they knew fractions all along. Then they spread the lie around the whole school: "I did really well in my division test!" Of course no one believed them. It only bothered the girls even more. Most girls thought they should have gotten an A instead of a C, because they studied harder and longer than anyone else. But Laura kept on studying fractions very hard. There had never been any question in Laura's mind that both her parents deserved better lives. Now maybe someday she could help them get those better lives. Qu quasi-likelihood approaches are widely used to analyze spatial point processes. Essentially, these methodologies allow us to make use of information from likelihood functions without having to impose a specific underlying distribution on our data. We can thus easily incorporate additional information or constraints into our models in order to improve performance. In this abstract, we present an overview of the main concepts and techniques involved in quasi-likelihood methods for spatio-temporal point process analysis. Specifically, we focus on the conceptual framework for choosing an appropriate likelihood function that takes into account both spatial and temporal correlations. Furthermore, we explore various practical considerations when using quasi-likelihoods, including model selection criteria, regularization techniques, and handling missing observations. Finally, we discuss some of the recent advances and challenges in extending quasi-likelihood methods to more complex spatio-temporal systems, such as those involving multiple types of observations.

Jet schemes are a popular method for solving advection problems in computational fluid dynamics. These schemes are designed to accurately capture behavior of advection-dominated flows, which are common in many engineering and scientific applications. In this paper, we review the basic principles of jet schemes and discuss their various implementations. We also present some recent advances in the development of jet schemes, including use of high-order methods and adaptive mesh refinement. Finally, we discuss some of challenges and open issues associated with the use of jet schemes, and provide some suggestions for future research. Overall, this paper provides comprehensive overview of jet schemes for advection problems and their applications.

Connection structure provides the basic insight that images are composed of small regions—nodes, edges or vertices—that communicate and interact with one another in meaningful ways across a large volume of semantic space. This notion has been well-tethered to the idea of word embeddings on an existing neural network context; however, it appears that these same conceptual constructs may also be used by a new approach to connectionist verification without any explicit mapping to word embeddings. RLCcorrector adds reinforcement learning functionality to this traditional proofreading paradigm (see [1] http://arxiv.org/abs/1308.4824), and integrates it with existing machine pattern recognition algorithms such as Gaussian Process and Markov chains. RLCcorrectors allow for both error detection (using unsupervised feature learning) and inference (by using high-level supervised models that utilize the features present in the evidence). For errors, we use word vectors that encode information about the locations of the locations of words within a sentence and then detect similar occurrences in different documents. With the current algorithm, if two adjacent documents have not yet touched each other, our model suggests that their occurrence should correspond to some common location. A few moments later when they begin crossing over, the error becomes more apparent. Thus, this system can quickly learn patterns such as the positions of words contained inside sentences based on prior knowledge to correct erroneous matches that might otherwise elude prediction. [2][3] We show how RLCcorrectors can extend commonly used automatic annotation systems like Wordnet and Snippets to include connectionist approaches, adding validation and support information. The end-to-end process required for connecting word embeddings and connectionist training methods yields improved readability and overall comprehension through higher levels of abstraction than previously available. In Proceedings of ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining. Springer International Publishing. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to structured output learning called multi-utility learning, which enables training models that can handle multiple annotation-specific loss functions. Traditional approaches to structured output learning rely on a single loss function, which may not capture all the relevant information and nuances of different types of annotations. Our proposed method allows for the use of multiple loss functions, each tailored to specific aspects of the output structure. We develop a general framework for multi-utility learning, which encompasses various applications such as image segmentation, natural language processing, and speech recognition. We also introduce an efficient algorithm that simultaneously optimizes the multiple utilities by balancing their corresponding loss functions. Furthermore, we provide theoretical analysis on the properties of our algorithm, including consistency and convergence guarantees under certain conditions. Experiments conducted on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in comparison to traditional methods. Additionally, we perform ablation studies to analyze the contribution of each utility and show how they complement each other in improving overall performance. Our work has significant implications for real-world applications where multiple outputs are often involved. By incorporating domain knowledge into the training process through multiple loss functions, our model is better equipped to make accurate predictions, leading to improved performance and robustness. This research paves the way for future exploration in combining different types of loss functions for multimodal tasks, ultimately advancing the field of machine learning toward more sophisticated and reliable models.

This paper investigates a general framework to discover categories of unlabeled scene images according to their appearances (i.e., textures and structures). We jointly solve the two coupled tasks in an unsupervised manner: (i) classifying images without pre-determining the number of categories, and (ii) pursuing generative model for each category. In our method, each image is represented by two types of image descriptors that are effective to capture image appearances from different aspects. By treating each image as a graph vertex, we build up an graph, and pose the image categorization as a graph partition process. Specifically, a partitioned sub-graph can be regarded as a category of scenes, and we define the probabilistic model of graph partition by accumulating the generative models of all separated categories. For efficient inference with the graph, we employ a stochastic cluster sampling algorithm, which is designed based on the Metropolis-Hasting mechanism. During the iterations of inference, the model of each category is analytically updated by a generative learning algorithm. In the experiments, our approach is validated on several challenging databases, and it outperforms other popular state-of-the-art methods. The implementation details and empirical analysis are presented as well.

We have discovered that injury to a peripheral nerve and electrical stimulation of C-fibers each cause an increase in the permeability of the BSCB and the BBB. The increase in permeability is delayed in onset, peaks at about 24 hours and is dependent upon action potential propagation. As the increase is mimicked by applying capsaicin to the nerve, the most parsimonious explanation for our findings is that the increase in permeability is mediated by activation of TRPV1-expressing primary sensory neurons. Our findings may be relevant to the development of pain and neuroplastic changes in the CNS following nerve injury. In addition, our findings may provide the basis for developing methods to purposefully open the BBB when needed to increase brain penetration of therapeutic agents that might normally be excluded by an intact BBB.

Abstract: Fundus image segmentation is a crucial task in ophthalmology, which Aims To identify and separate different retinal structures from fundus images. However, achieving generalizable segmentation performance on unseen datasets Remains a significant challenge due to the domain shift problem. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called Domain-oriented Feature Embedding (DoFE) to address this issue. DoFE is designed to learn a domain-invariant feature representation that can be used for generalizable fundus image segmentation. By incorporating domain-specific information into the feature embedding process, DoFE encourages the model to focus on The most relevant features that are consistent across different domains. This is achieved through a domain-oriented contrastive loss function that guides The model to learn a shared feature space across different domains. we evaluate the effectiveness of DoFE On several unseen datasets and compare it with state-of-the-art methods. The results demonstrate that DoFE outperforms existing methods in terms of segmentation accuracy, especially when the target dataset is significantly different from the source dataset. We also perform a series of Ablation studies to analyze The contribution Of different components in DoFE, providing insights into the working mechanism of the proposed approach. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: * We propose a novel approach called Domain-oriented feature Embedding (DoFE) for generalizable Fundus image segmentation on unseen datasets. * DoFE learns a domain-invariant feature representation by incorporating domain-specific information into the feature embedding process. * DoFE outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several unseen datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in addressing the domain shift problem. * We provide a thorough analysis of the contribution of different Components in DoFE, offering insights into the working mechanism of The proposed approach. Overall, this paper makes an important contribution to the field of fundus image segmentation by introducing a novel approach That can effectively address the domain shift problem and improve segmentation performance on unseen datasets.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to segmenting images based on weak labels, called Points2Polygons. Our method uses adversarial networks to learn a context-based segmentation model that can accurately separate objects from their surroundings, even in cases where the object boundaries are not well-defined or there is significant background noise. Traditional image segmentation methods rely on hand-crafted features and heuristics, which often lead to suboptimal performance when dealing with complex scenes or low-quality data. Moreover, obtaining high-quality labels for training these models can be time-consuming and expensive. In contrast, our approach leverages recent advances in deep learning to learn a segments representation directly from the input data, without relying on manual feature engineering. The key insight behind Points2Polygons is to use adversarial training to learn a polygon-based representation of the image, where each polygon corresponds to a coherent region of the scene. This allows us to effectively capture object boundaries and handle irregularly shaped objects, while also propagating information across neighboring regions to produce more accurate segmentations. We evaluate Points2Polygons on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes, comparing it against state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms. We introduce $\textit{InExtremIS}$, a weakly supervised 3D approach to train a deep image segmentation network using particularly weak train-time annotations: only 6 extreme clicks at the boundary of the objects of interest. Our fully-automatic method is trained end-to-end and does not require any test-time annotations. From the extreme points, 1D bounding boxes are extracted around objects of interest. Then, deep geodesics connecting extreme points are generated to increase the amount of "annotated" voxels within the bounding boxes. Finally, a weakly supervised regularised loss derived from a Conditional Random Field formulation is used to encourage prediction consistency over homogeneous regions. Extensive experiments are performed on a large open dataset for Vestibular Schwannoma segmentation. $\textit{InExtremIS}$ obtained competitive performance, approaching full supervision and outperforming significantly other weakly supervised techniques based on bounding boxes. Moreover, given a fixed annotation time budget, $\textit{InExtremIS}$ outperforms full supervision. Our code and data are available online.

Segmenting images of low quality or with missing data is a challenging problem. Integrating statistical prior information about the shapes to be segmented Can improve the segmentation results significantly. Most shape-based segmentation algorithms optimize an energy functional And find a point Estimate for the object to be segmented. This does not provide a measure of the degree of confidence in that result, neither does it provide a picture of Other probable solutions based on the data and the priors. With a statistical view, addressing these issues would involve the problem of characterizing the posterior densities of the shapes of the objects to be segmented. For such characterization, we propose a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) Sampling-based image segmentation algorithm that uses statistical shape priors. In addition to better characterization of the Statistical structure of the problem, such an approach would also have the potential to address issues with getting stuck at local optima, suffered by existing shape-based segmentation methods. Our approach is able to characterize the posterior probability density in the space of shapes through its samples, and to return multiple solutions, potentially from different modes of a multimodal probability density, which would be encountered, E.g., in segmenting objects from multiple shape classes. We present promising results on a variety of data Sets. We also provide an extension for segmenting shapes of objects with parts that can go through independent shape Variations. This Extension involves the use of local shape priors on Object parts and provides robustness to limitations in shape training data size.

C. elegans has a higher number of Psis in its snRNAs compared to yeasts, but a lower number compared to snRNAs of sequenced vertebrates. The majority of modification positions found in C. elegans snRNAs match with modifications that exist in other species, when compared with other sequenced snRNAs. Nevertheless, C. elegans snRNAs have two distinctive positions that have been altered: position 28 on U2 snRNA and position 62 on U4 snRNA. The two adjustments are situated in parts of the snRNAs that connect with U6 snRNA, either inside the spliceosome or the U4U6 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particle (snRNP). It's possible that Psi's existence may enhance the molecular bonding between the snRNAs.

Abstract: Bayesian reasoning might be the appropriate method for evaluating uncertainty in hypotheses that depend on unknown underlying parameters, theta. One classical example is the probability of Bob winning an automobile if he makes three correct choices of doors in games such as Wheel of Fortune and Let’s Make a Deal. And it would seem natural to use the additional information that he receives each time he makes a decision to modify his belief about his winnings, such as the fact that if he picks door two, he will have only a 50% (the ‘statistical’) chance of picking the right door the next time, whereas picking either door one or two gives him a 75% chance. But what are these prior probabilities? Do they even make sense, given the structure of the games themselves? If they do, then what are their values and how do we determine them before a game begins, given all the possibilities, both the ones that are visible and those that are hidden behind closed doors, behind whose curtains all the egresses must be unlocked.

In this paper, we present CHASE (Robust Visual Tracking via Cell-Level Differentiable Neural Architecture Search), a novel approach to visual object tracking that leverages the power of differentiable neural architecture search (NAS) to optimize deep neural networks for robust tracking performance. Unlike traditional NAS methods that rely on coarse-grained searches over predefined architectures, CHASE performs cell-level differentiable search, allowing it to explore a vast space of possible network architectures and identify optimal designs tailored specifically to each target object. CHASE is built upon a recently proposed differentiable rendering engine, which enables efficient and accurate rendering of synthetic images that mimic real-world scenarios. By combining this capability with advanced optimization techniques and a carefully designed loss function, CHASE is able to learn high-performance trackers in an end-to-end manner, without requiring manual feature engineering or domain knowledge. Extensive experiments conducted on several challenging benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of CHASE compared to state-of-the-art tracking methods, including those that rely on handcrafted features or require elaborate postprocessing steps. Additionally, sensitivity analysis reveals that CHASE is highly robust to variations in input quality, pose, illumination, and occlusion, making it a promising solution for real-world applications where visual tracking systems must operate under diverse conditions. The main contributions of this work can be summarized as follows: * We introduce CHASE, a novel method for robotic visual tracking using cell-level differentiable neural architecture search. * CHASE conducts a comprehensive search over the space of possible network architectures, leading to optimized trackers tailored to individual objects. * Extensive evaluations show that CHASE outperforms existing state-of-the-art trackers while demonstrating impressive generalization capabilities across various scenarios. * Our study highlights the benefits of employing differentiable NAS in computer vision tasks, particularly in visual tracking applications. Overall, our research presents a significant breakthrough in the field of visual object tracking by harnessing the strengths of differentiable neural architecture search. This article discusses the application of the method of diophantine approximation to the study of translation surfaces and planar resonant sets. The authors use methods of number theory such as the theory of continued fractions and diophantine approximation to study the geometry and dynamics of these objects. The paper begins by presenting the basic definitions and properties of translation surfaces and planar resonant sets, and their importance in many areas of mathematics, such as dynamical systems, algebraic geometry, and number theory. The authors present a sequence of results on diophantine approximation of translation surfaces and planar resonant sets, including the approximation of geometric and dynamical properties, such as curvature and the behaviour of trajectories. The authors also study the relations between diophantine approximations and the properties of translation surfaces and planar resonant sets, and show how information about the former can be used to infer information about the latter. They demonstrate the power of their method by a large number of examples, including the study of periodic orbits and the calculation of Lyapunov exponents. The paper concludes by discussing the consequences of their results for the study of translation surfaces and planar resonant sets, and by indicating several problems and some possible directions for future research. The paper is an important contribution to the theory of dynamical systems and to number theory, and shows how the method of diophantine approximation can be used to study the geometry and dynamics of complex systems.

Multiple myeloma, a malignancy of plasma cells, can have significant impacts on kidney function due to various mechanisms such as proteinuria, light chain deposition disease, and renal impairment. In this study, we aimed to develop a mathematical model that captures the effects of multiple myeloma on kidney function and investigates the dynamics of disease progression. A compartmental model was developed, which comprises equations describing the kinetics of total immunoglobulin (IgG) and light chains in both intact and fragmented forms, as well as their deposition rates in the kidneys. The model also accounts for glomerular filtration rate (GFR), albuminuria, and proteinuria. We used parameter estimation techniques to estimate model parameters from patient data. The simulation results show good agreement with clinical observations, indicating that our model accurately represents the underlying biological processes. Our simulations reveal that increases in IgG and free light chain (FLC) levels lead to elevated proteinuria and worsening GFR, which further deteriorate renal function over time. The model also predicts that transient changes in FLC levels significantly influence long-term renal outcomes. Moreover, interventions that effectively reduce FLC levels are predicted to improve kidney function and slow disease progression. Our findings highlight the importance of targeting pathways that control FLC production and/or promote their clearance to mitigate the progression of kidney injury in patients with multiple myeloma. This model serves as a valuable tool for personalized medicine approaches, allowing physicians to simulate treatment strategies tailored to individual patients based on their unique characteristics, ultimately improving management and optimized care for those affected by multiple myeloma.

This paper presents a comparative study of statistical skin detection algorithms for sub-continental human images. The study evaluates the performance of three popular algorithms, namely, Otsu's method, Interactive Data Language (IDL), and K-means clustering. The algorithms were tested on a dataset of sub-continental human images, and the results were analyzed based on accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The study found that K-means clustering algorithm outperformed the other two algorithms in terms of accuracy and F1-score. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of the findings and future directions for research in skin detection algorithms for sub-continental human images.

Joint segmentations are well suited to extract information about objects from noisy data such as ultrasound images (1). Recent studies have shown that when object reconstruction performance reaches certain thresholds over multiple iterations then a hierarchical posterior probability model (HBPM) or more generally, a generalised Gaussian prior with multiple local maxeima can perform admirably in this task at lower cost than stochastic gradient descent, a well described approach at scale (2, 3). Although many optimisation models provide similar solutions, none of them has demonstrated good reconstructions at similar scales using sparse (not fully dense distributed layers) networks, which is currently a requirement for practical use beyond 1 ms resolution. Here we introduce an HBPM called HMMP which achieves high local inference sizes because it employs only one spatial kernel, thus eliminating the need of having a global kernel. We also extend our model so that the posterior distribution does indeed reflect the information contained within the image; i.e., hierarchical predictions may be generated using HMMP without any additional non-linearities required by previous works. With these three advantages, HMMP outperforms other algorithms at high-dimensional datasets with low noise, i.e., 2 μW/cm2 (6) to 1 pico W/cm2 and greater (~10 ppb, ) in an example experiment using 5 Hz high-resolution ultrasound signal and 16 mm depth plane geometry. These findings demonstrate for our initial test cases the feasibility and potential applications of extending the power and strength of HMMP via parallelization and increasing hyperparametre tuning space. Moreover, the success seen here allows us to further analyse the underlying causes for this scaling trade-off as well which will help develop methods to increase performance and reduce bandwidth.

Rock and Roll music is no longer an important part of the cultural conversation. This is obviously not to say that there is no longer rock music being made, that it is not enjoyed or appreciated by many people around the world, or that it does not still have a significant cultural impact in certain contexts. However, it is true that in recent years, other genres have taken center stage in popular culture and media, such as pop, hip hop, and electronic dance music. This shift can be attributed to various factors, such as changing tastes and preferences among younger generations, the increasing availability and accessibility of music from different parts of the world, and the rise of digital streaming platforms and social media. Nonetheless, rock and roll music will always have a place in music history and continue to inspire and influence future generations of musicians and music lovers.

We investigate relations between best selling artists in last decade on phonographic market and from perspective of listeners by using the Social Network Analyzes. Starting network is obtained from the matrix of correlations between the world's best selling artists by considering the synchronous time evolution of weekly record sales. This method reveals the structure of phonographic market, but we claim that it has no impact on people who see relationship between artists and music genres. We compare 'sale' (based on correlation of record sales) or 'popularity' (based on data mining of the record charts) networks with 'similarity' (obtained mainly from survey within music experts opinion) and find no significant relations. We postulate that non-laminar phenomena on this specific market introduce turbulence to how people view relations of artists.

Laboratory researchers, from ignorance or by design, often analyse their results before the final number of experimental units (humans, animals, tissues or cells) has been reached. If this is done in an uncontrolled fashion, the pejorative term 'peeking' has been applied. A statistical penalty must be exacted. This is because if enough interim analyses are conducted, and if the outcome of the trial is on the borderline between 'significant' and 'not significant', ultimately one of the analyses will result in the magical P 0.05. I suggest that Armitage's technique of matched-pairs sequential analysis should be considered. The conditions for using this technique are ideal: almost unlimited opportunity for matched pairing, and a short time between commencement of a study and its completion. Both the Type I and Type II error-rates are controlled. And the maximum number of pairs necessary to achieve an outcome, whether P 0.05 or P 0.05, can be estimated in advance.

In this work, we take an image data and use it with two deep neural connections (CNNs) in order to produce an unsupervised multidimensional discriminative feature decomposition that efficiently reflects features about the images. We exploit the dual architecture for picture segmentation which can perform on average ~2% more than existing multi-dimensional hierarchical deconvolutional algorithms because of its inability to handle non-uniform inputs and effectively capture features of sparsely sampled pictures. The obtained algorithm learns to quickly decode feature maps from different image data in parallel, thus enabling deep models to process small scale unsupervised data sets.

In recent years, deep neural networks have made unprecedented progress in computer vision and other areas with an abundance of labeled data. However, creating rich training labels remains costly or impossible on many interesting tasks due to complexity and subjectivity. An increasingly popular solution to this issue is to train network models by minimizing some distance metric between weak labeled observations (e.g., points) and segmented images as determined by human annotators instead of creating exact boundaries themselves [1]. This relaxation naturally allows for incorporating additional information, such as contextual relationships that help constrain image interpretation. In contrast, typical approaches using point ground truth often ignore the spatial relationship between supervised structures, which can lead to poor generalization. Thus, we propose Points2polygons, an adversarially trained ConvNet capable of jointly utilizing multiple complementary sources of labeling (i.e., both weak labels and dense polygon outlines obtained through manual boundary editing) simultaneously during adversarial training without any need to retrain our model when faced with new weak labels only for all applications. Points2polygons improves over state-of-the-art methods for semantic and instance segmentation from coarse (weak) and complete dense polygon labels by 5%-6%, consistently across various application domains. While our focus is primarily on improving performance using existing datasets containing dense annotations as unlabeled auxiliary ground truth, including our new ones specifically created for validation, our findings should also have important theoretical implications within the ongoing debate regarding the role of strong or weak labels in Deep Learning as well.

We introduce the notion of a positive opetope and positive opetopic cardinals as certain finite combinatorial structures. The positive opetopic cardinals to positive-to-one polygraphs are like simple graphs to free omega-categories over omega-graphs, c.f. [MZ]. In particular, they allow us to give an explicit combinatorial description of positive-to-one polygraphs. Using this description we show, among other things, that positive-to-one polygraphs form a presheaf category with the exponent category being the category of positive opetopes. We also show that the category of omega-categories is monadic over the category of positive-to-one polygraphs with the `free functor' being an inclusion.

RLCorrector: Reinforced Proofreading for Connectomics Image Segmentation Abstract: Connectomics, the study of the neural connections within the brain, relies heavily on accurate image segmentation to identify and trace neural fibers. However, current segmentation methods often produce errors, particularly in the presence of complex fiber crossings and other challenging features. To address this challenge, we propose RLCorrector, a novel reinforcement learning-based approach that leverages proofreading techniques to improve the accuracy of connectomics image segmentation. RLCorrector combines the strengths of deep learning-based segmentation methods with the accuracy and efficiency of proofreading techniques. Our approach consists of two main components: a segmentation model and a proofreader. The segmentation model generates an initial segmentation of the input image, which is then passed through the proofreader. The proofreader uses reinforcement learning to learn a policy that corrects errors in the segmentation, iteratively refining the output until an accurate segmentation is achieved. We evaluate RLCorrector on several benchmark datasets and compare its performance to state-of-the-art segmentation methods. Our results show that RLCorrector significantly improves upon existing methods, with an average accuracy increase of 15% across all datasets. We also demonstrate the versatility of our approach by applying it to various segmentation tasks, including fiber tract segmentation and synapse detection. Our work has important implications for the field of connectomics, as accurate image segmentation is crucial for understanding the structure and function of the brain. RLCorrector offers a promising solution for improving the accuracy and efficiency of connectomics image segmentation, and has the potential to enable new applications and insights in neuroscience research.

Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in the field of healthcare, with applications ranging from disease diagnosis to treatment planning. However, the complexity and variability of medical images make it challenging to develop accurate and robust segmentation models. In this paper, we propose a novel self-supervised clustering network for medical image segmentation. Our approach leverages spatial information to guide the clustering process, allowing the model to learn meaningful representations of the image data. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving state-of-the-art performance on various segmentation tasks. Our work provides a valuable contribution to the field of medical image segmentation, offering a new approach to tackle the challenges posed by this important problem.

This paper examines the network structure of the phonographic market and identifies characteristic similarities between musicians. By analyzing the collaboration patterns among musicians, we uncover the underlying structure of the market and reveal clusters of musicians with similer styles, genres, or influences. We use a dataset of musical collaborations to build a network representation of the market, where musicians are represented as nodes and collaborations are represented as edges between nodes. We then apply community detection algorithms to identify clusters of musicians with high collaboration density. Our results show that the phonographic market exhibits a hierarchical structure, with a few highly connected musicians acting as hubs and many peripheral musicians with fewer collaborations. We also find that musicians within the same cluster tend to have similer styles, genres, or influences, indicating that the market is organized around specific musical themes or trends. Additionally, we observe a strong correlation between the similarity of musicians' styles and their collaboration patterns, suggesting that musicians tend to collaborate with others who share their musical characteristics. Our findings have implications for the music industry, suggesting that musicians who collaborate with others in their cluster are more likely to acheive success and that the market is organized around specific musical themes or trends. The paper contributes to the understanding of the structure and dynamics of the phonographic market and provides insights into the factors that influence the success of musicians. Keywords: phonographic market, network structure, collaboration patterns, community detection, musicians' similarity.

In this paper, we present a novel result in the field of process calculi, specifically in context of the $\pi$-calculus. We prove that the $\pi$-calculus is both behaviourally complete and orbit-finitely executable. Behavioural completeness is property that ensures that any process calculus can simulate the behaviour of any other process calculus. This means that the $\pi$-calculus is capable of modelling and analysing the behaviour of wide range of systems, including those that are not directly representable in the calculus itself. Orbit-finiteness, on the other hand, is property that guarantees that calculus has finite number of possible orbit-equivalence classes, where two processes are considered to be in the same orbit if they have same observable behaviour. This property is important because it allows for efficient analysis and verification of processes, as it reduces the number of possible processes that need to be considered. The combination of behavioural completeness and orbit-finiteness makes $\pi$-calculus a powerful tool for analysis and verification of systems. It allows for the modelling and analysis of wide range of systems, while also providing finite and manageable number of possible processes to consider. Our proof of the behavioural completeness and orbit-finiteness of $\pi$-calculus is based on series of technical results and constructions, which we present in detail in paper. Our approach draws on a range of techniques from category theory, logic, and theoretical computer science, and provides a novel and insightful perspective on $\pi$-calculus and its properties. Overall, our results demonstrate the versatility and expressive power of $\pi$-calculus, and provide a solid foundation for its use in wide range of applications, including the analysis and verification of distributed systems, programming languages, and other systems with complex behaviour.

This article examines coarse to fine lifting and is given as an example of an optimization paradigm that can be applied using computational graph theory (CGT). The technique was trained using a data set composed predominantly of images taken at high spatial frequency. The image resolution was increased progressively by adding more pixels and iteratively selecting best parameters. By contrast, most similar techniques in neural processing were developed using relatively low values of the input parameters and are less suitable for use on such large scales. Instead, this approach works with lower magnification, but not smaller ones. It uses two general methods. A first one allows choosing a small value of loss function that leads to accurate extraction with same level as before the search. Second it focuses only on parameter search while not including feature selection stage that occurs after set image has been processed. In both cases, we used two different datasets provided by Kaggle competition, image dataset of real objects (with maximum number of frames) and a 3D mesh created by a multirotor copter (40000 vertices). Here we present detailed results and explain how these models could contribute to improvements towards highly efficient algorithms.

Sir Vivian Richards believes Anderson is a worthy heir to Sir Ian Botham (pictured in August 2014) As one of the greatest batsmen to have lived and a long-time friend of Botham, Richards is well placed to judge the scale of Anderson's achievements and his endorsement is ringing. To address these issues, we propose a novel approach called CHASE (Cell-level differentiable Neural architecture SEarch) to robust visual tracking. Our method first adopts a multi-object tracking framework that uses a cellular neural network encoder to extract features of objects at both local and global levels, followed by a decoder that generates bounding boxes, distances, and directions of all visible objects from previous frames. We then incorporate differentiable neural architecture search, enabling our system to learn an optimized network structure that improves overall tracking performance on synthetic and real-world datasets. Experiments show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmark datasets in terms of precision and stability, demonstrating the value of our proposed optimization algorithm in improving robustness during tracking.

Arthritis is inflammation of the joints. Arthritis comes in well over 100 different forms, from genetic disorders, to viral infections, to the result of physical trauma. Anyone at any age can be diagnosed with arthritis, it's not just an "old person" disease. Some forms of arthritis is directly responsible for bone and joint degeneration, like osteoarthritis, some degeneration happens from trauma and arthritis is a side effect, and other forms are degenerative because cronic inflammation is itself damaging. I don't know if all forms are bone and joint degenerative, but it's the only way I understand how arthritis gets worse. Just because you have a genetic marker for arthritis doesn't mean that you actually have arthritis. Talk to your doctor and don't let him go until you are satisfied. I don't know if they can even positively identify arthritis this early, depending on which variation you may or may not have. That genetic marker may be all the sign you'll get. Ask your doctor and google a bit about how to minimize developing arthritis.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for weakly supervised image segmentation using inter-extreme points geodesics. Our method leverages the geometric properties of inter-extreme points to learn a mapping between the input image and a set of labelled images. We use this mapping to generate segmentation masks for the input image without requiring any explicit supervision. Our approach is based on the idea of using geodesics to find the shortest path between two points in a manifold. We extend this idea to the context of image segmentation by defining a manifold of labelled images and finding the shortest path between the input image and a set of labelled images. We use this path to generate a segmentation mask for the input image. Our approach is weakly supervised, meaning that we only require a small number of labelled images to generate accurate segmentation masks. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and speed.

There has been growing interest and research work on active contour models which are also called snakes, since 1987 when they were proposed by Kass, Weinberg & Terzopoulos with subsequent extensions to their formulation such as Level set method (OSVMT) introduced by Osher et al.. Though snakes could be very effective in segmenting some images like human lung images, they may perform poorly or even fail if the initial position fails due to improper initialization on the image(s). In this study we propose an energy-based approach that addresses the snake model's drawbacks of poor convergence near boundaries, improves its robustness to noise and reduces computational complexity through use of gradient information available both in a neighborhood region around the curve itself and image domain respectively at each iteration. To improve upon OSVMT , we derive an analytic solution using first derivatives rather than an evolutionary partial differential equation; while still retaining nonlinear interpolation features inherent in level sets. Further, our new implementation significantly reduces computation time and memory requirement over existing ones while ensuring reasonable accuracy and flexibility over complex structures without any loss of generality.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to weakly supervised segmentation called Inter Extreem Points Geodesics (IEPG). This method leverages the concept of extreem points, which are points in the image that have the highest similarity to the boundary of the object of interest, and geodesic distances, which provide a metric for comparing the similarity between pixels. The IEPG algorithm consists of two main steps: 1) extracting extreem points from the image using a modified Canny edge detector, and 2) computing the geodesic distance matrix between all pairs of extreem points. The resulting matrix is then used to construct a graph, where each node represents an extreem point and edges connect points with similer geodesic distances. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes. Our experiments show that IEPG outperforms traditional weakly supervised segmentation methods, such as random walker and GCUT, in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the impact of different parameters on the performance of IEPG, providing insights into how to optimize its use in practice. Our work has important implications for applications where obtaining large amounts of annotated data is difficult or expensive, such as medical imaging or satellite imagery. By leveraging weak annotations, IEPG enables accurate segmentation without requiring a large amount of manual annotation effort.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for simultaneous traffic sign detection and boundary estimation using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Existing methods often treat these tasks as separate processes, first detecting signs and then estimating their boundaries. Our proposed method combines both tasks into a single stage, improving efficiency and accuracy. We propose a CNN architecture that incorporates spatial pyramid pooling to extract multi-scale contextual information and effectively capture diverse sign sizes and orientations. Moreover, we introduce an innovative boundary prediction module that refines the estimated bounding box coordinates by predicting the distance from the sign's center to its edges. This enables accurate boundary estimation even in cases where the sign is partially occluded or has similar appearance to the background. Our approach was evaluated on several publicly available datasets, including synthetic and real-world images with various lighting conditions, weather conditions, and scenarios. The results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in terms of detection accuracy and boundary precision. Specifically, it achieves an Intersection over Union (IoU) score of 0.8461 on the German Traffic Sign dataset, which represents a significant improvement over previous approaches. The contributions of this work can be summarized as follows: * A single-stage framework for simultaneous traffic sign detection and boundary estimation using CNNs * An efficient architecture combining spatial pyramid pooling and a boundary prediction module * State-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness and robustness of our method This research has important implications for applications such as autonomous driving, intelligent transportation systems, and traffic violation monitoring. By accurately detecting and delineating traffic signs in real-time, our approach can enhance road safety and improve driver experience.
