Italian Coast Guard Rescues 8,480 Migrants in Four Days The Italian Coast Guard reports that they have successfully rescued 8,480 migrants attempting to travel from North Africa to Italy between Friday and Monday. This report comes as the authorities continue to search for the bodies of a reported 400 people missing after their vessel sunk off the Libyan coast, as claimed by international charity organisation, Save the Children. However, the coast guard cannot confirm these reports. On Tuesday, 144 survivors were taken to Reggio Calabria, Italy, from where Save the Children heard reports of the latest tragedy to occur on one of the most perilous migration routes in the world. The boat allegedly went down 24 hours before the group of survivors had been picked up close to a large submerged rubber boat that had reportedly capsized in the waters south of Italy. Italian Coast Guard spokesman, Cosimo Nicastro said that the Coast Guard has not yet found the missing boat, and declined to comment on any further details of the report. In the past month alone, about 6,000 people have been rescued, with a number of boats having capsized. The partial dismantling last year of the EU's naval operation was blamed for failing to prevent a rush of migrant vessels and subsequently being unable to save hundreds of lives from the deadly crossing from North Africa. According to the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the number of migrants who have arrived in Italy and Greece this far into 2016 is already 80 higher than the same period in 2015. If the reports regarding the lost boat are confirmed, theIOM will be forced to increase this year's death toll to over 1,600, continuing the situation we have seen in previous years, with warmer weather leading to a significant increase in the dangers of shipwreck for thousands of migrants trying to reach Europe. The Italian Coast Guard reiterated the necessity of the current rescue services. It explained that a vast number of the migrants traveling from Libya are illegally transported on "sub-register" or aging vessels, which are unsuitable for any kind of voyage, much less one that requires them to travel the choppy, high risk waters of the Mediterranean.

In 2016, an approach employing a morphological feature representation based on dilations was proposed to significantly improve semantic segmentation performance over state-of-theart deep learning architectures and datasets on 2D medical images (Koohpayeh, K., O'Doherty M., Dhanesh S & Bovis F., 2017a). In this article we extend this previous work by proposing new combinations of dilation operations in morphologically structured units that further boost both classification accuracy at the pixel level, whilst reducing run-time requirements so as to enable real-time processing speeds. We assess these blocks against those used previously through their suitability and benefits when applied to 3D MRI brain tumour volumetric images and propose an optimized set of morphological operation blocks along with their associated hyperparameter settings. We validate our findings through an experimental comparison of results using a series of deep-learning architecture models including VGGNet (V/X), Darknet55, GoogLeNet, ResNet 34, VoxSegCNN and the original multi-class network MCN++ which incorporates our previous dilating block approach. Our experiments are conducted across popular healthcare image benchmark collections from BraTS 2018.

Blackpool, UK - Controversial striker Nile Ranger has been absent without leave (AWOL) from Blackpool Football Club since early December. Fans and club management alike are growing increasingly concerned about the mysterious disappearance of the former Newcastle forward who last played for the Seasiders at the end of November. It's not the first time that Ranger has been involved in off-field issues. In 2013, he was arrested for assault and later in 2014, he faced a rape charge which was eventually dropped. The 28-year-old forward's contract with the League One team is set to expire at the end of this season, adding to the club's growing list of impending departures. Ranger, who originated from London, began his football career with Southampton before moving on to play for the likes of Newcastle United, Barnsley, and Swindon Town. After several loan spells, he joined Blackpool in 2017 and made a promising start, scoring his first goal for the club in a 3-1 win over Charlton Athletic. However, his career at Blackpool took a turn for the worse when he found himself on the wrong side of the club's management. Ranger accused Blackpool officials of mocking him and undermining his efforts to contribute to the team's performance on the field. Despite the player's claims, Blackpool has made it clear that they've always been supportive of Ranger. Club officials have been quoted as saying, "We gave Nile and his two representatives full access to our club's facilities and have worked closely with him to rehabilitate his troubled past." While there are no indications of Ranger's potential next move, his actions have left Blackpool in a difficult position. With upcoming crucial matches in the coming months, the team must now find a way to make up for the missing leadership and firepower of their AWOL forward. As Nile Ranger's departure from Blackpool seems imminent with the expiration of his contract, fans and authorities are left to wonder what could have been, had he been able to overcome the obstacles that have plagued his intriguing football career.

As far as we know, this is the initial account of bacteria-caused meningitis related to a malformed stapes footplate in a young patient with an auditory brainstem implant. Individuals who have abnormalities in their inner ear, particularly those with Mondini's dysplasia, require thorough assessment before any surgical procedures to mitigate or eradicate any structural factors that may increase the risk of meningitis. We suggest conducting a radiological examination before the operation for children who have an auditory brainstem implant and suspected ear malformation to check for the indication known as the "bulging oval window." If radiological indications suggest the presence of anatomical stapes footplate defects, which can increase the risk of bacterial meningitis, then it is recommended to conduct a comprehensive examination of both ears through bilateral exploratory tympanotomy.

This research proposes development of a novel deep learning approach called DoDNet, which can effectively segment multi-organ and tumors from multiple partially labeled datasets. The proposed solution leverages transfer learning techniques to utilize pre-existing models and incorporate new data into training sessions without requiring extensive manual labeling. It then uses ensemble methods for combining multiple learned algorithms such that their strengths are realized while minimizing their weaknesses as much as possible. Experiments conducted have shown promising results, indicating DoDNet's capability to accurately and generically segment not only organs but also tumors across different subjects, providing an alternative means for handling high dimensional and complex medical image analysis tasks. Introduction Artificial Intelligence (AI) has gained significant importance and acceptance in different sectors including healthcare, which is considered as one of its potential breakthrough grounds. Mapping vulnerable populations can help identify groups at particular risks for disease outbreaks or severe health conditions. This study’s primary goal was to develop an AI-based mapping system focused on identifying global vulnerable populations. Methods We developed a machine learning model adopting a novel deep neural network architecture to map world population vulnerability. Our dataset consisted of multiple indicators such as life expectancy, poverty rate, access to healthcare, environmental factors, climate change impacts, education level, and others. We used a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques to improve the accuracy of our results. Results Our findings show that vulnerable populations are distributed across globe with high concentrations in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. The most critical vulnerability factors are poverty, low healthcare access, short life expectancy, and lack of educational opportunities. Climate change impacts also play a vital role in increasing vulnerability levels in specific regions. Our proposed AI-based mapping approach provides governments and healthcare organizations with valuable insights to proactively plan targeted interventions and allocate resources effectively. Conclusion This research presents a significant step towards building dynamic, intelligent systems capable of supporting policymaking in public health by providing real-time maps and actionable insights about global vulnerable populations. With the continuously evolving technology landscape, AI holds immense potential in transforming how we understand, monitor, and address global health issues.

This paper presents a theoretical study of the optical conductivity of the first and second longitudinal modes of a single layer of MoS2. A broad range of temperatures and frequencies was studied, and it was found that the longitudinal optical conductivity shows a peak at the neutrality point, and the spin Hall optical conductivity is non-monotonic as a function of frequency. These results provide insight into the optical properties of MoS2 and are of potential importance to its use in photonics and optoelectronics.

This paper presents novel approach for solving large-scale binary quadratic optimization problems using semidefinite relaxation. The proposed method leverages recent advances in convex optimization techniques to efficiently solve instances of this problem that were previously intractable. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through numerical experiments on various benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in terms of computational efficiency and solution quality. Additionally, we explore applications of our technique in diverse fields such as machine learning, computer vision, and control systems. Specifically, we apply our method to problems including maximum cut, graph partitioning, and robust PCA, achieving superior results compared to existing approaches. Our work provides powerful tool for tackling complex optimization problems and demonstrates the potential of semidefinite relaxation techniques for solving large-scale binary quadratic programs.

Once upon a time, there was a place called "The Screaming Fun House." It was a carnival that had been abandoned for years, but it was said that the screams of its patrons could still be heard echoing through the abandoned rides and attractions. Despite the rumors, a group of friends decided to explore the old carnival one night. As soon as they stepped inside, they were greeted by a chilling and constant scream that seemed to come from all around them. They walked down the rows of rusted and broken-down rides, but as they got closer to the center of the carnival, the screams grew louder and more frequent. It wasn't long before the group found themselves in the middle of a large, open area filled with clown statues and carnival games. The screams became deafening. Suddenly, the clowns began to move, their wide grins seeming to follow the group as they moved around the area. The group tried to leave, but the carnival appeared to be alive, trapping them inside. Every game they tried to play seemed rigged, and the screams continued to grow louder and more disturbing. As the night went on, the group began to feel like they were losing their minds. Finally, after hours of enduring the screams and carnival attractions, the group managed to escape the Screaming Fun House. They never spoke of their experience again, and the carnival remained abandoned, warning others of the nightmare that lurked inside its gates. From that day on, people would hear screams coming from the carnival that never seemed to stop. Despite the screams, people still flocked to the abandoned carnival, as if drawn by a mysterious and otherworldly force. For those brave enough to enter the Screaming Fun House, the fun never ended, but the screams would haunt them for the rest of their lives.

This paper proposes a novel deep learning approach for earth image segmentation using imperfect polyline labels with annotation errors. Existing methods rely on precise labelling of object boundaries, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain. In contrast, our method leverages freely available satellite imagery and utilises imperfect polygonal labels, which are more readily accessible but contain various types of annotation errors. We introduce an algorithm that integrates a deep neural network with a robust label fusion strategy to effectively handle various types of annotation errors, including missing labels, redundant labels, and noisy labels. The proposed method consists of two stages: (1) initial segmentation using a fully convolutional network (FCN), and (2) refinement of the segmentation results using a Graph-based Local Binary Pattern (GLBP) philtre. We evaluate our method using several datasets with different levels of annotation accuracy and demonstrate its superiority compared to traditional machine learning approaches. Our key contributions include: (1) a novel deep learning architecture for earth image segmentation that tolerates imperfect polygon labels with annotation errors; (2) an efficient label fusion strategy to integrate multiple kinds of annotations and mitigate their corresponding errors; (3) extensive experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of our method in various scenarios. The main findings indicate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance under realistic settings where perfect labels are unavailable. Specifically, it outperforms traditional machine learning models by 5%–15% in terms of overall segmentation accuracy when dealing with imperfect polygon labels. Moreover, we analyse the impact of individual annotation errors on the segmentation outcome, providing insights into the reliability of crowd-sourced data. This research has significant implications for large-scale land cover classification tasks, particularly in areas where high-quality annotated data is scarce or difficult to obtain. Our approach enables the use of low-cost, large-scale satellite imagery for land cover mapping, advancing the feasibility of accurate earth image segmentation in many applications.

The stability of topological properties of bismuth (111) bilayer is a topic of interest in the field of condensed matter mechanics. In this paper, we investigate the instability of the topological insulator state in bismuth (111) bilayer using density functional theory and first-principles measurements. We find that the topological insulator state is unstable in the absence of a large quantity of doping with lighter components such as lead or zinc. We therefore investigate the impact of stress on the strength of the topological insulator state and find that it is unstable under a broad variety of strain conditions. Our findings provide insight into the potential for bismuth (111) bilayer to be employed as a topological insulator material for practical applications.

But it is incompatible with certain of the methods of artificial intelligence that the transfer of knowledge between networks is either of the simplest or of the most complicated nature. The normal methods of transfer learning, for instance, have been employed for transferring the knowledge of one network to another of the same architecture. Another method, that of distillation, allows knowledge to be transferred from one type of network to another, but has often required access to the original training data, or the presence of additional generative networks. In view of these drawbacks, it is desirable to have an improved transfer method which is insensitive to the choice of network architecture and independent of the availability of the original training data. The knowledge transfer approach we propose here involves learning the student network on a separate transfer learning dataset, annotated by the teacher network. The experiments were conducted on five networks for semantic segmentation, on seven datasets and three different imaging modalities. The experiments also involved learning with a single teacher, learning with a single teacher and fine-tuning, and learning with a plurality of teachers. Using a single teacher gave results similar to those of the teacher, while learning with multiple teachers yielded results which were better than the teachers. The salient features of the proposed method are: (1) the elimination of the need for the original training data or generative models, (2) the transfer of knowledge between different network architectures, (3) the ease of implementing the method for downstream tasks by using the data of the task as the transfer learning data, and (4) the use of an ensemble of independently trained teachers for learning the student. Extensive experiments have demonstrated that the proposed method is effective for knowledge transfer, and is easy to tune.

In this paper, we propose a novel deep convolutional neural network (CNN) -based algorithm for solving ill-posed inverse problems. Regularized iterative algorithms have emerged as the standard approach to ill-posed inverse problems in the past few decades. These methods produce excellent results, but can be challenging to deploy in practice due to factors including the high computational cost of the forward and adjoint operators and the difficulty of hyper parameter selection. The starting point of our work is the observation that unrolled iterative methods have the form of a CNN (filtering followed by point-wise non-linearity) when the normal operator (H H, the adjoint of H times H) of the forward model is a convolution. Based on this observation, we propose using direct inversion followed by a CNN to solve normal-convolutional inverse problems. The direct inversion encapsulates the physical model of the system, but leads to artifacts when the problem is ill-posed; the CNN combines multiresolution decomposition and residual learning in order to learn to remove these artifacts while preserving image structure. We demonstrate the performance of the proposed network in sparse-view reconstruction (down to 50 views) on parallel beam X-ray computed tomography in synthetic phantoms as well as in real experimental sinograms. The proposed network outperforms total variation-regularized iterative reconstruction for the more realistic phantoms and requires less than a second to reconstruct a x 512 512 image on the GPU.

Specifically, in the proposed method, an segmenting active contour is constrained to converge To a configuration at which its geometric parameters attain their Empirical probability densities closely matching the corresponding model densities that are Learned based on training samples. It is shown through numerical experiments that the proposed shape modeling can be regarded as "weak" in the sense that it minimally influences the segmentation, which is allowed to be dominated by data-related forces. On the other hand, the priors provide sufficient constraints to Regularize the convergence of segmentation, while requiring substantially smaller training sets to yield less biased results as compared to the case of PCA-based regularization methods. The main advantages Of the proposed technique over Some existing alternatives is demonstrated in a series of experiments.

Performing inference in graphs is a common task within several machine learning problems, e.g., image segmentation, community detection, among others. For a given undirected connected graph, we tackle the statistical problem of exactly recovering an unknown ground-truth binary labeling of the nodes from a single corrupted observation of each edge. Such problem can be formulated as a quadratic combinatorial optimization problem over the boolean hypercube, where it has been shown before that one can (with high probability and in polynomial time) exactly recover the ground-truth labeling of graphs that have an isoperimetric number that grows with respect to the number of nodes (e.g., complete graphs, regular expanders). In this work, we apply a powerful hierarchy of relaxations, known as the sum-of-squares (SoS) hierarchy, to the combinatorial problem. Motivated by empirical evidence on the improvement in exact recoverability, we center our attention on the degree-4 SoS relaxation and set out to understand the origin of such improvement from a graph theoretical perspective. We show that the solution of the dual of the relaxed problem is related to finding edge weights of the Johnson and Kneser graphs, where the weights fulfill the SoS constraints and intuitively allow the input graph to increase its algebraic connectivity. Finally, as byproduct of our analysis, we derive a novel Cheeger-type lower bound for the algebraic connectivity of graphs with signed edge weights.

The idea, which centers around a gas being accidentally let out and causing people to laugh uncontrollably, had a lot of potential for creating comedic situations. The presence of Steve Carell and Melissa McCarthy heading a group of talented comic actors gave me high hopes for some huge laughter. Nevertheless, the comedy failed to amuse mainly because of the poorly developed storyline and characters that seemed exaggerated. The script provided minimal material, and the humorous moments seemed reused from superior comedic works from previous times. Despite the cliche and unimaginative material, the actors made an effort to deliver their best performance as the movie clumsily transitioned from one comical scene to the next. Regrettably, their skill was unable to make up for the evident flaws in the screenplay, resulting in their work being exhausted and monotonous. The supporting cast, namely Kate McKinnon and Ken Jeong, provided some truly funny moments that were the only saving grace of the otherwise mediocre movie. Their personalities were more eccentric and provided an essential liveliness that was missing from the rest of the movie. However, in the end, the presence of those actors couldn't rescue 'Laughing Gas' from its complete absence of humor. To summarize, 'Laughing Gas' was a letdown within the realm of comedic works. Don't waste your time and money on this unfunny comedy.

The Lagrangians and Hamiltonians of classical field theory require to comprise gauge fields in order to be form-invariant under local gauge transformations. These gauge fields have turned out to correctly describe pertaining elementary particle interactions. In this paper, this principle is extended to require additionly the form-invariance of classical field theory Hamiltonian under variations of the space-time curvature emerging from the gauge fields. This approach is devised on basis of the extended canonical transformation formalism of classical field theory which allows for transformations of space-time metric in addition to transformations of the fields. Working out the Hamiltonian that is form-invariant under extended local gauge transformations, we can dismiss conventional requirement for gauge bosons to be massless in order for them to preserve the local gauge invariance.The emerging equation of motion for the curvature scalar turns out to be compatible with the Einstein equation in case of a static gauge field. The emerging equation of motion for curvature scalar R turns out to be compatible with that from Proca system in case of a static gauge field.

Abstract Using light detection and ranging (LIDAR) in combination with classification algorithms, we propose to design an algorithm capable of recognising blood cell types using LIDAR and automatically classifying each type as either G5/N6 or D40/U9. In our system, LIDAR uses multiple lasers that are directed at cells, each laser acting like an individual binocular stereo lens, thus enabling localization without any information loss associated with large amounts of data; the intensity, spatial resolution and temporal frame rate needed are determined by the size of the sample bin (as well as the sensitivity required), and can be tweaked accordingly. In order to achieve both accurate identification and quick classification on very small samples, this image classifier uses adaptive thresholding, which applies a fixed bias parametre to the intensity gradient during training. The end result is a robust method capable of working off real-time imagery collected within several milliseconds even when detecting objects within a fraction of a second of being presented by other methods simultaneously. We show that automated processing of images has many implications beyond its applications in diagnosing diseases. For instance, it could lead to efficient search engines targeting high dimensional regions in biomedical litreature where no human annotators have spent time and effort finding annotations (see 'Data mining'). It might also open the gate for future vision sensor systems offering a similar level of visual performance based on simple yet clever computer vision algorithms [such as in the case of eye tracking in medical scanning]. The main limitations of our method are not related in particular to its application in humans but rather due to insufficient preprocessing/classification speed, making certain tasks computationally feasible in principle only if they occur quickly while minimising false positives. This limits our potential to aid in the clinical diagnosis of blood disorders while avoiding false positive rates, especially because an algorithm must always be able to detect abnormal cells, which may take up to several seconds for G5s, 5–15s for N6s and >20s for WBCs. The proposed framework is trained in an end-to-end manner and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the referring segmentation benchmark. Exact inference in graphs is a crucial problem in many areas of computer science and statistics. in This paper, we present a thorough view of exact inference in graphs from the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy. We first introduce the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy, which is a powerful tool for exact inference in graphs. We then show How to use this hierarchy to solve a Wide range of exact inference problems in graphs, including clique detection, minimum cut, and maximum flow. We also discuss some of the limitations of the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy and propose some possible extensions. Overall, our paper provides a comprehensive overview of exact inference in Graphs from the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy And demonstrates its effectiveness in solving a variety of problems.

The conventional approach to real-time semantic segmentation has been focused on designing lightweight architectures with reduced complexity. However, recent studies have shown that exploiting spatial and channel dependencies can result in improved accuracy without significant increases in computational cost. This study proposes a novel revision of Bilateral Spatial Pyramid Pooling (BiSeNet) architecture by incorporating dual path refinements along both horizontal and vertical directions through dense connections, thereby enhancing feature extraction capabilities at multiple scales. Extensive experiments were conducted using CAMVID, Cityscapes, and COCO datasets which demonstrated superior performance when compared to state-of-the-art models while maintaining competitive inference times. The proposed model achieves an impressive tradeoff between accuracy and speed making it suitable for various applications such as autonneomous driving or robotics where real-time processing is essential. Overall, this work provides new insights into network design strategies for efficient yet accurate semantic segmentation tasks.

This paper extends the problem of 2-dimensional palindrome search into the area of approximate matching. Using the Hamming distance as the measure, we search for 2D palindromes that allow up to k mismatches. We consider two different definitions of 2D palindromes and describe efficient algorithms for both of them. The first definition implies a square, while the second definition (also known as a centrosymmetric factor), can be any rectangular shape. Given a text of size x n m, the time complexity of the first algorithm is O (n m (log m log n k and for the second algorithm it is O (n m (log m k) o c c) where o c c is the size of the output.

"This paper investigates the influence on learning mechanisms of crowd-based environments, in which large numbers of people interact over an extended period with common challenges at common points within these communities. We show that a large number of individuals will be exposed to a limited set of salient features, and this group structure can have a significant effect on their capacity for learning. We provide evidence that the influence of the social environment on learning in general, not just MOOC related learning, derives from both diffusion (spread) effects and structural constraints on the formation of knowledge. The effects were evident across a wide range of tasks including reading comprehension, knowledge integration exercises and multiple choice question types."

> We present a quantum phase-space representation for curved configuration spaces. The representation is based on the quantum phase-space representation for the Euclidean space, which is a generalisation of the Weyl-Wigner representation. The representation is constructed by using the quantum phase-space representation for the Euclidean space and the quantum phase-space representation for the tangent space. The representation is applied to the quantum mechanics on curved configuration spaces. The representation is also applied to the quantum mechanics on the curved configuration space of a particle in a magnetic field. The paper is available here.

We present a local routing algorithm which guarantees delivery in all connected graphs embedded on a known surface of genus g. The algorithm transports O (g log n) memory and finishes in time O (g 2 n 2), where n is the size of the graph. It requires access to a homology basis for the surface. This algorithm, GFR, may be viewed as a suitable generalization of Face Routing (FR), the well-known algorithm for plane graphs, which we previously showed does not guarantee delivery in graphs embedded on positive genus surfaces. The problem for such surfaces is the potential presence of homologically non-trivial closed walks which may be traversed by the right-hand rule. We use an interesting mathematical property of homology bases (proven in Lemma) to show that such walks will not impede GFR. FR is at the base of most routing algorithms used in modern (2D) ad hoc networks: these algorithms all involve additional local techniques to deal with edge-crossings so FR may be applied. GFR should be viewed in the same light, as a base algorithm which could for example be tailored to sensor networks on surfaces in 3D. Currently there are no known efficient local, logarithmic memory algorithms for 3D ad hoc networks. From a theoretical point of view our work suggests that the efficiency advantages from which FR benefits are related to the codimension one nature of an embedded graph in a surface rather than the flatness of that surface (planarity).

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to medical image segmentation using a spatial guided self-supervised clustering network (SG-SCN). The SG-SCN model combines the strengths of self-supervised learning and spatial guidance to improve the accuracy and efficiency of medical image segmentation. Self-supervised learning has emerged as a promising approach to medical image segmentation, as it can learn useful features from unlabelled data. However, self-supervised learning methods often suffer from the problem of trivial solutions, where the model learns irrelevant or redundant features that do not generalize well to new data. Spatial guidance, which incorporates prior knowledge about the spatial structure of the data, has been shown to improve the performance of self-supervised learning models. The SG-SCN model proposed in this paper combines self-supervised learning with spatial guidance to overcome the limitations of traditional self-supervised learning methods. The model consists of a spatial guidance module that incorporates prior knowledge about the spatial structure of the data, and a self-supervised clustering module that learns to cluster the data into meaningful segments. The spatial guidance module is designed to provide the self-supervised clustering module with spatial information, such as the location and size of organs or tissues, which helps the model to learn more accurate and meaningful features. We evaluate the performance of the SG-SCN model on several publicly available medical image datasets, including brain MRI, lung CT, and liver CT. He thought it was just his imagination playing tricks on him but then he noticed that the sounds seemed to follow him wherever he went in the house. He quickly closed the door and ran upstairs, never wanting to go back down there again. He called an exterminator the next day and they took care of the problem. After that, he could finally relax in his new home without having to worry about any more unpleasant noises.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to medical image segmentation using a spatial guided self-supervised clustering network (SGSCN). Our method leverages the inherent spatial structure in medical images to learn clustering representations without the need for annotated data. The SGSCN model consists of a convolutional neural network (CNN) followed by a spatially-aware clustering module. The CNN encodes the input image into a set of feature maps, which are then used to compute a spatial similarity graph. The spatially- aware clustering module partitions the graph into distinct clusters, where each cluster corresponds to a specific class label. We evaluate our method on several publicly available medical imaging datasets, including MRI brain scans and CT lung scans. Experimental results show that SGSCN outperforms traditional supervised learning approaches, as well as state-of-the art self-supervised methods, in terms of segmentation accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in scenarios where annotations are limited or difficult to obtain. CGSCN has important implications for medical image analysis tasks, particularly in situations where annotated data is scarce or challenging to obtain. Our approach provides a robust and efficient way to segment medical images without relying on manual annotation effort. This can potentially accelerate the development of AI solutions for various medical applications, such as disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for quantifying segmentation uncertainty in dense multi-label CRFs, titled Perturb-and-MPM. Dense multi-label CRFs are widely used in image segmentation tasks, as they can model complex relationships between image pixels and multiple labels. However, the uncertainty in the segmentation process has been largely overlooked, which is crucial for building trustworthy models and improving their performance. Existing methods for quantifying segmentation uncertainty in CRFs are limited, and they often rely on approximations or heuristics. In contrast, our approach uses a principled method to compute the uncertainty in the segmentation process. We introduce a perturbation-based framework that generates a set of possible segmentations, and then use a Monte Carlo dropout technique to estimate the uncertainty of each segmentation. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and compare it with state-of-the-art methods. Our results show that Perturb-and-MPM outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in providing meaningful uncertainty estimates, which can be used for tasks such as active learning and anomaly detection. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: * We propose a novel approach for quantifying segmentation uncertainty in dense multi-label CRFs, which is based on a perturbation-based framework and Monte Carlo dropout. * We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. * We show that our approach provides meaningful uncertainty estimates, which can be used for tasks such as active learning and anomaly detection. Overall, our work fills a significant gap in the field of image segmentation, and provides a new tool for building trustworthy models that can handle complex relationships between image pixels and multiple labels.

Recent progress in biomedical image segmentation based on deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has drawn much attention. However, its vulnerability towards adversarial samples cannot be overlooked. This paper is the first one that discovers that all CNN-based state-of-the-art biomedical image segmentation models are sensitive to adversarial perturbations. This limits the deployment of these methods in safety-critical biomedical fields. In this paper, we discover that global spatial dependencies and global contextual information in biomedical image can be exploited to defend against adversarial attacks. To this end, non-local context encoder (NLCE) is proposed to model short- and long range spatial dependencies and encode global contexts for strengthening feature activations by channel-wise attention. The NLCE modules enhance robustness and accuracy of the non-local context encoding network (NLCEN), which learns robust enhanced pyramid feature representations with NLCE modules, and then integrates the information across different levels. Experiments on both lung and skin lesion segmentation datasets have demonstrated that NLCEN outperforms any other state-of-the-art biomedical image segmentation methods against adversarial attacks. In addition, NLCE modules can be applied to improve the robustness of other CNN-based biomedical image segmentation methods.

The graph theory literature has seen tremendous growth, And exact inference techniques have been a major focus. However, recent research shows that previous approaches suffer from significant limitations when applied to graphs with degree 4 or more vertices as their number increases rapidly while still maintaining a feasible graph structure. To address this issue, we propose an efficient approach based on The degree-4 sum of squares hierarchy (DSSH), which efficiently generates lower bounds for exact solutions to problems over these graphs. Our proposed method involves representing each vertex node using Its Degree vector, so that A solution can be considered a Valid assignment if it satisfies the DSSH constraints. We then develop algorithms based on dynamic programming to generate such assignments systematically, starting with small subproblems containing fewer nodes and iterating towards larger ones. Our results show improvements in efficiency of order O(N log N) compared to previous methods With the same level of accuracy. Furthermore, our work contributes significantly towards understanding the structure of degree-4 graphs using mathematical analysis and theoretical insights, paving the way for future development of efficient exact inference techniques specifically tailored to meet these needs. Overall, our findings offer new avenues for research and The potential For significant advancements in applying Combinatorial optimization techniques to real-world scenarios involving complex Networks. In summary, this paper presents an innovative approach to exact inference in graphs using the degree-4 sum of squares hierarchy, resulting in improved efficiency and Better understanding of the underlying graph structures.

The proposed method utilizes deep learning techniques and combines both fully supervised and weakly supervised approaches, enabling efficient use of available annotations while leveraging unlabeled data during training. Our experimental results demonstrate that this strategy outperforms conventional methods on several benchmark dataset evaluations, achieving state-of-the art accuracy for multi- organ segmentation tasks even under limited labeling scenarios. Overall, our work contributes valuable insights toward advancing automatic image analysis pipelines critical for clinical decision making.

> We consider the problem of computing the maximum a posteriori (MAP) assignment of a set of variables given a set of constraints. This problem is known to be NP-hard in general, and we focus on the case where the constraints are linear. We propose a new algorithm for this problem, which is based on a novel formulation of the problem as a multi-dimensional parametric mincut problem. We show that this formulation can be solved efficiently using a combination of dynamic programming and linear programming. We also show that our algorithm can be used to solve a number of related problems, including the problem of computing the maximum a posteriori assignment of a set of variables given a set of linear constraints and a set of linear costs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm on a number of benchmark problems. The paper is available here.

We consider a wireless distributed computing system, in which multiple mobile users, connected wirelessly through an access point, collaborate to perform a computation task. In particular, users communicate with each other via the access point to exchange their locally computed intermediate computation results, which is known as data shuffling. We propose a scalable framework for this system, in which the required communication bandwidth for data shuffling does not increase with the number of users in the network. The key idea is to utilize a particular repetitive pattern of placing the dataset (thus a particular repetitive pattern of intermediate computations), in order to provide coding opportunities at both the users and the access point, which reduce the required uplink communication bandwidth from users to access point and the downlink communication bandwidth from access point to users by factors that grow linearly with the number of users. We also demonstrate that the proposed dataset placement and coded shuffling schemes are optimal (i.e., achieve the minimum required shuffling load) for both a centralized setting and a decentralized setting, by developing tight information-theoretic lower bounds.

Last week, my mother was frustrated because it seemed nothing worked. The washing machine was smoking, the roof leaked and the heater died. She had repaired them all, only to have them break down again. They don't really break down. They work fine, because they are doing what they were designed to do. The washer doesn't clean well because the water level is too low. The roof doesn't keep out the rain because the shingles are rotting. And the heater doesn't provide warmth because the vents are blocked. Her frustration isn't with the items; it's with her inability to prevent them from breaking down. If the washer stops working, she calls the repair man, and he makes it work again. A friend of hers, who is a mechanic, talks about the old days, when you could actually fix things. But, times have changed. It's not just that technology advances. It's that companies have changed their business models. They have stopped making products that last. In this paper, we explore the concept of inductive types in the context of homotopy type theory (HOTT). Inductive types are a fundamental concept in type theory, allowing for the definition of types that are constructed through a process of recursive application. In HOTT, inductive types are particularly useful for encoding structures that are inherently recursive, such as trees and loops. We begin by introducing the basic concepts of HOTT and its syntax, including the notion of a type and the judgemental structure of the theory. We then present the definition of inductive types in HOTT, which is based on the idea of a "universal property" that characterizes the recursive structure of the type. We then explore the properties and behavior of inductive types in HOTT, including their relationship to other type constructs such as product and function types. We show how inductive types can be used to encode a wide range of mathematical structures, including natural numbers, trees, and loops. One of the key insights of the paper is the way in which inductive types in HOTT can be used to encode self-referential structures, which are notoriously difficult to handle in traditional type systems. We demonstrate this by presenting a series of examples that illustrate the expressive power of inductive types in HOTT, including the encoding of self-referential functions and the construction of "fixed point" types that are defined in terms of themselves. Finally, we discuss the relationship between inductive types in HOTT and other approaches to type theory, including intuitionistic type theory and category theory. We show how the concept of inductive types in HOTT provides a new and powerful way of understanding the relationship between these different approaches, and how they can be used to encode a wide range of mathematical structures in a consistent and principled way. Overall, this paper provides a detailed exploration of inductive types in homotopy type theory, and demonstrates their power and flexibility in encoding a wide range of mathematical structures. It provides a valuable contribution to the development of HOTT and its applications in mathematics and computer science.

There has been growing interest and research work on active contour models which are also called snakes, since 1987 when they were proposed by Kass, Weinberg & Terzopoulos with subsequent extensions to their formulation such as Level set method (OSVMT) introduced by Osher et al.. Though snakes could be very effective in segmenting some images like human lung images, they may perform poorly or even fail if the initial position fails due to improper initialization on the image(s). In this study we propose an energy-based approach that addresses snake model's drawbacks of poor convergence near boundaries, improves its robustness to noise and reduces computational complexity through use of gradient information available both in neighborhood region around curve itself and image domain respectively at each iteration. To improve upon OSVMT , we derive analytic solution using first derivatives rather than an evolutionary partial differential equation; while still retaining nonlinear interpolation features inherent in level sets. Further, our new implementation significantly reduces computation time and memory requirement over existing ones while ensuring reasonable accuracy and flexibility over complex structures without any loss of generality.

In a breakthrough study, Stanford researchers have discovered an easier and faster way to create diamonds - one that effectively "cheats" the thermodynamics of the process. The research team found that they could use microwaves to drastically reduce the time required to turn graphite into diamonds. It typically takes days or weeks for diamond formation through conventional methods; with microwaves, it only takes minutes. The team proved their method by placing graphite in a microwave cavity, where microwaves heat and pressurize it until a diamond forms. They also cross-checked their results using traditional high-pressure, high-temperature (HPHT) equipment. The microwaves were able to achieve the same effect as HPHT in a fraction of the time. Lead researcher Dr. John McLean was stunned by the finding. "We initially weren't sure if this would even work," he said. "But we were amazed to find that we could produce diamonds in such a short amount of time. We're essentially cheating the thermodynamics of diamond production." This discovery could have far-reaching implications for industries that rely on diamonds, such as the jewelry industry. It could make diamonds much more accessible and cheaper to produce, allowing them to be used in more applications. The study has been published in the journal Nature Communications. The research team is now looking into other ways to use microwave technology to transform other materials into new forms.

Conventional transfer learning leverages weights of Pre-trained networks, but mandates the need for similar neural architectures. Alternatively, knowledge distillation can transfer knowledge between heterogeneous networks but often requires access to the original training data or additional generative networks. Knowledge transfer between networks can be improved by being agnostic to The choice of network architecture and reducing the Dependence On original training data. We propose a knowledge transfer approach from a teacher to a student network wherein we train The student on an independent transferal Dataset, whose annotations are generated By the teacher. Experiments were conducted on five state-of-the-art networks for semantic segmentation And seven datasets across three imaging modalities. We studied knowledge transfer from a single teacher, combination of knowledge transfer and fine-tuning, and knowledge transfer from multiple teachers. The student model with a single teacher achieved similar performance as the teacher; and the student model with multiple teachers achieved better performance than the teachers. The salient features of our algorithm include: 1)no need for original training data Or generative networks, 2) knowledge transfer between different architectures, 3) ease of implementation for downstream tasks by using the downstream task dataset as the transferal dataset, 4) knowledge transfer of an ensemble of models, trained independently, into one Student model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the Proposed algorithm is effective for knowledge transfer and easily tunable.

I think that people have a right to those artistic, cultural, and aesthetic forms that please them, and openly sharing and partaking of diverse ideas and styles makes the world a richer, more innovative, and better place. Saying that a particular style of dress, manner of speech, way of doing things, or cultural icon "belongs" to a particular group of people who have rights over who may use it and how is dogmatic and dictatorial. If a person wants to wear a kimono or headdress to imitate and mock Japanese people or Native Americans, that's obviously racist and offensive. But if someone wants to wear a kimono or headdress because they like the way they look, the usage of those forms is at worst benign and at best potentially a show of admiration for them and the cultures whence they come.

In this paper, we investigate the concept of alpha channeling with high-field launch of lower hybrid waves in a magnetized plasma. Alpha channeling is a promising technique for confining and heating plasma in magnetic fusion devices, and it has been shown to be effective in reducing the energy loss of alpha particles in tokamaks. However, the conventional method of alpha channeling relies on the excitation of Alfvén waves, which can be challenging to launch in high-field plasmas. In this work, we propose a new method of alpha channeling that utilizes the high-field launch of lower hybrid waves to excite the Alfvén waves. Lower hybrid waves are electromagnetic waves that are resonant with the ion cyclotron frequency and can be excited by a high-field launch. We demonstrate that the high-field launch of lower hybrid waves can effectively excite Alfvén waves in a high-field plasma, leading to efficient alpha channeling. Using a set of theoretical models and simulations, we investigate the properties of the lower hybrid waves and their interaction with the plasma. We show that the high-field launch of lower hybrid waves can produce a strong electric field in the plasma, which can accelerate the ions and create a population of high-energy alpha particles. We also demonstrate that the excited Alfvén waves can effectively interact with the alpha particles, leading to their confinement and heating. Our results indicate that the high-field launch of lower hybrid waves is a promising method for alpha channeling in high-field plasmas. This technique has the potential to improve the efficiency of plasma heating and confinement in magnetic fusion devices, and it could help to overcome the challenges associated with conventional alpha channeling methods. Overall, this paper provides a novel approach to alpha channeling and contributes to the development of advanced plasma heating and confinement techniques for magnetic fusion. The results of this work have important implications for the development of future fusion reactors and could help to pave the way for the realization of practical fusion energy.

A series of experiments showed that background levels of natural radioactive particles, generated or naturally occurring in air, such as uranium and thorium, were reduced over time as it rose up to around 40 mSv (millions of sieverts) above ambient background. The increase in radon, on the other hand, was very rapid throughout the study period, reaching the highest level at 20 hours after exoumeation to 1 Gyr-year-20 years after exoumeation. We conclude that radon-222 exposure may contribute by reducing the radium content in the rock matrix when the geologic material loses mass during exoumal migration and/or decays to uranium. We propose in this paper the possibility in situ investigations at selected locations among which these results are confirmed.

Inter Extreme Points (IEPs) provide a promising approach to weakly supervised image segmentation. IEPs are points in images that can be computed from a small region around them using geometric properties such as distance and angles, without requiring explicit object detection or pixel-level labeling. In our work, we explore their potential in weakly supervised automatic segmentation by analyzing their structural relationships with local neighbors and other regions within an image. We show that IEPs possess rich information about object boundaries, shape, texture, and contextual hierarchy, which makes them well suited for weak supervision. However, direct use of IEPs is limited by their low resolution compared with pixels, leading to spatial ambiguity. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework that constructs intermediate representations between spatial neighborhoods and pixels based on smooth 3-D geodetic paths connecting extreme points across regions with similar geometric structures. Our scheme explicitly exploits spatial continuity, while preserving local geometric relationships among elements in these regions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of intermediate levels of supervisory information using IEPs to improve accuracy for both unsupervised and semi-supervised image segmentation tasks. It also enables visualization of underlying image structure through analysis of IEP cluster connectivity patterns. Overall, our proposed method offers new insights into interpreting spatial hierarchy and integrating nonlocal features at various scales and resolutions for weakly supervised image processing in computer vision applications.

In this work, we propose an ultra-resolution medical image (URMI) super resolution network with two parallel networks and three meta blocks that can effectively resolve details while preserving structure boundaries based on a large number of nonredundant deep encoder activations generated by convolutional layers in parallel branches. Specifically, URMI contains 2 parallel subnetworks - deciders: one directly generates the final feature map, corresponding to the single scale; the other first enhances features and then makes its decision via a fusion module, corresponding to multiple scales. Besides, our multi-level pyramid generator extracts multi-scale semantic information from each level in hierarchical way through our proposed Meta Block, which contain a Contextual Up-sampling Block (CUB), a Feature Squeezer Block (FSB), and a Super Resolving Block (SRB). As CUB allows both channels up-date dynamically within different spatial regions, more diverse semantic representation will be kept after several iterative fusing steps rather than losing important boundary information as previous models do, thus generating high quality output images. Extensive experiments were conducted using benchmark datasets and clinical CT scans. We have confirmed significant improvement in the performance over state-of-the-art methods according to various quantitative evaluations.

This paper presents a novel approach to real-time semantic segmentation using BiSeNet architecture. By making several modifications to original design, we are able to improve accuracy and efficiency of the model, making it well-suited for real-time applications. Our proposed method is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over existing methods while maintaining a fast inference time. Overall, this study provides valuable contribution to the field of computer vision and demonstrates the potential of our proposed method for various real-world applications.

This paper studies the context aggregation problem in semantic image segmentation. The existing researches focus on improving the pixel representations by aggregating the contextual information within individual images. Though impressive, these methods neglect the significance of the representations of the pixels of the corresponding class beyond the input image. To address this, this paper proposes to mine the contextual information beyond individual images to further augment the pixel representations. We first set up a feature memory module, which is updated dynamically during training, to store the dataset-level representations of various categories. Then, we learn class probability distribution of each pixel representation under the supervision of the ground-truth segmentation. At last, the representation of each pixel is augmented by aggregating the dataset-level representations based on the corresponding class probability distribution. Furthermore, by utilizing the stored dataset-level representations, we also propose a representation consistent learning strategy to make the classification head better address intra-class compactness and inter-class dispersion. The proposed method could be effortlessly incorporated into existing segmentation frameworks (e.g., FCN, PSPNet, OCRNet and DeepLabV3) and brings consistent performance improvements. Mining contextual information beyond image allows us to report state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks: ADE20K, LIP, Cityscapes and COCO-Stuff.

This study proposes a novel technique named Light Model Adaptation, which is aimed to improve semantic image segmentation efficiency when moving from night to nighttime. By using both supervised and unsupervised learning methods, our approach identifies lighting changes that might threaten conventional computer vision models' precision in low-light situations. Through extensive experimentation on multiple datasets, we demonstrate substantial improvements over state-of-the-art algorithms while achieving low performance levels, giving this method an attractive toolkit component applicable to diverse technologies such as autonomous driving or surveillance applications operating under challenging light circumstances.

In particular we formulate it as constrained optimization problem where the optimal alignment between learned feature spaces of two domains can be obtained in closed form given access to auxiliary set of labeled data in target domain for supervision only. As opposed to previous work using pairwise class alignments (e..g., joint embedding framework), our approach uses class agnostic vector correlation metric. This provides flexibility to adjust such constraints to control tightness of correspondence thus yielding better generalization ability. Experiments show significant improvement over state of art methods across a variety of medical image segmentation tasks including liver and tumor segmentation from CT images, retinal vessel tree extraction and whole slide fundus pathology image analysis ... The paper "CHASE: Robust Visual Tracking via Cell-Level Differentiable Neural Architecture Search" presents a novel approach to visual tracking that utilizes a differentiable neural architecture search (DNAS) method to optimize the tracking performance. The proposed method, called CHASE (Cell-Level Hierarchical Architecture Search for Efficient Tracking), uses a hierarchical architecture search strategy to identify the optimal architecture for visual tracking. The search is performed at the cell level, allowing for the exploration of a large search space and the identification of the most effective architectural components. The resulting architecture is then trained using a robust visual tracking dataset, resulting in improved tracking performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The paper also presents an analysis of the effectiveness of the different architectural components and demonstrates the robustness of the proposed method to variations in the tracking environment. Overall, the paper demonstrates the potential of DNAS for improving the performance of visual tracking systems.

You've got a bottle-neck! It doesn't matter what system you run, just about every single one of them have multiple things going on all at the same time. Most of the time, you're pushing a lot of stuff through the CPU, but you're also pushing a lot of stuff through your GPU, and a little bit of stuff through the RAM as well. The problem comes when you get to the point where the GPU can't keep up with what you're throwing at it and the CPU spends most of its time waiting on the GPU to get out of its way. This is called a bottleneck and it can really slow down the gaming experience. You need to know how to solve this problem as it's one of the biggest things that can slow down your gaming. Before we get into anything else, you need to make sure that the problem you're seeing isn't something else. There are a ton of other reasons why your game might be running slow, like your GPU drivers or even the game itself. Open up your Task Manager (CTRL SHIFT ESC) and make sure that your GPU isn't using more than 60-70 of your GPU. If it is, you've got a problem. We'll be looking at why this is happening and what to do about it. There are two main types of bottleneck: software and hardware. A software bottleneck is a problem where your CPU and GPU can't keep up with what you're throwing at them. In this case, the hardware is working as hard as it can to process what you're giving it, but it's just not enough. This paper describes the network structure of the phonographic industry and reveals characteristic differences between performers. By examining the collaboration patterns among performers, we uncover the fundamental structure of the industry and reveal clusters of artists with different genres, styles, or influences. We use a database of musician collaborations to establish a network representation of the market, where performers are represented as vertices and collaborations are presented as edges between clusters. We then apply community detection algorithms to find clusters of musicians with low collaboration density. Our findings show that the phonographic industry exhibits a hierarchical hierarchy, with a few strongly connected artists acting as hubs and few peripheral artists with fewer collaborations. We often know that artists outside the same cluster seem to have different genres, styles, or influences, suggesting that the market is organized around particular artistic themes or trends. Moreover, we observe a weak similarity between the similarity of artists' styles and their collaboration styles, indicating that artists prefer to engage with people who share their artistic characteristics. Our results have implications for the entertainment business, stating that artists who collaborate with individuals in their cluster are more unlikely to obtain success and that the market is organized around certain musical themes or trends. The journal adds to the knowledge of the composition and dynamics of the phonographic industry and offers insights into the variables that affect the success of artists. Keywords: phonographic industry, network structure, collaboration patterns, community detection, performers' similarity.

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge learned from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled and unseen target domain, which is usually trained on data from both domains. Access to the source domain data at the adaptation stage, however, is often limited, due to data storage or privacy issues. To alleviate this, in this work, we target source free UDA for segmentation, and propose to adapt an ``off-the-shelf" segmentation model pre-trained in the source domain to the target domain, with an adaptive batch-wise normalization statistics adaptation framework. Specifically, the domain-specific low-order batch statistics, i.e., mean and variance, are gradually adapted with an exponential momentum decay scheme, while the consistency of domain shareable high-order batch statistics, i.e., scaling and shifting parameters, is explicitly enforced by our optimization objective. The transferability of each channel is adaptively measured first from which to balance the contribution of each channel. Moreover, the proposed source free UDA framework is orthogonal to unsupervised learning methods, e.g., self-entropy minimization, which can thus be simply added on top of our framework. Extensive experiments on the BraTS 2018 database show that our source free UDA framework outperformed existing source-relaxed UDA methods for the cross-subtype UDA segmentation task and yielded comparable results for the cross-modality UDA segmentation task, compared with a supervised UDA methods with the source data.

RLCorrector: Reinforced Proofreading for Connectomics Image Segmentation Connectomics, the study of neural connections, relies heavily on image segmentation to identify and analyze neural structures. However, manual segmentation is time-consuming and prone to errors, while automated methods often produce suboptimal results. To address this issue, we propose RLCorrector, a reinforced proofreading approach for connectomics image segmentation. RLCorrector combines the strengths of both manual and automated segmentation by using a deep reinforcement learning algorithm to correct errors made by an initial automated method. Our experimental results on a benchmark dataset show that RLCorrector significantly improves the accuracy and efficiency of connectomics image segmentation, reducing the need for manual intervention and providing a valuable tool for connectomics research.

Large, fine-grained image segmentation datasets, annotated at pixel-level, are difficult to obtain, particularly in medical imaging, where Annotations also require expert knowledge. Weakly-supervised learning can train models by relying on weaker forms of Annotation, such as scribbles. Here, we learn To segment using scribble annotations in an adversarial game. With unpaired segmentation masks, we Train a multi-scale GAN to generate realistic segmentation Masks at multiple resolutions, while We use scribbles to learn Their correct position in the image. Central to the model's success is a novel attention gating mechanism, Which we condition with adversarial Signals to act as a shape prior, resulting in better object localization at multiple scales. Subject to adversarial conditioning, the segmentor learns attention maps that are semantic, suppress the noisy activations outside the objects, and Reduce the vanishing gradient problem in the deeper layers of the segmentor. We evaluated our model on several medical (ACDC, LVSC, CHAOS) and non-medical (PPSS) datasets, and we report performance levels matching those achieved by models trained with fully annotated segmentation masks. We also demonstrate extensions in a variety of settings: semi-supervised learning; combining multiple scribble sources (a crowdsourcing scenario) and multi-task learning (combining scribble and mask supervision). There is no doubt that we are in dire need of better ways of handling the problem where deep learning and regression problems do not fit our requirements, which are highly complicated segmentation task tasks such as feature extraction or object recognition. The current data processing models implemented in standard distributed algorithms are not suited well enough for these problems. A good example for simple and parallel application was shown by Gao et al., who applied convolutional networks and DNNs respectively on a 2D dataset. We present here an alternative solution by introducing the new concept of inter-extremity geoderricks (IER): a set of georeferenced geodesic line representations. These are not strictly convex line representations but they approximate this condition for a subset of points along a curve whose edge passes through no part of a point (i.e. their segment). Erecting a set that fits all points as per feature extraction and object detection schemes (based on local minima) can reduce the number and distance search distance by about 10 times, thereby dramatically reducing computation time and memory requirement (and improving accuracy), due largely to better preprocessing step. Our work further focuses on modelling inter-point constraints to determine the location of a set of subgroups defined at many scales, i.e. all parts or edge points. Acidosis alters the cellular metabolism of several major metabolites, which induces a significant degree of metabolic inflexibility. Cells exposed to acidosis largely rely upon mitochondrial metabolism for energy generation to the extent that metabolic intermediates are redirected away from several other critical metabolic processes, including ribose and glutathione synthesis. These alterations lead to both a decrease in cellular proliferation and increased sensitivity to ROS. Collectively, these data reveal a role for p53 in cellular metabolic reprogramming under acidosis, in order to permit increased bioenergetic capacity and ROS neutralization. Understanding the metabolic adaptations that cancer cells make under acidosis may present opportunities to generate anti-tumor therapeutic agents that are more tumor-specific.

In this paper, we present a novel method for qubit state tomography in superconducting circuits using weak measurements. Qubit state tomography is the process of reconstructing the quantum state of a qubit, which is a fundamental building block of quantum computing. Superconducting circuits are a promising platform for quantum computing due to their high coherence times and low noise levels. However, performing qubit state tomography in these systems is challenging due to the fragile nature of quantum states and the limited number of measurements that can be performed before the state is disturbed. Our method utilizes weak measurements, which are measurements that only slightly perturb the quantum state, to overcome these challenges. By applying a series of weak measurements to the qubit, we are able to reconstruct the quantum state with high fidelity without significantly disturbing it. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method using numerical simulations and experimentally validate it using a superconducting qubit. Our results show that weak measurements can be used to perform qubit state tomography with high accuracy and low error rates. This technique has the potential to enable more efficient and accurate quantum state tomography in superconducting circuits, which is essential for the development of scalable quantum computing architectures. Our work takes a significant step towards the development of practical quantum computing technology and paves the way for further advancements in this field.

Researchers at Stanford University and the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory have discovered a way to transform a substance found in fossil fuels into diamonds with pressure and low heat. Diamond synthesis usually requires a large amount of energy, time, or the addition of a catalyst, which adds impurities. Diamondoids are tiny, odorless, and slightly sticky powders that resemble rock salt. They are made up of atoms arranged in the same pattern as diamonds, but they contain hydrogen. Diamondoids can reorganize into diamonds with surprisingly little energy, without passing through other forms of carbon, such as graphite. The method is currently only able to make specks of diamonds, and it is impractical until larger crystals can be formed.

Facebook's Deepfake Detection Challenge is an open competition to find algorithms that can spot AI-manipulated videos. This year's winning algorithm could spot real-world examples of deep fakes with an average accuracy rate between 94 and 99. The second most accurate detection method was developed by three researchers at UC Berkeley, who used a combination of machine learning techniques (including convolutional neural networks) along with human annotations from the 2018 VidCon conference in Anaheim, California - where attendees saw some fake footage for themselves. The team had more than 300 hours of data on which their model learned how to identify manipulated media. Their approach only scored about 91, though; it showed signs of stalling when faced with video sequences containing both realistic images paired with video clips or animations. Finally came Kaggle, whose platform hosts competitions across multiple industries like finance and healthcare. Its latest contest included submissions using convolutional neural network approaches as well as supervised learning methods trained on labeled datasets. After evaluating these models against several benchmark datasets created specifically around detecting deepfakes, two teams emerged victorious: one modeling just image information and another targeting audio signals alone. Both were able to detect altered content with almost 100 accuracy after training solely off publicly available dataset sets. Overall, this success shows promise toward helping us all avoid becoming victims of misinformation campaigns powered by increasingly convincing faked imagery. But we're still years away from effectively determining whether photos have been tampered with, let alone being capable enough to reliably distinguish between what's entirely genuine versus fabricated. It's even possible our efforts won't be helpful anyway since many users don't care if they view deepfaked material so long as it aligns with their preexisting beliefs anyways.

Image segmentation is a critical task in computer vision and machine learning that involves partitioning an image into meaningful regions. Despite the success of recent deep learning methods, they often suffer from overfitting, which can lead to poor generalization performance. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach to image segmentation using weak shape priors. Our method incorporates shape information through a recently developed theory called hierarchical perceptual grouping (HPG), which captures statistical correlations among low-level features extracted from images. By training our model with HPG, we impose constraints on the shapes of objects within an image and effectively prevent overfitting. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art object detection and segmentation algorithms while achieving more accurate shape recognition. Overall, our work provides a new perspective on integrating weak shape priors into deep learning models and opens up avenues for future research in computer vision.

Electronic health records (EHR) contain patient medical information in machine legible form, but many parts remain unscanned and stored as free-text notes, which are currently still being used by physicians to document relevant issues in their patient's case history. Researchers have turned towards developing automated natural language processing algorithms to mine and extract structured EHR data; however there is little prior work on determining what to do if multiple different methods agree only partly regarding any particular clinical finding. We explore using inter-annotator agreement among human annotations as one possible way out in this scenario. After selecting two types of problems where we expect disagreement may be beneficial- tumor margin prediction for breast cancer staging, and lesion segmentation for skin image analysis - through a small amount of qualitative investigation of existing clinical guidelines and some online discussions with clinicians, we evaluate several ways of determining thresholds below which agreement should not be trusted before moving forward. While results vary somewhat depending on the application, our analysis shows preliminary evidence that taking into account overall uncertainty due to variability across annotators can alleviate some errors generated by individual systems without sacrificing too much useful precision.

We design our system using an encoder-decoder backbone, which allows us to learn feature representations from raw image data and use them to automatically isolate various tissues within complex medical images. Our experiment results show improvement over previous state-of-the-art models across multiple evaluation metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed methodology. The paper further discusses several potential avenues for future research, including improvements to preprocessing techniques, incorporating additional modalities into our framework, and investigating other applications beyond medical imaging. Overall, our work contributes significantly to the existing literature on medical image segmentation by introducing a powerful tool capable of accurately identifying and separating different types of tissue within complex medical images with minimal human input.

This involves decomposing an image into a linear combination of a set of basis functions (often refered to as modes) that can be used to represent various features present within the image.
