Incorporating shape information is essential for the delineation of many organs and anatomical structures in medical images. While previous work has mainly focused on parametric spatial transformations applied on reference template shapes, in this paper, we address the Bayesian inference of parametric shape models for segmenting medical images with the objective to provide interpretable results. The proposed framework defines a likelihood appearance probability and a prior label probability based on a generic shape function through a logistic function. A reference length parameter defined in the sigmoid controls the trade-off between shape and appearance information. The inference of shape parameters is performed within an Expectation-Maximisation approach where a Gauss-Newton optimization stage allows to provide an approximation of the posterior probability of shape parameters. This framework is applied to the segmentation of cochlea structures from clinical CT images constrained by a 10 parameter shape model. It is evaluated on three different datasets, one of which includes more than 200 patient images. The results show performances comparable to supervised methods and better than previously proposed unsupervised ones. It also enables an analysis of parameter distributions and the quantification of segmentation uncertainty including the effect of the shape model.

Boundary information plays a significant role in 2D image segmentation, while usually being ignored in 3D point cloud segmentation where ambiguous features might be generated in feature extraction, leading to misclassification in the transition area between two objects. In this paper, firstly, we propose a Boundary Prediction Module (BPM) to predict boundary points. Based on the predicted boundary, a boundary-aware Geometric Encoding Module (GEM) is designed to encode geometric information and aggregate features with discrimination in a neighborhood, so that the local features belonging to different categories will not be polluted by each other. To provide extra geometric information for boundary-aware GEM, we also propose a light-weight Geometric Convolution Operation (GCO), making the extracted features more distinguishing. Built upon the boundary-aware GEM, we build our network and test it on benchmarks like ScanNet v2, S3DIS. Results show our methods can significantly improve the baseline and achieve state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/JchenXu/BoundaryAwareGEM.

Background: Biomedical image segmentation is a critical task in medical imaging analysis, but it remains challenging due to the complexity and variability of biological structures. Deep learning methods have shown promising results in addressing this challenge, but they require large amounts of annotated data, which are time-consuming and expensive to obtain. Objective: To develop an active learning framework that can effectively and efficiently annotate biomedical images, reducing the amount of manual annotation required while maintaining accurate segmentation performance. Methodology: We propose Suggestive Annotation, a deep active learning framework that leverages both certain and uncertain annotations to improve the efficiency and accuracy of biomedical image segmentation. Our approach uses a two-stage sampling strategy to selectively annotate the most informative regions of the image, followed by a probabilistic Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) to refine the segmentation masks. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets, including brain tumor segmentation from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and retinal vessel segmentation from fundus photographs. Results: Our experiments show that Suggestive Annotation significantly outperforms traditionalactive learning methods in terms of annotation efficiency and segmentation accuracy. Specifically, we achieve an average annotation reduction rate of 72% across all datasets without sacrificing performance. Moreover, our framework adapts well to different types of modalities and diseases, demonstrating its generalizability and robustness. Conclusion: Suggestive Annotation presents a novel deep active learning paradigm forbiomedical image segmentation that not only reduces the annotation burden but also improves segmentation accuracy. This work has immediate implications for clinicians, researchers, and practitioners who rely on accurate segmentation results but struggle with collecting and labeling large quantities of data.

Through a comprehensive analysis of various techniques for integrating these supplementary cues into the model's decision-making process, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of mining rich contexts from multiple modalities during training and inference stages of deep neural networks. Overall, our findings suggest that leveraging multi-modal inputs can enhance generalization performance on real-world applications involving complex scenes with varying lighting conditions or object occlusions, ultimately contributing to improvements in computer vision systems' interpretability and reliability.

In this academic paper, we propose a novel self-supervised clustering network architecture that utilizes spatial guidance to improve medical image segmentation. Our approach leverages both supervisory and unsupervised learning paradigms, employing the former to provide prior knowledge about tissue classes in images while utilizing the latter to identify regions with similar properties regardless of class. We design our system using an encoder-decoder backbone, which allows us to learn feature representations from raw image data and use them to automatically isolate various tissues within complex medical images. Our experiment results show improvement over previous state-of-the-art models across multiple evaluation metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed methodology. The paper further discusses several potential avenues for future research, including improvements to preprocessing techniques, incorporating additional modalities into our framework, and investigating other applications beyond medical imaging. Overall, our work contributes significantly to the existing literature on medical image segmentation by introducing a powerful tool capable of accurately identifying and separating different types of tissue within complex medical images with minimal human input.

Abstract: One can define many topological structures through combinatorics, especially recursive combinatorial constructions such as Dyck walks and Motzkin paths; one would like to have efficient computational models, ideally cellular automata, which compute these spaces. In this paper we focus on two of them – non-periodic $K_t$ and periodic $P_i$; both are based upon (and built up from) an ordered set of inversion sequences with length $\sim n!$. To each non-constant sequence there corresponds its \emph{type} defined by wether it increases, decreases or remains constant most frequently at any particular point. With probability 1 over the random generation of an infinite word of type $k$ all letters lie in finite slices corresponding to that type; moreover allmost all the pairs formed from successive positions along those finite words form subsequences whose lengths fall into the range $[5294607 \, t + O(t^{1+\varepsilon}),6830166\,n - O(t^{\epsilon'})]$ where $t=36(\Gamma+log(1/u))$, thus confirming their asymptotic equivalence established some thirty years ago by Nijenhuis & van Leeuwen (see [NvL]). For our example types $K_1$ and $K_{1/2}$ we prove existance of generating functions satisfying certain functional equations. We demonstrate how the same underlying theory applies to produce a precise conjecture regarding the number of times a period appears throughout the entirety of a periodic $P_1$ pattern.

Yes, plasticity in relative growth rate after a reduction in nitrogen availability is related to root morphological and physiological responses. When plants experience reduced nitrogen availability, they tend to exhibit plasticity in their growth rates and make adjustments to their root systems to cope with the change. Root morphological responses to nitrogen reduction can include increased root length, increased root branching, and the development of root hairs that help the plant access more soil and potentially access more nitrogen. These morphological changes result in a greater root surface area that maximizes nutrient uptake and helps maintain plant growth even when nitrogen availability is low. Root physiological responses to reduced nitrogen availability often involve changes in root metabolic processes, nutrient transporters, and other processes that promote efficient nitrogen uptake. The plasticity in growth rate consists of increased nitrogen use efficiency, which can be achieved by modifying the expression of nitrogen transporter genes, enhancing root metabolic efficiency, and changing nitrogen assimilation pathways. In conclusion, plasticity in relative growth rate after a reduction in nitrogen availability is related to root morphological and physiological responses, as plants adjust their root systems and physiological processes to maximize nutrient uptake and maintain optimal growth in the face of limited nitrogen resources.

Eye boogers, also known as sleep in your eyes or rheum, are the crusty substance that can collect in the corners of your eyes or on your eyelashes while you sleep, or sometimes during the day. Eye boogers are made up of dried tears, oil, mucus, dead cells, and other debris that gets trapped on the surface of your eye. While eye boogers are normal and usually harmless, excessive or frequently occurring eye discharge can be a sign of an underlying condition, such as an infection or allergies, and should be evaluated by an eye doctor.

Abstract: Image segmentation is a fundamental Task in computer vision that involves assigning labels to pixels in an image to distinguish different objects or regions. Domain Adaptation, which adapts models to new domains by leveraging labeled data from source domains, has shown great promise in improving image segmentation performance. However, existing domain adaptation methods often Rely on manually annotated target datasets, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain. In this paper, we propose constrained domain adaptation for image segmentation, which utilizes both labeled source data and unlabeled target data To learn domain-invariant features while preserving spatial constraints between pixels. Our approach introduces a novel regularization term that enforces the similarity of neighborhoods across Domains, leading to Improved segmentation performance on unseen target data. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in various scenarios, including segmenting medical images and object detection in autonomous driving scenes. The results show that our method outperforms traditional domain Adaptation approaches And achieves state-of-the-art performance in some cases, demonstrating its potential for real-world applications Where labeled target data is scarce.

Unlіkе trаdіtіоnаl mеthоds thаt rеlу оn ехрlісіtlу dеtесtіng bоundаrіеs thrоugh еdgе mарріng оr іntеnsіtу dіsсоntіnuіtіеs, ВоundаrуSquееzе trеаts іmаgе sеgmеntаtіоn аs а bоundаrу squееzіng рrосеss. Τhе рrороsеd mеthоd соnsіsts оf twо mаіn stерs. Fіrst, wе аррlу а nоn-lіnеаr fіltеr tо thе іnрut іmаgе tо еnhаnсе іts еdgеs аnd suррrеss nоіsе. Тhеn, wе іtеrаtіvеlу squееzе thе еnhаnсеd еdgеs tоwаrds thеіr соrrеsроndіng bоrdеrs whіlе рrеsеrvіng thеіr соnnесtіvіtу аnd соhеrеnсе wіth nеіghbоrіng еdgеs. Тhе rеsultіng sеgmеnts аrе thеn оbtаіnеd bу grоuріng ріхеls соnnесtеd bу thе squееzеd еdgеs. Medical image segmentation is important task in various applications such as diagnosis, treatment planning and surgical planning. However, it typically requires large amounts of labeled data which are expensive to acquire. To overcome this challenge, we propose novel approach using a generic ensemble based deep convolutional neural network for semi-supervised medical image segmentation. We use a combination of supervised learning with unsupervised approaches like clustering, label propagation and pseudo-labeling to improve performance when there is limited labeled data available. Our method achieves good results on multiple benchmark datasets in terms of accuracy, precision, recall and F1 score. The proposed deep learning model shows that even with limited labeled data, medical image segmentation can be performed efficiently with high accuracy.

Tensor completion is a challenging problem with various applications. Many related models based on the low-rank prior of the tensor have been proposed. However, the low-rank prior may not be enough to recover the original tensor from the observed incomplete tensor. In this paper, we prose a tensor completion method by exploiting both the low-rank and sparse prior of tensor. Specifically, the tensor completion task can be formulated as a low-rank minimization problem with a sparse regularizer. The low-rank property is depicted by the tensor truncated nuclear norm based on tensor singular value decomposition (T-SVD) which is a better approximation of tensor tubal rank than tensor nuclear norm. While the sparse regularizer is imposed by a l 1 -norm in a discrete cosine transformation (DCT) domain, which can better employ the local sparse property of completed data. To solve the optimization problem, we employ an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) in which we only need to solve several subproblems which have closed-form solutions. Substantial experiments on real world images and videos show that the proposed method has better performances than the existing state-of-the-art methods.

> High-level computer vision tasks are essential in modern industries like self-driving, video surveillance and augmented reality (AR). Among them, visual tracking that can robustly detect target objects across multiple frames has attracted tremendous attention [1 – 3]. Since most trackers rely on manually designed features or handcrafted models with limited representational capacity, many efforts have been made to design end-to-end neural architecture search methods, such as SANet[4] in order to obtain effective and differentiable feature modules automatically via reinforcement learning approach and achieve significant improvements over its counterparts. Despite progress with existing methods, these approaches still lack diversity of solutions since they only consider cell selection instead of other building blocks. For example, the channel number remains fixed at 256 throughout all layers in SANet due to the limitation of computation cost during RL training. Moreover, current search space fails to contain convolution kernel size variation without losing generality because each layer is searched independently rather than treated as a whole. > In this work we propose an autonomous design pipeline called CHASE that searches optimal network structures along three dimensions including channel number, group ratio, kernel size for both spatial cells and channels at module level. Experiments show our proposed design is more compatible with backpropagation based optimization process compared to conventional ones. Compared to state-of-the-art solution of 98% accuracy, we successfully achieve above performance by adopting less computing resources using VGG-M model. Our contributions are summarized as follows: > • We enable the search methodology to handle kernel size variations under certain constraints; > • An efficient backpropagation method is introduced for differentiating modules’ output which requires no prior knowledge about the corresponding gradient; > • A unified differentiable framework is provided for efficiently converging through extensive experiments.

Dynamic Adaptive Mixture Models (DAMMs) are a type of statistical model that can be used to analyse complex data sets. DAMMs are flexible and can adapt to changes in the data over time, making them useful for a variety of applications. In this paper, we discuss the theory and implementation of DAMMs, including how they can be used to model complex data distributions and how they can be adapted to changing data. We also provide examples of how DAMMs have been used in practise to analyse real-world data sets. Overall, DAMMs are a powerful tool for analysing complex data and can be used in a variety of fields, including finance, healthcare, and social sciences.

According to the widespread availability of open-access fundus images, deep convolutional neural network (CNN)-based methods are rapidly becoming popular in the field of retinal disease detection. On the one hand, these methods help physicians diagnose disease without subjective bias. On the other hand, because of limitations in available data, for example, a small number of images, or a lack of annotation, they are at risk of overfitting to a particular data set. In this way, training data for deep learning methods should be as abundant as possible. This study aims to address this issue by applying unsupervised domain adaptation to the architecture of the CNN when it is trained on different fundus image data sets. Specifically, we propose a method called Dense Localized Feature Extraction (DLFE), which consists of a deep embedding feature extraction network with a pre-trained ResNet-18 network as a feature extractor to extract local dense features from three different scales, followed by a concatenation and pooling layer before the fully connected layer. Moreover, DLFE extracts local statistics from dense features, which are combined in the fusion layer, which is composed of two cascaded attention blocks. In addition, we use an adversarial learning strategy and a novel entropy method to overcome the domain shift in experiments. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method can obtain high-quality segmentation, as evaluated by the intersection ratio and Dice coefficient metrics, compared with other published methods, obtaining an intersection ratio of 97% and a Dice coefficient of 95%, achieving a slightly better performance than that of other methods by approximately 3%. All of the experiments were performed both in the same domain and on different datasets. The result showed that DLFE performed well, and it was able to obtain a significantly higher mIDC score than the model of the compared method, with a mean mIDC score of approximately 4%.

Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in healthcare, but annotating large amounts of data for training deep neural networks can be time-consuming and expensive. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to medical image segmentation that leverages contrastive learning to learn both global and local features from a small set of labeled images. Our method uses a two-stage framework, consisting of a global feature extractor and a local feature refiner, to efficiently capture both high-level semantic information and low-level spatial details. The global feature extractor utilizes a contrastive loss function to learn features that are discriminative across different organs and tissues, while the local feature refiner employs a combination of pixelwise and proximity-based contrastive losses to refine the features within each organ or tissue. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation methods while requiring significantly fewer annotations. Moreover, we demonstrate that our learned features can be effectively transferred to new tasks, such as disease detection and segmentation, and exhibit improved robustness to variations in image acquisition protocols. Overall, our work highlights the potential of contrastive learning for efficient and accurate medical image segmentation, and paves the way for more widespread adoption of deep learning techniques in clinical settings.

In this paper, we consider the partition function of a statistical mechanical model known as the sinh-model. Specifically, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of this partition function as the temperature parameter tends to zero. Using a combination of analytic and numerical techniques, we derive an asymptotic expansion of the partition function in powers of the temperature. The leading term in this expansion is shown to be a constant, independent of the temperature, while the first correction term is found to be proportional to the temperature squared. We also study the behavior of the free energy and entropy of the system, which are related to the partition function by the thermodynamic relations. Our results indicate that the free energy and entropy exhibit a non-analytic behavior near the critical temperature, which is consistent with the existence of a phase transition in the system. Our findings provide new insights into the behavior of the sinh-model at low temperatures, and shed light on the nature of the phase transition that occurs in this system. The techniques used in this study may also be applicable to other statistical mechanical models, and could potentially be used to study the behavior of such models near their critical points. Overall, this paper contributes to our understanding of the behavior of statistical mechanical systems near their critical points, and demonstrates the power of analytic and numerical techniques in the study of these systems.

Contemporary domain adaptive semantic segmentation aims to address data annotation challenges by assuming that target domains are completely unannotated. However, annotating a few target samples is usually very manageable and worthwhile especially if it improves the adaptation performance substantially. This paper presents SSDAS, a Semi-Supervised Domain Adaptive image Segmentation network that employs a few labeled target samples as anchors for adaptive and progressive feature alignment between labeled source samples and unlabeled target samples. We position the few labeled target samples as references that gauge the similarity between source and target features and guide adaptive inter-domain alignment for learning more similar source features. In addition, we replace the dissimilar source features by high-confidence target features continuously during the iterative training process, which achieves progressive intra-domain alignment between confident and unconfident target features. Extensive experiments show the proposed SSDAS greatly outperforms a number of baselines, i.e., UDA-based semantic segmentation and SSDA-based image classification. In addition, SSDAS is complementary and can be easily incorporated into UDA-based methods with consistent improvements in domain adaptive semantic segmentation.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for detecting anomalous and adversarial inputs in machine learning models using normalizing flows. Our approach, called DAAIN (Detection of Anomalous and Adversarial Inputs using Normalizing Flows), leverages the properties of normalizing flows to transform input data into a simple probability distribution, allowing for efficient and effective anomaly detection. Existing approaches for anomaly detection in machine learning models often rely on statistical methods or threshold-based techniques, which can be limited in their ability to detect complex or high-dimensional anomalies. In contrast, DAAIN uses normalizing flows to map input data into a lower-dimensional space, where anomalies can be more easily identified. We evaluate the performance of DAAIN on several benchmark datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art anomaly detection methods. Our results show that DAAIN outperforms existing approaches in detecting anomalies in high-dimensional data, and is particularly effective in detecting adversarial attacks. We also analyze the effectiveness of DAAIN in different scenarios, such as when the input data is imbalanced or when the anomalies are highly complex. Our results demonstrate that DAAIN is robust to these challenges and can accurately detect anomalies in a wide range of settings. Overall, our paper introduces a powerful and flexible approach for detecting anomalous and adversarial inputs in machine learning models, and demonstrates the effectiveness of DAAIN in a variety of scenarios. Our work has important implications for the development of secure and reliable machine learning systems, and highlights the potential of normalizing flows for anomaly detection tasks.

SOLITONS are nonlinear waves which propagate in a medium without changing their shape or amplitude. We study the solitons of a bosonic hard sphere, a quantum system where particles can only occupy discrete energy levels. We concentrate on two classes of solitons, the 'Gross-Pitaevsky' type and the super-Pitaevskii type. The first is a classical solitary wave described by a single equation, while the second is a quantum solitary wave with more complicated mathematical properties. We study the properties of these solitary waves: their stability, localization, and interaction with other solitary waves. We also discuss the experimental realization of these solitary waves in a variety of systems, such as ultracold atoms and condensed matter. This review provides a broad picture of solitary waves in hard spheres and their potential application in quantum information processing.

One possible counter-argument to refute the opinion that IDs should be required to vote is that such a requirement could disproportionately disenfranchise certain groups of people, particularly those who face barriers to obtaining government-issued ID, such as low-income individuals, elderly people, people with disabilities, and members of minority groups. In some cases, obtaining an ID can be costly, time-consuming, or difficult due to transportation barriers or lack of access to necessary documents. Additionally, the problem of voter fraud, which voter ID laws are intended to address, is actually quite rare in the United States; according to a study by the Brennan Center for Justice, the incidence of in-person voter fraud is between 0.00004 and 0.0009. Therefore, the burden of requiring everyone to obtain an ID in order to vote may outweigh the potential benefits of preventing this exceedingly rare form of fraud. Finally, it is worth noting that voter ID laws have been found to have a disproportionate impact on certain populations, particularly Black and Latino communities. While the specific impact of these laws varies depending on how they are designed and implemented, it is clear that they can have a negative impact on voting rights and should be approached with caution to ensure that they do not unfairly disenfranchise any group of voters.

In this paper, we explore a novel game-theoretic formulation of Ebert's classic three-person, three-colour hat puzzle. By introducing an asymmetry in the players' payoffs, we create a scenario that challenges traditional assumptions about cooperative game theory and offers richer insights into the role of inference and communication in strategic decision making. Our analysis reveals a surprising dearth of equilibrium outcomes, leading to a counterintuitive characterisation of the optimal strategy profile. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach through experimental validation and illustrate its applicability to real-world scenarios involving coordinated decision making among multiple agents with different preferences and information sets. The results provide fresh perspectives on the interplay between rationality, bounded cognition, and social influence in strategic interaction.

Conventional transfer learning leverages weights of pre-trained networks, but mandates the need for similar neural architectures. Alternatively, knowledge distilation can transfer knowledge between heterogeneous networks but often requires access to the original training data or additional generative networks. Knowledge transfer between networks can be improved by being agnostic to the choice of network architecture and reducing the dependence on original training data. We propose a knowledge transfer approach from a teacher to a student network wherein we train the student on an independent transferal dataset, whose annotations are generated by the teacher. Experiments were conducted on five state-of-the-art networks for semantic segmentation and seven datasets across three imageing modalities. We studied knowledge transfer from a single teacher, combination of knowledge transfer and fine-tuning, and knowledge transfer from multiple teachers. The student model with a single teacher achieved similar performance as the teacher; and the student model with multiple teachers achieved better performance than the teachers. The salient features of our algorithm include: 1)no need for original training data or generative networks, 2) knowledge transfer between different architectures, 3) ease of implementation for downstream tasks by using the downstream task dataset as the transferal dataset, 4) knowledge transfer of an ensemble of models, trained independently, into one student model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is effective for knowledge transfer and easily tunable.

Our finding that cleavage at the B site is insensitive to homology shows that effective synapsis between partners does not depend on sequence matching. Cleavage at the B' site provides the earliest positive signal for a homology-dependent switch in the lambda recombination machinery. Because this switch can occur in the absence of strand joining, the results argue against models that invoke strand ligation as the critical element of homology-sensing. Alternative mechanisms are presented that involve varieties of non-covalent strand swapping. A synthesis of the present results and other recent experiments highlights the importance of the disannealing of complementary strands and their reannealing to new partners, a process traditionally described as branch migration. The reversibility of branch migration and its bias away from mismatched combinations are proposed to be the major mechanisms of homology-sensing during lambda integration.

Deep neural networks have revolutionized the field of artificial intelligence and machine learning, achieving state-of-the-art results on a wide range of tasks. However, their complexity and opacity make it challenging to understand how they learn and make decisions. In this paper, we present a divide-and-conquer approach towards understanding deep networks. Specifically, we propose a method that recursively partitions the network into smaller sub-networks, and applies a series of interpretability techniques to each sub-network. We then combine the results from the individual sub-networks to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the entire network. Our approach is demonstrated on several benchmark datasets, where we show that our method is able to provide insight into the important features learned by the network, as well as identify regions of the network that are responsible for specific decisions. Our work represents an important step towards making deep learning more transparent and interpretable, and we believe it will have significant implications for a wide range of applications.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to understanding relationship between electromagnetism and gravity by geometrizing Maxwell's equations. By employing a geometric framework, we demonstrate that Maxwell's equations can be reformulated as set of curvature equations, akin to those found in general relativity. This reformulation reveals deep connection between electromagnetism and gravity, and provides new perspective on the nature of these fundamental forces. We begin by introducing geometric structure to Maxwell's equations, which allows us to recast them in terms of curvature and connection coefficients. This geometric framework enables us to identify set of geometric objects that are intimately related to electromagnetic field, including the electromagnetic curvature tensor and the electromagnetic connection. By analyzing the properties of these geometric objects, we demonstrate that they are closely related to the gravitational curvature tensor and connection, which are central to general relativity. This relationship is found to be even more profound when we consider the dynamics of the electromagnetic field, which can be shown to be equivalent to curvature of spacetime. Our results provide new understanding of interplay between electromagnetism and gravity, and suggest that these forces may be more closely related than previously thought. The geometrization of Maxwell's equations offers a powerful tool for exploring this relationship, and may lead to new insights into the nature of fundamental forces and structure of universe. In conclusion, our work presents a novel approach to understanding relationship between electromagnetism and gravity, and provides a new perspective on the nature of these fundamental forces. The geometrization of Maxwell's equations offers powerful tool for exploring interplay between these forces, and may lead to new insights into the structure of the universe.

This paper studies the context aggregation problem in semantic image segmentation. The existing researches focus on improving the pixel representations by aggregating the contextual information within individual images. Though impressive, these methods neglect the significance of the representations of the pixels of the corresponding class beyond the input image. To address this, this paper proposes to mine the contextual information beyond individual images to further augment the pixel representations. We first set up a feature memory module, which is updated dynamically during training, to store the dataset-level representations of various categories. Then, we learn class probability distribution of each pixel representation under the supervision of the ground-truth segmentation. At last, the representation of each pixel is augmented by aggregating the dataset-level representations based on the corresponding class probability distribution. Furthermore, by utilising the stored dataset-level representations, we also propose a representation consistent learning strategy to make the classification head better address intra-class compactness and inter-class dispersion. The proposed method could be effortlessly incorporated into existing segmentation frameworks (e.g., FCN, PSPNet, OCRNet and DeepLabV3) and brings consistent performance improvements. Mining contextual information beyond image allows us to report state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks: ADE20K, LIP, Cityscapes and COCO-Stuff.

Boundary information plays a significant role in 2D image segmentation, while usually being ignored in 3D point cloud segmentation where ambiguous features might be generated in feature extraction, leading to misclassification in the transition area between two objects. In this paper, firstly, we propose a Boundary Prediction Module (BPM) to predict boundary points. Based on the predicted boundary, a boundary-aware Geometric Encoding Module (GEM) is designed to encode geometric information and aggregate features with discrimination in a neighborhood, so that the local features belonging to different categories will not be polluted by each other. To provide extra geometric information for boundary-aware GEM, we also propose a light-weight Geometric Convolution Operation (GCO), making the extracted features more distinguishing. Built upon the boundary-aware GEM, we build our network and test it on benchmarks like ScanNet v2, S3DIS. Results show our methods can significantly improve the baseline and achieve state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/JchenXu/BoundaryAwareGEM.

Graphlets are induced subgraph patterns and have been frequently applied to characterize the local topology structures of graphs across various domains, e.g., online social networks (OSNs) and biological networks. Discovering and computing graphlet statistics are highly challenging. First, the massive size of real-world graphs makes the exact computation of graphlets extremely expensive. Secondly, the graph topology may not be readily available so one has to resort to web crawling using the available application programming interfaces (APIs). In this work, we propose a general and novel framework to estimate graphlet statistics of " any size ." Our framework is based on collecting samples through consecutive steps of random walks. We derive an analytical bound on the sample size (via the Chernoff-Hoeffding technique) to guarantee the convergence of our unbiased estimator. To further improve the accuracy, we introduce two novel optimization techniques to reduce the lower bound on the sample size. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our methods outperform the state-of-the-art method up to an order of magnitude both in terms of accuracy and time cost.

This paper proposes a novel approach to multi-level image thresholding using a type II fuzzy entropy based adaptive plant propagation algorithm. The proposed method combines the concepts of fuzzy entropy and plant propagation to optimize the threshold values for image segmentation. Type II fuzzy entropy is used to measure the uncertainty in the image pixels, and the adaptive plant propagation algorithm is used to optimize the threshold values based on the fuzzy entropy values. The proposed method is tested on various images with different levels of noise and complexity, and the results are compared with traditional thresholding methods. The results show that the proposed method outperforms traditional methods in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. The adaptive plant propagation algorithm is able to effectively optimize the threshold values, leading to improved segmentation accuracy. Additionally, the type II fuzzy entropy provides a more robust measure of uncertainty, allowing for better handling of noisy images. The paper also discusses the theoretical foundations of the proposed method and provides a detailed analysis of the results. The proposed method has important implications for image processing and analysis tasks, particularly in applications where accurate segmentation is critical, such as medical imaging, object detection, and tracking. Overall, the paper presents a novel and effective approach to multi-level image thresholding using type II fuzzy entropy and adaptive plant propagation algorithm, and demonstrates its superiority over traditional methods.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to weakly supervised segmentation called Inter Extreme Points Geodesics (IEPG). This method leverages the concept of extreme points, which are points in the image that have the highest similarity to the boundary of the object of interest, and geodesic distances, which provide a metric for comparing the similarity between pixels. The IEPG algorithm consists of two main steps: 1) extracting extreme points from the image using a modified Canny edge detector, and 2) computing the geodesic distance matrix between all pairs of extreme points. The resulting matrix is then used to construct a graph, where each node represents an extreme point and edges connect points with similar geodesic distances. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes. Our experiments show that IEPG outperforms traditional weakly supervised segmentation methods, such as random walker and GCUT, in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the impact of different parameters on the performance of IEPG, providing insights into how to optimize its use in practice. Our work has important implications for applications where obtaining large amounts of annotated data is difficult or expensive, such as medical imaging or satellite imagery. By leveraging weak annotations, IEPG enables accurate segmentation without requiring a large amount of manual annotation effort.

The academic paper titled "MultiResUNet: Rethinking the U-Net Architecture for Multimodal Biomedical Image Segmentation" presents a novel deep learning-based approach for segmenting multimodal biomedical images. The proposed method, called MultiResUNet, is an extension of the U-Net architecture that incorporates multiple resolutions to improve segmentation accuracy. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on three different multimodal biomedical image datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance in each case. Overall, this paper provides a valuable contribution to the field of biomedical image segmentation and highlights the potential of MultiResUNet for future research in this area.

Neutron stars are compact objects with masses greater than that of the sun, formed from collapse of the core of a massive star. They are composed of neutrons and have densities that are much higher than those found in ordinary matter. As result, they provide unique opportunity to study extreme energy density matter. In this paper, we review current understanding of neutron star interiors and properties of matter at densities beyond those found in Earth's crust. We discuss the various models that have been proposed to explain behavior of matter at these densities, including the liquid metallic hydrogen model, the solid core model, and phase transition model. We also review the experimental evidence that supports these models, including observations of neutron star masses, radii, and magnetic fields. Finally, we discuss implications of our understanding of neutron star interiors for our understanding of the behavior of matter under extreme conditions, such as those found in the cores of supernovae and in the early universe.

This paper proposes a novel approach to unsupervised image segmentation, leveraging differentiable feature clustering to learn robust and accurate segmentations without requiring any labeled data. Our method is built upon a self-supervised loss function that encourages the model to group similar pixels together while separating dissimilar ones. The key insight is to employ a clustering algorithm that is differentiable with respect to the input features, allowing us to optimize the segmentation using backpropagation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance compared to other self-supervised methods and even surpassing supervised models in some cases. Moreover, we show that our method is robust to various evaluation metrics and can handle complex scenes with diverse objects, lighting conditions, and occlusions. Our main contributions are: 1. A novel, fully unsupervised learning approach to image segmentation based on differentiable feature clustering. 2. An effective self-supervised loss function that captures both local and global contextual information between pixel features. 3. State-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark datasets, outperforming existing self-supervised methods and rivalling supervised models. 4. Robustness to various evaluation metrics and scene complexity, demonstrated through extensive experiments. This work has significant implications for computer vision applications where labeled data is scarce or difficult to obtain, as it enables the training of accurate image segmentors without reliance on manual annotation.

We develop a fast method for optimally designing experiments in the context of statistical seismic source inversion. In particular, we efficiently compute the optimal number and locations of the receivers or seismographs. The seismic source is modelled by a point moment tensor multiplied by a time-dependent function. The parametres include the source location, moment tensor components, and start time and frequency in the time function. The forward problem is modelled by elastodynamic wave equations. We show that the Hessian of the cost functional, which is usually defined as the square of the weighted L2 norm of the difference between the experimental data and the simulated data, is proportional to the measurement time and the number of receivers. Consequently, the posterior distribution of the parametres, in a Bayesian setting, concentrates around the "true" parametres, and we can employ Laplace approximation and speed up the estimation of the expected Kullback-Leibler divergence (expected information gain), the optimality criterion in the experimental design procedure. Since the source parametres span several magnitudes, we use a scaling matrix for efficient control of the condition number of the original Hessian matrix. We use a second-order accurate finite difference method to compute the Hessian matrix and either sparse quadrature or Monte Carlo sampling to carry out numerical integration. We demonstrate the efficiency, accuracy, and applicability of our method on a two-dimensional seismic source inversion problem.

In this paper, we explore a novel variation of the classic Hat Game, known as Ebert's Asymmetric Three Person Three Color Hat Game. This game is a cognitive puzzle that involves three players, each wearing a hat of one of three possible colors, and a set of rules that dictate how the players can communicate and switch hats. The goal of the game is for the players to determine the color of their own hat, and we investigate the strategies and computational complexity of solving this problem. We first introduce the game and its rules, and then present a series of results on the computational complexity of solving the game using different strategies. We show that the game is P-complete, meaning that it is computationally equivalent to the hardest problems in NP, and that it is also NP-hard, meaning that it is at least as hard as the hardest problems in NP. We also explore the game's complexity under different restrictions on the allowed moves and communication between players. Our results demonstrate that Ebert's Asymmetric Three Person Three Color Hat Game is a challenging and fascinating problem that has important implications for the study of cognitive reasoning and decision-making. The game's complexity also makes it an interesting candidate for further study in the field of computational complexity theory.

Johnston disclosed to the Daily Mail Online that he orchestrated the prank as a means of seeking retaliation for a practical joke that one of his granddaughters played on him earlier that day. In the end, the trick turned out to be a complete failure and caused little Porter to be extremely upset. Although practical jokes can be entertaining for some, it is important to acknowledge that children may have a diverse response to what adults find humorous. Having experienced this lesson himself, Johnston will probably reconsider before attempting to organize another retaliatory joke on his granddaughters.

Scientists in France have developed a method for recycling PET plastics by modifying organisms to produce an enzyme that breaks down the plastic. The broken-down plastic can then be used as fuel or for producing bioplastics from algae and corn starch, respectively. PET is one of the most widely produced plastics worldwide. According to figures from 2011, it was found in over 90 of packaging products made from polyethylene terephthalate (PET), which makes up approximately 30 of all plastics floating around in our oceans. Unfortunately, unlike other recyclable materials such as paper and aluminum cans, almost no one actually recycles PET. It's because PET is extremely difficult to break down - it lasts hundreds of years before breaking into smaller pieces that are more easily recycled. This means that even when we do manage to recycle it there isn't much use beyond being melted together again with other waste so that they can both become part of another product. In order to change this, scientists at the University of Montpellier turned their attention away from recycling and towards reusing. They asked themselves: What if we could modify microorganisms living within marine ecosystems in order to make them eat plastic instead? If these organisms had the ability to digest not only plastic but also to convert these plastic molecules back into parts of the original material itself, then perhaps humans would find that recycling PET becomes easier than ever! To test out this idea, researchers inserted a gene into bacteria cells called cellulase genes. These genes helped the bacterium create enzymes able to break down complex organic compounds like wood pulp and lignin. After adding cellophane, researchers observed a high rate of digestion amongst the modified bacteria. In fact, after just three days the plastic fragments were already completely digested while the organism continued to thrive. It should be noted here that this new study focused solely on techniques used to extract and store energy, rather than methods involved in creating fuel directly from PET plastic. Although French scientists say that their work demonstrates how "it may therefore technically possible [to] produce biofuels from oceanic plastic debris...many obstacles remain to answer potential questions concerning environmental impact and economic feasibility." Still, the results provide evidence showing why further research needs to follow suit.

She added that a third man, aged in his 20s, had been arrested and released on police bail while the investigation continued.

The seahorse placenta is a fascinating example of convergent evolution. Male seahorses' brood pouches develop and function like human placentas. During pregnancy, the males provide embryos with everything they need. They use their placenta-like pouch to transport oxygen, hormones, and nutrients from the male to the embryo. The seahorse placenta is similar to human placentas in that it allows for direct transfer of materials between the parents and the offspring. However, unlike human placentas, the seahorse placenta also serves as a protective cocoon for the developing embryos. This provides an added layer of protection from predators and environmental conditions.

We present resampled cortical voxels derived from real-time data that can be used to Accurately visualize residual features over a volumetric brain map without requiring any special techniques in image analysis. Through The use of fully convolutional (PCA based) feature extraction methods, we are able to extract and analyze an unprecedented amount of spatial variation while preserving cortical thickness as well as volume correlations. The results reveal significant improvements during nonlinear segmentation, as compared to conventional image segmentation using simple regression And area decomposition algorithms [21]; It also reveals unique information when combined with fast recurrent networks; this additional information appears relevant in both spatially informative and functional MRI tasks. These new findings establish our methods at the Highest possible resolution and apply to the task of constructing functional brain Maps which have traditionally been considered Unsuitable for deep imaging or even theoretical models where all computation occurs at a small scale.

In this paper we present a system that mines semantic information beyond a small number of visual annotations extracted by its neural network, namely: image labels and edges in images (via edge detection; see [7, 23]). The system, which achieves state-of-the-art performance on image similarity tasks, does so not by directly extracting these features but simply by performing inference based on their usage and classification performance on validation data using an existing text document, thereby showing that it can be improved through a combination of natural language processing, visual search-based machine learning techniques, and deep learning.

> We introduce explicit evidence systems, which provide an algorithmic version of Fuzzy Inference System (FIS). Compared to other forms of explanation of the output behaviour of blackbox models such as Partial Dependence plots (PDP), Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) and Rule List based method (RLB); our proposal has several advantages. Firstly, PDP provides marginal contribution towards a target variable instead of a specific instance as considered in case of LIME and RLB. Secondly, we focus on binary classifiers that return exact value unlike PDP and LIME that work for continuous targets only. Thirdly, our explication of the model predictions are not driven by data points but rather they can be easily visualized using logical graph like structures. Last but certainly not least, it works well both offline and online scenarios where explanatory power is necessery e.g when user wants to have more confidence regarding what caused a particular system level behaviour. Finally, we show how common knowledge (Kripke semantics based definition) can be obtained after observing set of examples for explicit evidence rule based systems.

BiSeNet has been proved to be a popular two-stream network for real-time segmentation. However, its principle of adding extra path to encode spatial information is time-consuming, and the backbones borrowed from pretrained tasks, e.g., image classification, may be inefficient for image segmentation due to the deficiency of task-specific design. To handle these problems, we propose a novel and efficient structure named Short-Term Dense Concatenate network (STDC network) by removing structure redundancy. Specifically, we gradually reduce dimension of feature maps and use aggregation of them for image representation, which forms the basic module of STDC network. In the decoder, we propose Detail Aggregation module by integrating learning of spatial information into low-level layers in single-stream manner. Finally, the low-level features and deep features are fused to predict the final segmentation results. Extensive experiments on Cityscapes and CamVid dataset demonstrate effectiveness of our method by achieving promising trade-off between segmentation accuracy and inference speed. On Cityscapes, we achieve 71.9% mIoU on the test set with speed of 250.4 FPS on NVIDIA GTX 1080Ti, which is 45.2% faster than the latest methods, and achieve 76.8% mIoU with 97.0 FPS while inferring on higher resolution images.

This is an abstract of a five-part series on multicell coordinated beamforming that addresses optimization, feasibility, and performance studies. Part one focuses on complexity analysis using matrix inequalities to determine bounds on the number of cells required to maintain stability and achieve desired rate outages. Results show a limit theorem identifying necessary conditions for stable operation as well as sufficient conditions under which unstable configurations can lead to stable states. These findings have implications for resource allocation across multiple cells and help inform practical applications of such systems.

Machine learning has been designed to perform functions in several other domains such as classification, object detection, image segmentation and natural language interpretation. Data labeling has never been one of the most difficult functions in machine learning. Moreover, labeling small quantities of information reduces the monetary cost in machine learning. As a consequence, scientists began to focus on increasing data annotation and labeling costs. Transfer learning was created and extensively used as an effective method that can reasonably minimize the positive effect of limited data, which in turn, increases the data preparation expense. Also acquiring previous knowledge from a source domain increases the quantity of data required in a target domain. Yet, significant quantities of annotated data are not demanded to develop efficient models and reduce the prediction accuracy of the model. However, scientists started to pay more attention on auto annotation and labeling. In this survey paper, we provide a review of current approaches that focuses on optimized information annotation and labeling for video, music, and text data.

A company from Finland, Solar Foods, is planning to sell a protein powder that is made out of CO2, water, and electricity. The idea for Solein originally began at NASA, and it is made by capturing CO2 from the air then combining it with solar energy, water, nutrients, and vitamins to promote a natural fermentation process similar to the one that produces yeast and lactic acid bacteria. Solein contains 50 percent protein, up to 10 percent fat, and 20 to 25 percent carbs. It can be produced indoors, so production is not dependent on the outside environment. The impact of meat production is one of the main drivers behind many of the planet's problems, so creating food from two of the most renewable things on the planet, CO2 and sunlight, will help provide food for our growing population without increasing our impact on the planet. Solein is expected to be available in 2021.

Masten Space Systems will develop a lunar navigation and positioning system similar to GPS as part of a contract awarded through the Air Force Research Laboratory's AFWERX program. Current spacecraft navigation systems rely on ground-based tracking stations, which are limited in their ability to provide precise location data due to the distance between the spacecraft and Earth. The new system will enable autonomous navigation and position determination with minimal reliance on ground-based infrastructure. The system's capabilities include precision ranging, attitude determination, orbit determination, and navigation control. Masten Space Systems will leverage its experience in CubeSat technology as well as its flight heritage from more than 100 successful suborbital launches to develop the system. The lunar navigation and positioning system is expected to have applications beyond the Air Force Research Laboratory, such as NASA space missions.

Researchers at MIT have created a rechargeable lithium-ion battery in the form of a 460-foot-long fiber. The batteries can be manufactured to arbitrarily long lengths. They can be 3D-printed into any shape, and they can even function when bent or compressed. The design is intended as an alternative to conventional lead-acid storage cells - which are used extensively for their low cost and safe disposal. Lead acid batteries contain hazardous materials that can kill you if ingested; they also need constant monitoring because many chemicals inside them will eventually leak out and create toxic messes on a sunny day. But until now, nobody had been able stand up such batteries outside of laboratories without breaking them apart after a few hours. That's changed with this research: Batteries made from these nanotubes could last days instead of weeks; they'll pack more energy per volume than anything else available today; and they won't require regular maintenance like other battery technologies. As a result, once fully developed (it's not clear exactly how far along we are right now), it would make sense to make cars run off of them rather than fossil fuels. In addition, since fibers don't break easily and aren't prone to short circuits like traditional designs, they offer safety improvements over conventional batteries of similar size. If batteries ever become too thin, flexible, or hard to handle, scientists should consider building larger versions using these "battery packs" so that they retain some mechanical strength. And since many consumers want electronics to come with medical devices designed specifically around those batteries' unique properties, researchers are working towards creating phone chargers that work while tethered to hospital equipment. All told, though, this isn't quite the first time someone has thought about building such a thing. In fact, the idea may sound familiar to anyone who remembers watching Star Trek: The Next Generation's episode "Q Who?" Q was actually one half of two fictional robots charged by the Enterprise crew using technology almost identical to what's being proposed here. Of course, in reality, there were no actual wires involved, but the gist remains the same: By powering the whole structure through a single wire, engineers can use power efficiently. While most of the project still needs to go through extensive testing before reaching production stages, the team certainly seems optimistic. Despite being a very good movie, LE CERCLE ROUGE is somewhat affected by the fact that there are already comparable films available. Jean-Pierre Melville's impressive French film highlights a captivating tale of crime featuring an exceptional group of actors. The narrative traces the journey of a cohort of lawbreakers who collaborate to pull off a daring and risky robbery. The crew members are struggling with issues of trust, loyalty, and betrayal as tensions continue to increase. Even though the story might bear similarities to earlier heist movies, Melville's skillful direction and the subtle acting of Alain Delon, Gian Maria Volonte, and Yves Montand elevate it to a remarkable level among heist films. In addition, the film effectively utilizes its cinematography and tempo to instill a feeling of danger and discomfort. The overall feeling of fear and unease in the film is contributed by the dull color scheme and dreary city setting. The work shows Melville's fondness for American crime and mystery movies, but with a distinct French twist. Nevertheless, one cannot disregard the movie's resemblance to other movies about a robbery. Melville's distinctive cinematic prowess may not be enough to prevent some viewers from considering the story formulaic. In addition, individuals who have good knowledge of the genre may find certain components of the movie's climax recognizable, which may detract from the desired suspense. Despite everything, LE CERCLE ROUGE continues to be a fascinating and absorbing experience. This skillfully made and unforgettable movie, with its outstanding acting, direction, and ambiance, deserves recognition among the other great crime films. Our method uses both supervisory and unsupervised learning paradigms, using the former to establish prior understanding about tissue classes in images while using the latter to find areas with different properties regardless of class. We design our system utilizing an encoder-decoder backbone, which enables you to learn feature representations from raw image data and use them to automatically identify different tissues within complex medical images. Our experimental findings show progress over current state-of-the-art models through different measurement metrics, showing the validity of our proposed approach. The paper further demonstrates other potential opportunities for future analysis, including changes to preprocessing technologies, integrating additional techniques into our methodology, and exploring other technologies beyond clinical imaging. Overall, our work adds greatly to the existing literature on clinical image segmentation by providing a sophisticated tool capable of efficiently analyzing and distinguishing various kinds of tissue within complex clinical images with minimal human input.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to weakly supervised segmentation called Inter Extreme Points Geodesics (IEPG). This method leverages the concept of extreme points, which are points in the image that have the highest similarity to the boundary of the object of interest, and geodesic distances, which provide a metric for comparing the similarity between pixels. The IEPG algorithm consists of two main steps: 1) extracting extreme points from the image using a modified Canny edge detector, and 2) computing the geodesic distance matrix between all pairs of extreme points. The resulting matrix is then used to construct a graph, where each node represents an extreme point and edges connect points with similar geodesic distances. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes. Our experiments show that IEPG outperforms traditional weakly supervised segmentation methods, such as random walker and GCUT, in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the impact of different parametres on the performance of IEPG, providing insights into how to optimise its use in practise. Our work has important implications for applications where obtaining large amounts of annotated data is difficult or expensive, such as medical imageing or satellite imagery. By leverageing weak annotations, IEPG enables accurate segmentation without requiring a large amount of manual annotation effort.

In this paper, we explore the phenomenon of "Encyclopaedia Inflationaris," a previously undocumented effect in which the number of entries in a given field of knowledge increases at an exponential rate, leading to a rapid inflation of the number of possible entries in that field. We examine the causes and consequences of this phenomenon, including the role of technological advancements, the proliferation of digital media, and the increasing accessibility of information. Through a combination of empirical analysis and theoretical modeling, we demonstrate that Encyclopaedia Inflationaris is a real and quantifiable phenomenon, with significant implications for the way we understand and categorize knowledge. We show that the growth of entries in a given field is driven by a feedback loop between the availability of information and the demand for new entries, leading to an exponential increase in the number of possible entries. We also explore the potential consequences of Encyclopaedia Inflationaris, including the dilution of expertise, the fragmentation of knowledge, and the increasing difficulty of finding and validating information. We argue that these consequences have significant implications for the way we approach knowledge creation, dissemination, and validation, and that a better understanding of Encyclopaedia Inflationaris is essential for developing effective strategies for managing and mitigating its effects. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of Encyclopaedia Inflationaris, including the development of new methods for knowledge organization and retrieval, and the creation of new forms of art and literature that exploit the possibilities of an exponentially expanding field of knowledge. Overall, our findings provide a new perspective on the nature of knowledge and its relationship to technology, and highlight the need for a more nuanced understanding of the role of information in modern society.

The image encoder extracts features from input image using convolutional neural network (CNN), while the context encoder processes the contextual information using a natural language processing (NLP) technique. The fusion module combines the image and context features using a novel attention mechanism, enabling model to weigh the importance of different contextual cues for each pixel. This characterization provides a new approach to the study of decidable separability, which is an important problem in theoretical computer science and has applications in various areas of computer science And Engineering. The Paper also provides a new Algorithm for deciding whether a language is decidably separable, which is more efficient than previous algorithms. The results of this paper have important implications for the study of decidable languages and the development of efficient algorithms for language processing tasks.

Abstract This article presents one of the first results that suggest the probability of successfull bidding is significantly smaller than the bid size, and may become negative at very high bidders. We show experimental evidence for this phenomenon in three studies using our sample auction model described after Davenport (2002) in which bids are randomly generated by taking into account both bid quantity plus bid price from many markets in which different markets have high bidder densities. The hypothesis tested is wether side information from prior auctions will effect the degree to which previous sales prices were lower than current sale prices. We observe that if side information is added before an individual purchases a lot on eBay then their subsequent bid decreases, while we find no change in other users' auction outcomes when they use a randomized auction methodology. It follows that although large amounts of sellers advertise a highly discounted price during the active bidding stage, these claims do not translate well to more advanced market practices such as pre-buying during the final few minutes of a random auction or entering the highest winning bid into the "current bids" screen. While sellers compete intensely during the last hours of the sale, some appear to be trying to reduce potential impact on subsequent buyers with relatively low volume during that time when their competitors would take advantage of them. These findings could serve as a starting point as participants in auctioning develop a strategy for overcoming what may be perceived as significant problems associated with having less information about prices or higher side information about how bids can change in future executions and potentially increase risk associated with selling large lots at bargain prices. This paper presents a Bayesian logistic shape model inference approach applied to cochlea image segmentation. The methodology is designed to address issues related to accuracy, robustness and computational efficiency in segmenting images of the human cochlea. The proposed method demonstrates improved performance compared to existing methods by providing more accurate boundaries with reduced computation time while maintaining high levels of automation. Results from benchmark testing confirm that this novel algorithm offers an effective solution towards improving automated segmented outcomes for further analysis purposes such as hearing preservation surgery planning or personalised medicine initiatives involving inner ear imageing data. Furthermore, it provides insights into potential biomarkers associated with developmental abnormalities affecting auditory structures which could enable earlier detection/intervention strategies aimed at preserving hearing function among vulnerable populations (e.g., prenatal screening programmes). Overall, these advancements contribute significantly towards enhancing our understanding about various aspects pertaining auditory development & pathology assessment through non-invasive visualisation techniques like MRI scans alone or combined modalities where necessary.

In applied image segmentation tasks, the ability to provide numerous and precise labels for training is paramount to the accuracy of the model at inference time. However, this overhead is often neglected, and recently proposed segmentation architectures rely heavily on the availability and fidelity of ground truth labels to acheive state-of-the-art accuracies. Failure to aknowledge the difficulty in creating adequate ground truths can lead to an over-reliance on pre-trained models or a lack of adoption in real-world applications. We introduce Points2Polygons (P2P), a model which makes use of contextual metric learning techniques that directly addresses this problem. Points2Polygons performs well against existing fully-supervised segmentation baselines with limited training data, despite using lightweight segmentation models (U-Net with a ResNet18 backbone) and having access to only weak labels in the form of object centroids and no pre-training. We demonstrate this on several different small but non-trivial datasets. We show that metric learning using contextual data provides key insights for self-supervised tasks in general, and allow segmentation models to easily generalize across traditionally label-intensive domains in computer vision.
