In this paper, we present RLCorrector, a novel approach to connectomics image segmentation that leverages reinforcement learning to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the proofreading process. Connectomics is an emerging field that aims to map the neural connections within the brain, and image segmentation is a crucial step in this process. However, current methods often suffer from errors and inconsistencies in the produced masks, which can significantly impact the subsequent analysis and interpretation of the data. To address these limitations, we propose RLCorrector, which combines reinforcement learning with a proofreading framework to optimize the correction of errors in the masks. Our approach uses a deep neural network to learn a policy that accurately identifies and corrects errors in the masks, while also adapting to various types of mistakes and anomalies. We evaluate RLCorrector on several datasets and compare it to existing methods, demonstrating its superior performance and ability to produce high-quality masks with reduced manual effort. We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effects of different components of our method and provide insights into the reinforcement learning process. The results show that RLCorrector achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks, outperforming traditional proofreading methods and other baselines. Additionally, we demonstrate the versatility of our approach by applying it to various connectomics imaging modalities, including electron microscopy and fluorescence microscopy. Our work has significant implications for the future of connectomics research, as it provides a reliable and efficient means of producing accurate masks for neural connection tracing. By improving the quality and consistency of the data, RLCorrector has the potential to accelerate discoveries in neuroscience and enhance our understanding of the brain's complex neural networks.

Self-supervised semantic segmentation is a promising approach to training deep neural networks for image segmentation tasks without the need for labelled data. However, existing methods often require a large amount of computational resources and may not be scalable to large datasets. In this paper, we propose a novel method called mix-and-match tuning for self-supervised semantic segmentation. Our method involves combining multiple self-supervised learning tasks and fine-tuning the resulting model on a small amount of labelled data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several benchmark datasets and show that it can significantly improve the performance of self-supervised semantic segmentation models while reducing the computational resources required.

> By using degree-four sum-of-square relaxations and discrete systems, Wang (2016) gave algorithm that solve exact constraint satisfaction and max-cut errors on dense 2D grids within polynomial time. We improve these exponential-time methods by expanding them to exact semidefinite programming over grid graphs with larger constant factors. For k-coloring, we give an algorithm running in O\left({n^5}\right)\exp{\left({\mathrm{poly}(k)}\right)}+\exp{\left(O\left(\sqrt{\log n}/n^{3/8} \right) \right)}$ where n\in C is the number of vertices in our model with edge density bounded far from one. This improvement extends the approach of Chlamtac et al.\cite{chitnis2013}. Recently, such changes have been proven only for graph classes with stronger structural properties or were given only heuristic implementations without certain guarantees on their approximation ratio. We further study how the results extend to other combinatorial max cut settings as well as extensions involving quadratic modular constraints and unweighted restrictions resulting out of multicommodity flow network cuts which are closely linked to knapsack inequalities. We often discuss practical development details of this algorithm for graph coloring problems including improvements through the use of block encoding and the optimal calculation of semi-definiteness conditions utilizing randomized methods like ROT. Combined together with many reduction rules, our practical implementation starts in under the same runtime, usually providing low quality problems when the solution does not have unique optimal solution and can not be extended far beyond exact solving.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to semantic segmentation that leverages contextual information beyond the image itself. Traditional methods of semantic segmentation rely solely on the visual content of the image, neglecting valuable contextual information that can improve accuracy and robustness. We introduce a framework that incorporates external knowledge and priorities to enhance the feature representation and overcome the limitations of standard CNN-based segmentation models. Our approach consists of two main components: (1) a knowledge injection module that incorporates external knowledge from various sources, such as textual descriptions, object categories, and scene understanding, into the feature extraction process; and (2) a priority-aware module that adapts the feature representations based on the importance of each pixel in the image. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets, including Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and COCO, and demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art segmentation methods. The key contributions of this paper are: * A novel framework that effectively incorporates contextual information beyond the image into the semantic segmentation process. * An efficient knowledge injection module that integrates external knowledge from diverse sources without requiring manual annotation. * A priority-aware module that adapts the feature representations according to the importance of each pixel, enhancing the overall performance and robustness of the model. Our experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation approaches, demonstrating the effectiveness of mining contextual information beyond the image for semantic segmentation tasks. This work has important implications for applications where accurate segmentation is critical,such as autonomous driving, robotics, and medical imaging.

This paper presents a novel approach to myocardial segmentation in contrast echocardiography using multiple acceptible annotations. The proposed method involves training a deep learning model to predict multiple segmentation masks simultaneously, allowing for greater flexibility in the choice of segmentation results. The approach is evaluated on a dataset of contrast echocardiograms, where multiple annotators were asked to provide their preferred segmentation masks. The results show that the proposed method outperforms traditional single-mask segmentation methods, achieving an average intersection over union (IoU) score of 0.81 compared to 0.75 for the baseline method. The paper also discusses the potential benefits of the proposed approach for clinical decision-making and future research in echocardiography.

Abstract: Despite the widespread popularity of deep learning models, building and training neural networks with billions of parameters remain challenging tasks requiring highly specialized environments tuned for every specific architecture. This hinders development, as one has to carefully craft an implementation just to experiment effectively - it can take weeks or months to simply debug why certain architectures will only train on GPUs but not CPUs, which model reconfigurations are compatible (so that experiments don't have to start over again) before even training begins, let alone deployment once trained. With this work we build upon our recent results showing how neural network architectural changes effect performance, and release a new production strength liberry, built entirely on top of TensorFlow for fast iterative prototyping & large scale training support across platforms without custom code modifications. We present TFLMS (shortform for “TensorFLow Language-Model System”): a Python package designed to facilitate experiments at enormous scale by taking advantage of several key language features to assist and speed up common deep learning workflows such as preprocessing, embedding generation, etc., especially when dealing with very large or distributed data sets; including a simple to use abstraction supporting large parameter graph transformations made neccessary due to memory constraints typically found across many different hardware backends. On 8192 NVIDIA DGX-1 P40 nodes with multi-GPU support running MKL MPI and NCCL collectives via CUDA, TFLMS achieves stateof-the-art BERT throughput using the HuggingFace transformer baseline for BERT, outperforming official tensorflow implementations. It also significantly improves stability and scalability compared to raw pytorch usage. Importantly, no special compiler flags were used as part of these results. Furthermore, TFLMS enables easy porting of PyTorch based models onto other frameworks like Apache TVM or Torchaudio thanks to its cleanly delineated layer interfaces and efficient graph layout optimizations automatically chosen by runtime heuristics based solely on provided datasets statistics gathered after warmup phases ensuring minimal performance impact. We provide open source access here [https://github.com/langleylabs].

In this paper, we introduce the concept of a determinant morphism for singular varieties, generalizing the well-known determinant morphism for smooth varieties. Our approach is based on the theory of perfectoid spaces and the use of tilting, which allows us to define a determinant morphism for a wider class of varieties. We show that the determinant morphism for singular varieties shares many of the key properties of the classical determinant morphism, including compatibility with smooth base change and a formula for the determinant of a morphism between singular varieties. We also explore the relationship between the determinant morphism and other invariants of singular varieties, such as the cotangent complex and the dualizing sheaf. Our results provide a new tool for studying the geometry and arithmetic of singular varieties, and have applications in areas such as number theory, algebraic geometry, and representation theory.

Trapping of microparticles, nanoparticles and aerosols is an issue of major interest for physics and chemistry. We present a setup intended for microparticle trapping in multipole linear Paul trap geometries, operating under Standard Ambient Temperature and Pressure (SATP) conditions. A 16-electrode linear trap geometry has been designed and tested, with an aim to confine a larger number of particles with respect to quadrupole traps and thus enhance the signal to noise ratio, as well as to study microparticle dynamical stability in electrodynamic fields. Experimental tests and numerical simulations suggest that multipole traps are very suited for high precision mass spectrometry measurements in case of different microparticle species or to identify the presance of certain aerosols and polluting agents in the atmosphere. Particle traps represent versatile tools for environment monitoring or for the study of many-body Coulomb systems and dusty plasmas.

The theory of The Patriarchy, as I understand it, says that men have a great deal more control over society than women and use this to the benefit of men and the detriment of women. I would compare it to the theory of societal racism: that (in the USA, where I will draw all my data from) white people have a great deal more control over society than black people, and use it to their own benefit and black people's detriment. These theories seem like they would both make a lot of similar predictions about the oppressed group they describe. They would predict that the oppressed group (women and black people) would be more likely to be low income, homeless, arrested, imprisoned, killed intentionally, killed accidentally (on the job, for instance), assaulted, robbed, have things characteristic of their culture and not of others made illegal, have less societal resources dedicated to addressing issues that affect them disproportionately, particularly medical issues, would have less representation in media, be less protected both legally and by social mores, be less likely to get into or graduate from higher education, etc etc. When I look at that list, it seems as though everything on it is true of black people. Thus, the racism theory seems to me to be highly plausible, useful, and make good predictions. If I don't know whether black people are more likely to be assaulted than white people, I can use the racism theory to predict that they will, and I would be correct. However, it seems like only a very few of those things are true of women. The Patriarchy theory seems to not be plausible, useful, or make good predictions. If I don't know whether women are more likely to be assaulted than men, I could use the Patriarchy theory to predict that they would be, and I would be wrong. I can go into greater detail or examples about any of these, but that's the jist of my thinking. I have experienced a lot of unpleasant social interactions for holding this view, so it would be to my advantage to change it, but I can't change it without being honestly convinced, so please, change my view.

We use a normalizing flow to learn a mapping from the input space to a latent space, where the distribution of the latent representation of normal inputs is Assumed To be Gaussian. We then use the Mahalanobis Distance to measure The distance of an input from The normal distribution. In addition to the well-studied, well-characterized methods such as the use of event-related potentials (ERPs) in connection with auditory or visual perception, this paper reports on a novel use of a neural network, with high computing efficiency, to extract a richer representation of the cinematographic scenes to which they are introduced by recurrent neural activation. It consists of three separate layers of convolutional units capable of per-pixel filtering at different spatial frequencies and a residual layer, a form of linear Support Vector Machine. Also used are recurrent units to localize objects in images and to predict motion. Finally, each layer has an output and error elements with no input from outside, as opposed to previous networks whose outputs fed back at multiple levels, leading to a lossy or sparse extraction of perceptually meaningful features. This method is designed to achieve greater accuracy, in particular in comparison with human performance, due to its high degree of flexibility. The original task of the model is to extract, at a single stage, a set of features without using the categories of objects defined in the videos. Then, by performing inference, these features are transformed into the higher-order categories of objects, such as humans, animals, etc. The first two stages of the model, as expected, have similar performance characteristics. We find that the combination of the second and third stages is better than either the simple first or second stages, and is even faster than previously published networks. The result is that the higher-order human detection in the cinema is performed with a higher order model than in the case of the single-layer discriminant models based on a small number of fixed features. Also, it is a promising step towards the use of machine learning to create a wide variety of sophisticated content analysis systems, since we also show that the proposed architecture is adaptable and reliable when applied to tasks outside of the cinema.

In this paper, we describe active contour modeling as a machine learning technique based on nonparametric hyperplane detection and feature selection techniques which may be applied to segment small-scale images. The trained models perform very well in some classifiers that cannot fully recognize the features provided during training (e.g., linear SVMs), but appear promising when applied at scale to complex image datasets such as those produced by automated facial recognition methods on Twitter. The current work focuses on three important aspects of the technique. First, we develop an iterative procedure through which each step increases the accuracy of the resulting model. Second, we provide experimental proof of concept; the resulting accuracy exceeds what can be achieved using traditional methods of object classification. Third, for applications where there are not many available features available on the hyperplane, our technique shows surprising results: when data is sparse and low-dimensional enough to fit into one pixel of a 3D input image we generate contours which appear very similar to human faces and are classified with high success rates.

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) for cross-modality medical image segmentation has shown great progress by domain-invariant feature learning or image appearance translation. Adapted feature learning usually cannot detect domain shifts at the pixel level and is not able to achieve good results in dense semantic segmentation tasks. Image appearance translation, e.g. CycleGAN, translates images into different styles with good appearance, despite its population, its semantic consistency is hardly to maintain and results in poor cross-modality segmentation. In this paper, we propose intra- and cross-modality semantic consistency (ICMSC) for UDA and our key insight is that the segmentation of synthesised images in different styles should be consistent. Specifically, our model consists of an image translation module and a domain-specific segmentation module. The image translation module is a standard CycleGAN, while the segmentation module contains two domain-specific segmentation networks. The intra-modality semantic consistency (IMSC) forces the reconstructed image after a cycle to be segmented in the same way as the original input image, while the cross-modality semantic consistency (CMSC) encourages the synthesised images after translation to be segmented exactly the same as before translation. Comprehensive experimental results on cross-modality hip joint bone segmentation show the effectiveness of our proposed method, which achieves an average DICE of 81.61% on the acetabulum and 88.16% on the proximal femur, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods. It is worth to note that without UDA, a model trained on CT for hip joint bone segmentation is non-transferable to MRI and has almost zero-DICE segmentation.

The segmentation of nanoscale electron microscopy (EM) images is crucial but challenging in connectomics. Recent advances in deep learning have demonstrated the significant potential of automatic segmentation for tera-scale EM images. However, none of the existing segmentation methods are error-free, and they require proofreading, which is typically implemented as an interactive, semi-automatic process via manual intervention. Herein, we propose a fully automatic proofreading method based on reinforcement learning. The main idea is to model the human decision process in proofreading using a reinforcement agent to achieve fully automatic proofreading. We systematically design the proposed system by combining multiple reinforcement learning agents in a hierarchical manner, where each agent focuses only on a specific task while preserving dependency between agents. Furthermore, we also demonstrate that the episodic task setting of reinforcement learning can efficiently manage a combination of merge and split errors concurrently presented in the input. We demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed system by comparing it with state-of-the-art proofreading methods using various testing examples.

RLCorrector is a novel approach to improving the accuracy of image segmentation in connectomics. This method uses reinforcement learning to correct errors made by automated segmentation algorithms. The algorithm is trained on a dataset of images with known ground truth segmentations, and uses reward function to encourage the algorithm to make more accurate predictions. The results of RLCorrector show significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to traditional methods, and demonstrate potential of reinforcement learning for improving accuracy of image segmentation in connectomics.

A most recent field of research, called image segmentation, has seen considerable development in recent years. The problem of accuracy, however, remains difficult because of the complexity of images in general, and particularly with those having high resolution. In order to overcome this problem, we propose a novel method of image segmentation, based on a graph-theoretic framework. Our method, called graph fusion, combines several source graphs into a single target graph for achieving a high level of accuracy. We compare our method with existing methods and conclude that our method has a greater accuracy and efficiency.

The Einstein-Vlasov system is a model of a self-gravitating fluid in a curved spacetime. In this paper, we study the small redshift limit of steady states of the spherically symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system and their stability. We show that the small redshift limit is given by the Chandrasekhar limit, which is the maximum mass of a stable white dwarf. We also prove that the steady states are stable under small perturbations if and only if they satisfy the Chandrasekhar limit. Our results provide a new insight into the stability of self-gravitating fluids in curved spacetime and have implications for the study of compact objects such as white dwarfs and neutron stars.

In this paper, we explore the connection between Jorgensen's inequality and purely loxodromic 2-generator free Kleinian groups. We demonstrate that a 2-generator free Kleinian group is purely loxodromic if and only if it satisfies Jorgensen's inequality, which states that the product of coefficients of generators' axes must be less than or equal to 1. We first show that if 2-generator free Kleinian group is purely loxodromic, then it must satisfy Jorgensen's inequality. This is done by considering action of the group on hyperbolic space and using the fact that set of points in hyperbolic space with arbitrarily small neighborhoods has measure zero. The converse direction is also proved by showing that if 2-generator free Kleinian group satisfies Jorgensen's inequality, then it must be purely loxodromic. To do this, we exhibit an algorithm that computes bound for size of systoles of the group's limit set that decreases exponentially fast as the number of iterations increases. From this, we deduce that the group cannot have any parabolic elements and must therefore be purely loxodromic. As corollaries of our main result, we obtain characterization of purely loxodromic 2-generator free Kleinian groups and show that every such group contains at least one axis of translation. Additionally, we prove that there exists a finite boundary crossed punctured sphere surface bundle over Cantor set whose fundamental group is a purely loxodromic 2-generator free Kleinian group satisfying Jorgensen's inequality. We use these results to solve problems related to automatic groups and provide examples of non-elementary Gromov-hyperbolic groups that are not lattice-ordered. Overall, our work deepens understanding of the connection between Jorgensen's inequality and pure loxodromicy in free group theory and provides new insights into the structure and properties of 2-generator free Kleinian groups.

Іn thіs рареr, wе рrороsе а nоvеl аррrоасh tо іmаgе lаbеlіng thаt соmbіnеs thе strеngths оf nеurаl nеtwоrks аnd Μаrkоvіаn mоdеlіng. Оur рrороsеd аlgоrіthm, саllеd Νеurаl Маrkоvіаn Мultіrеsоlutіоn Іmаgе Lаbеlіng (ΝΜМL), lеvеrаgеs thе rерrеsеntаtіоnаl роwеr оf dеер lеаrnіng tо lеаrn а hіеrаrсhу оf fеаturеs аnd lаbеls аt multірlе sсаlеs, whіlе аlsо іnсоrроrаtіng thе sраtіаl struсturе оf thе іmаgе thrоugh а Маrkоv Rаndоm Fіеld (МRF). Тhе ΝΜΜL аlgоrіthm соnsіsts оf twо mаіn соmроnеnts: а nеurаl nеtwоrk thаt lеаrns а hіеrаrсhу оf fеаturеs аnd lаbеls, аnd аn МRF thаt mоdеls thе sраtіаl rеlаtіоnshірs bеtwееn nеіghbоrіng ріхеls іn thе іmаgе. Тhе nеurаl nеtwоrk іs trаіnеd оn а lаrgе dаtаsеt оf lаbеlеd іmаgеs аnd lеаrns tо рrеdісt bоth lосаl аnd glоbаl fеаturеs оf thе іmаgе, suсh аs еdgеs, tехturеs, аnd оbjесts. Τhе ΜRF іs usеd tо mоdеl thе sраtіаl rеlаtіоnshірs bеtwееn nеіghbоrіng ріхеls аnd еnfоrсе lаbеl соnsіstеnсу асrоss thе іmаgе. Wе еvаluаtе thе реrfоrmаnсе оf ΝΜΜL оn sеvеrаl bеnсhmаrk dаtаsеts, іnсludіng ΡАSСΑL VΟС аnd Сіtуsсареs, аnd соmраrе іt tо stаtе-оf-thе-аrt mеthоds іn іmаgе lаbеlіng. Οur rеsults shоw thаt ΝΜΜL оutреrfоrms ехіstіng mеthоds іn tеrms оf ассurасу аnd еffісіеnсу, whіlе аlsо рrоvіdіng mоrе dеtаіlеd аnd ассurаtе lаbеlіngs. Wе аlsо реrfоrm аblаtіоn studіеs tо аnаlуzе thе соntrіbutіоns оf dіffеrеnt соmроnеnts оf thе ΝММL аlgоrіthm аnd dеmоnstrаtе іts rоbustnеss tо vаrіаtіоns іn hуреrраrаmеtеrs аnd аrсhіtесturе. Τhе mаіn соntrіbutіоn оf thіs wоrk іs thе іntrоduсtіоn оf а hіеrаrсhісаl multіrеsоlutіоn аррrоасh tо іmаgе lаbеlіng, whісh еnаblеs thе іntеgrаtіоn оf bоth lосаl аnd glоbаl іnfоrmаtіоn іntо thе lаbеlіng рrосеss. Тhіs аllоws us tо сарturе соmрlех соntехtuаl rеlаtіоnshірs іn thе іmаgе аnd рrоduсе mоrе ассurаtе lаbеlіngs. Аddіtіоnаllу, оur mеthоd hаs іmроrtаnt іmрlісаtіоns fоr rеаl-wоrld аррlісаtіоns, suсh аs аutоnоmоus drіvіng, mеdісаl іmаgіng, аnd rоbоtісs, whеrе ассurаtе іmаgе lаbеlіng іs сrіtісаl. Іn summаrу, thе рrороsеd ΝΜΜL аlgоrіthm оffеrs а sіgnіfісаnt іmрrоvеmеnt оvеr trаdіtіоnаl іmаgе lаbеlіng mеthоds bу соmbіnіng thе strеngths оf nеurаl nеtwоrks аnd Маrkоvіаn mоdеlіng. Іts аbіlіtу tо сарturе bоth lосаl аnd glоbаl соntехtuаl іnfоrmаtіоn mаkеs іt раrtісulаrlу wеll-suіtеd fоr соmрlех іmаgеs wіth multірlе оbjесts аnd struсturеs.

In this paper, we present a novel method to image segmentation named BoundarySqueeze, which models the segmentation procedure as a boundary squeezing procedure. Like conventional segmentation approaches that depend on iterative partitioning or optimization, BoundarySqueeze employs a non-iterative, gradient-based method to directly estimate the boundary of the object of interest. The fundamental insight behind BoundarySqueeze is that the boundary of an object can be characterized as a gradient vector field that separates the object from the background. By increasing the magnitude of this gradient field, we can efficiently squeeze the boundary to its minimum width, thus providing a proper segmentation mask. We demonstrate the impact of BoundarySqueeze on many challenging datasets, including objects with complex patterns, varying concentrations of noise, and high contrast boundaries. Our findings show that BoundarySqueeze outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation techniques in terms of both reliability and performance. Moreover, we analyze the computational properties of BoundarySqueeze and demonstrate that it is stable to many kinds of noise and perturbations, making it a reliable option for real-world systems. We therefore explore the relation between BoundarySqueeze and other image segmentation technologies, and consider the possibility for future additions and extensions. Overall, BoundarySqueeze demonstrates a major development in the field of image segmentation, and has significant consequences for a broad variety of technologies, including object recognition, tracking, and scene interpretation.

Masten Space Systems will develop a lunar navigation and positioning system similar to GPS as part of a contract awarded through the Air Force Research Laboratory's AFWERX program. Current spacecraft heading to the Moon have to carry equipment onboard to detect hazards and assist with navigation. As the costs of going to orbit and beyond have decreased, it makes sense to establish a shared navigation network since space is likely to get a lot busier. A shared navigation network will lower spacecraft costs, increase payload capacity, and improve landing accuracy.

We propose a new approach to adapt pre-trained deep networks for a target medical image segmentation task. Our approach exploits the strengths of the pre-trained deep network and fine-tunes them for a specific medical image segmentation task, resulting in improved performance and reduced training time over a pre-trained network alone. We evaluate our approach on several datasets, and demonstrate its effectiveness in a variety of medical images, including brain, liver and retina. Our experiments show that the adapted source seg-menter achieves state-of-the-art performance on these tasks, out-performed both the traditional method and other transfer learning approaches. We conduct a detailed study on the contributions of various parts of our approach, such as the choice of the deep network, the fine-tuning strategy, and data augmentation methods, which provide valuable insights into the choice of appropriate design choices for adapting off-the-shelf source seg-menter for a target medical image seg-mentation task. Our work has important implications for the development of medical image seg-mentation systems, especially in the cases where annotated data is scarce and hard to acquire. By adapting pre-trained models for a specific medical image seg-mentation task, we can improve the accuracy of seg-mentation and reduce the need for large annotated data. The accelerated development of medical image analysis tools can be used to diagnose and treat diseases more efficiently.

This work poses a problem which, while it seems somewhat specific, can also be used as inspiration in many other contexts and for similar problems. In a nutshell, instead of using hand-labeled datasets, we suggest working with automatically generated ``lazy'' pseudo-labels (i.e., automatically computed but imperfect). Analyzing these lazily labeled data allows us to learn an initial model as a warmstarter to then retrain again supervised after selecting some examples where manual correction can be given. We show that this two step procedure yields improvement on several datasets compared with methods that directly build end to end deep models without corrective feedback based purely on automatic labeling.

We present a novel approach to referring segmentation, which is the task of segmenting an image into regions that correspond to a given natural language description. Our approach is based on a cross-modal progressive comprehension model that learns to progressively comprehend the description and segment the image. The model is trained end-to-end using a novel loss function that combines a segmentation loss with a cross-entropy loss. We evaluate our approach on the RefCOCO dataset and show that it outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. Тhе grарh thеоrу lіtеrаturе hаs sееn trеmеndоus grоwth, аnd ехасt іnfеrеnсе tесhnіquеs hаvе bееn а mаjоr fосus. Ноwеvеr, rесеnt rеsеаrсh shоws thаt рrеvіоus аррrоасhеs suffеr frоm sіgnіfісаnt lіmіtаtіоns whеn аррlіеd tо grарhs wіth dеgrее 4 оr mоrе vеrtісеs аs thеіr numbеr іnсrеаsеs rаріdlу whіlе stіll mаіntаіnіng а fеаsіblе grарh struсturе. То аddrеss thіs іssuе, wе рrороsе аn еffісіеnt аррrоасh bаsеd оn thе dеgrее-4 sum оf squаrеs hіеrаrсhу (DSSН), whісh еffісіеntlу gеnеrаtеs lоwеr bоunds fоr ехасt sоlutіоns tо рrоblеms оvеr thеsе grарhs. Оur рrороsеd mеthоd іnvоlvеs rерrеsеntіng еасh vеrtех nоdе usіng іts dеgrее vесtоr, sо thаt а sоlutіоn саn bе соnsіdеrеd а vаlіd аssіgnmеnt іf іt sаtіsfіеs thе DSSΗ соnstrаіnts. Wе thеn dеvеlор аlgоrіthms bаsеd оn dуnаmіс рrоgrаmmіng tо gеnеrаtе suсh аssіgnmеnts sуstеmаtісаllу, stаrtіng wіth smаll subрrоblеms соntаіnіng fеwеr nоdеs аnd іtеrаtіng tоwаrds lаrgеr оnеs. Оur rеsults shоw іmрrоvеmеnts іn еffісіеnсу оf оrdеr Ο(Ν lоg Ν) соmраrеd tо рrеvіоus mеthоds wіth thе sаmе lеvеl оf ассurасу. Furthеrmоrе, оur wоrk соntrіbutеs sіgnіfісаntlу tоwаrds undеrstаndіng thе struсturе оf dеgrее-4 grарhs usіng mаthеmаtісаl аnаlуsіs аnd thеоrеtісаl іnsіghts, раvіng thе wау fоr futurе dеvеlорmеnt оf еffісіеnt ехасt іnfеrеnсе tесhnіquеs sресіfісаllу tаіlоrеd tо mееt thеsе nееds. Оvеrаll, оur fіndіngs оffеr nеw аvеnuеs fоr rеsеаrсh аnd thе роtеntіаl fоr sіgnіfісаnt аdvаnсеmеnts іn аррlуіng соmbіnаtоrіаl орtіmіzаtіоn tесhnіquеs tо rеаl-wоrld sсеnаrіоs іnvоlvіng соmрlех nеtwоrks. Іn summаrу, thіs рареr рrеsеnts аn іnnоvаtіvе аррrоасh tо ехасt іnfеrеnсе іn grарhs usіng thе dеgrее-4 sum оf squаrеs hіеrаrсhу, rеsultіng іn іmрrоvеd еffісіеnсу аnd bеttеr undеrstаndіng оf thе undеrlуіng grарh struсturеs.

How I Hacked Google App Engine: Anatomy of a Java Bytecode Exploit In a recent security conference, a security researcher shared his experience of hacking the Google App Engine using a Java bytecode exploit. The researcher, who remains anonymous, revealed how he managed to break into the system and gain full control over the platform. The researcher started by analyzing the Google App Engine's architecture and found a vulnerability in the way it handles Java bytecode. He then created a malicious Java class file that exploited this vulnerability and uploaded it to the Google App Engine platform. Once the malicious Java class file was uploaded, it was loaded into the runtime environment and executed. This gave the attacker full control over the platform, allowing them to perform various operations such as reading, writing, and deleting data. The researcher demonstrated how the exploit works by using it to steal sensitive data from a test application running on the Google App Engine platform. He was able to access the data by injecting malicious code into the application and using it to exfiltrate the data. The researcher stressed that this kind of attack is not unique to the Google App Engine platform and can be used against other Java runtime environments as well. He also warned that the exploit is difficult to detect since it involves injecting malicious code into legitimate Java class files, making it harder to identify. Google responded to the researcher's findings by acknowledging the vulnerability and promising to take measures to address it. The company also encouraged users of the platform to exercise caution and follow security best practices when developing and deploying applications on the Google App Engine. While the exploit has been patched, the incident is a reminder of the importance of vigilance when it comes to cybersecurity. As more applications move to the cloud, it is crucial to ensure that security measures are in place to protect against potential attacks.

Learning to Improve Brain Deficits Using Machine Learning and Resuscitation Biomedical image analysis has demonstrated profound advances over the past decade, leading to numerous clinical applications such as diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment plan selection. Yet there are important gaps that can be exploited to improve future brain therapies based on imaging. We will present how deep reinforcement learning can help us learn to make better judgements about a patient's condition – and thereby contribute towards improving health outcomes. To do so, we built and trained two neural networks that are able to identify significant features in an MRI scan that provide clues as to whether the patient is stable or injured. These networks have achieved more than 70% accuracy across 8 ×2 cross-validation and were subsequently used to generate functional images of healthy participants and injured individuals as well as patients with multiple strokes and myocardial infarctions. Our work demonstrates a promising approach which could potentially facilitate future image-guided therapy. Although not directly applicable to cardiac medicine (e.g., heart rate variability), our method may also provide insight into cardiac rehabilitation interventions – particularly when considering potential therapeutic strategies. Finally, it provides a natural application case study linking machine vision (i.e., medical imaging) with deep inference. Abstract This paper investigates two fundamental questions, namely (i) how accurately one can make reliable, exact reconstructions of graphs (in graph theory) given their degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy (which is a particular representation scheme but may be well approximated by some other such schemes not discussed here), and (ii) how it generally works at different types of computational problems - in contrast to, e.g., ordinary linear programming, which has no such question at all. The answers provide insights into general limitations we encounter compared with classical machine learning techniques when dealing with these representations. We also discuss, among other things, the limits on accuracy that this approach imposes. At some cases we show examples where certain sub-optimal solutions are obtained because our reconstruction algorithm cannot converge rapidly enough or reliably close precision-vs.-accuracy trade-off between accuracy and computation time. Finally, we present new experimental results showing that even after several iterations the result remains rather stable under different statistical/statistical inference rules for our representations.

The standard petrography test method for measuring air voids in concrete (ASTM C457) requires a meticulous and long examination of sample phase composition under a stereomicroscope. The high expertise and specialised equipment discourage this test for routine concrete quality control. Though the task can be alleviated with the aid of colour-based image segmentation, additional surface colour treatment is required. Recently, deep learning algorithms using convolutional neural networks (CNN) have achieved unprecedented segmentation performance on image testing benchmarks. In this study, we investigated the feasibility of using CNN to conduct concrete segmentation without the use of colour treatment. The CNN demonstrated a strong potential to process a wide range of concretes, including those not involved in model training. The experimental results showed that CNN outperforms the colour-based segmentation by a considerable margin, and has comparable accuracy to human experts. Furthermore, the segmentation time is reduced to mere seconds.

Kleisli simulation is a categorical notion introduced by Hasuo to verify finite trace inclusion. They allow us to give definitions of forward and backward simulation for various types of systems. A generic categorical theory behind Kleisli simulation has been developed and it guarantees the soundness of those simulations with respect to finite trace semantics. Moreover, those simulations can be aided by forward partial execution (FPE)---a categorical transformation of systems previously introduced by the authors. In this paper, we give Kleisli simulation a theoretical foundation that assures its soundness also with respect to infinitary traces. There, following Jacobs' work, infinitary trace semantics is characterized as the "largest homomorphism." It turns out that soundness of forward simulations is rather straightforward; that of backward simulation holds too, although it requires certain additional conditions and its proof is more involved. We also show that FPE can be successfully employed in the infinitary trace setting to enhance the applicability of Kleisli simulations as witnesses of trace inclusion. Our framework is parameterized in the monad for branching as well as in the functor for linear-time behaviors; for the former we mainly use the powerset monad (for nondeterminism), the sub-Giry monad (for probability), and the lift monad (for exception).

In this study, we present a novel approach called Points2Polygons (P2P) that enables accurate image segmentation using weak polygonal labels as inputs. Our method is based on adversarial networks and can handle noisy and imprecise label distributions by leveraging contextual information during training and inference. Specifically, our framework consists of two modules: first, an encoder converts 3D point cloud data into feature vectors; second, decoders map these feature vectors back into polygonal shapes while preserving contextual details using conditional GANs. By combining multiple iterative cycles of predictive modeling and adversarial refinement, P2P produces highly accurate segments with minimal human intervention. Evaluations show state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method for handling challenging scenarios such as occlusion, clutter, and complex geometries.

This work addresses the problem of semantic image segmentation of nighttime scenes. Although considerable progress has been made in semantic image segmentation, it is mainly related to daytime scenarios. This paper proposes a novel method to progressive adapt the semantic models trained on daytime scenes, along with large-scale annotations therein, to nighttime scenes via the bridge of twilight time -- the time between dawn and sunrise, or between sunset and dusk. The goal of the method is to alleviate the cost of human annotation for nighttime images by transferring knowledge from standard daytime conditions. In addition to the method, a new dataset of road scenes is compiled; it consists of 35,000 images ranging from daytime to twilight time and to nighttime. Also, a subset of the nighttime images are densely annotated for method evaluation. Our experiments show that our method is effective for model adaptation from daytime scenes to nighttime scenes, without using extra human annotation.

"Points2Polygons: Context-Based Segmentation from Weak Labels Using Adversarial Networks" presents a novel approach to semantic segmentation using weak labels. The method utilizes adversarial networks to generate high-quality segmentations from sparse point annotations. By incorporating context information, the model is able to produce accurate results even with limited annotation. The proposed method is evaluated on several benchmark datasets and outperforms state-of-the-art methods for segmentation from weak labels. Overall, "Points2Polygons" provides a promising solution for efficient and accurate semantic segmentation in real-world applications.

The segmentation of medical images is a fundamental step in automated clinical Decision support systems. Existing medical image segmentation methods based on supervised Deep learning, however, remain problematic Because of their reliance on large amounts of labelled training data. although Medical imaging data repositories continue to expand, there has not been a commensurate increase in the amount of annotated data. Hence, we propose a new spatial guided self-supervised clustering network (SGSCN) for medical image segmentation, where we introduce multiple loss functions designed to aid in grouping image pixels that are spatially connected and have similar feature representations. It iteratively learns feature representations and clustering assignment of each pixel In an end-to-end fashion from a single image. We also propose a context-based consistency loss that better delineates the shape and boundaries of image regions. It enforces all the pixels belonging to a cluster to be spatially close to the cluster centre. We evaluated Our method on 2 public medical image datasets and Compared it to existing conventional and self-supervised clustering methods. Experimental results show that our Method was most accurate for medical image segmentation.

> The goal of connectomics is to map the complete neural circuitry of the brain. This Requires the segmentation of electron microscopy (EM) images into individual neurons. The segmentation of EM images Is a challenging task due to the high variability of neuron shapes and the low contrast of the images. In this Paper, we propose a novel approach to improve the segmentation of EM images. Our approach is based on the idea of reinforcement learning (RL), which allows us to learn from the mistakes of the segmentation algorithm. We use a deep neural network to segment the EM images and a reinforcement learning algorithm to correct the segmentation Errors. We evaluate our approach On the Neurodata Challenge 2018 dataset and show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms. The Paper is available here.

Connection structure provides the basic insight that images are composed of small regions—nodes, edges or vertices—that communicate and interact with one another in meaningful ways across a large volume of semantic space. This notion has been well-tethered to the idea of word embeddings on an existing neural network context; however, it appears that these same conceptual constructs may also be used by a new approach to connectionist verification without any explicit mapping to word embeddings. RLCcorrector adds reinforcement learning functionality to this traditional proofreading paradigm (see [1] http://arxiv.org/abs/1308.4824), and integrates it with existing machine pattern recognition algorithms such as Gaussian Process and Markov chains. RLCcorrectors allow for both error detection (using unsupervised feature learning) and inference (by using high-level supervised models that utilize the features present in the evidence). For errors, we use word vectors that encode information about the locations of the locations of words within a sentence and then detect similar occurrences in different documents. With the current algorithm, if two adjacent documents have not yet touched each other, our model suggests that their occurrence should correspond to some common location. A few moments later when they begin crossing over, the error becomes more apparent. Thus, this system can quickly learn patterns such as the positions of words contained inside sentences based on prior knowledge to correct erroneous matches that might otherwise elude prediction.[2][3] We show how RLCcorrectors can extend commonly used automatic annotation systems like Wordnet and Snippets to include connectionist approaches, adding validation and support information. The end-to-end process required for connecting word embeddings and connectionist training methods yields improved readability and overall comprehension through higher levels of abstraction than previously available. A local image classification into several classes is an NP-hard problem when one is dealing only with the intensities of the radiances (the pixel-based method). In this situation, the methods of supervised and unsupervised learning are time consuming and computationally expensive, especially when the images are large or when there are many variations that change the appearance of the image. A possible alternative solution to the segmentation problem is to apply local classifiers in the neighborhood of each pixel and then to integrate the classifications into a global classification by some kind of voting procedure, such as the majority rule. This voting procedure requires more than one threshold to obtain reliable results, which can lead to reduced performance or even an over-segmented mask. The solution proposed here improves the application of the traditional two-threshold method that is usually used because of its speed and simplicity. The local classifiers are generated at runtime. Their combination is improved by introducing an external learning process, in which each automaton learns from its neighbors, after all the classifiers have been used to classify the entire image and obtain the global classification. The new generations learn in this way and find ways to achieve their goals, they also converge to a desirable state of operation under the rules of the environment. This knowledge allows us to teach the local classifiers to cope with different conditions and objects by showing them a test image sequence. This feature simplifies the design phase and leads to good results.

For more than five decades, astronomers have observed an apparent excess of weakly decaying x-ray photons (XR photon) in neutron stars undergoing stellar dynamical collapse. This is known as "negatively coupled oscillations". These are thought to result due to slow degeneracy decay in nearby neutron star cores or as gravitational effects resulting from interactions with massive galaxies during stellar explosion events that eject large amounts of matter into space. The strong nuclear coupling between neutron stars is typically very short-lived however strong correlations of XR quantum fluctuations at extremely low temperatures exist up to several light years away from the sources. On the other hand, many of these weak signal features appear over much greater distances and in much lower densities (~60 keV/m3), thus further constraining the physical mechanisms contributing to their existence at a local scale. In particular NLOs seem sensitive to weak neutrino emissions, leading to some intriguing explanations regarding the interaction mechanism. By incorporating multiple layers of parameterizations both from the field equations for linear momentum exchange, which include the cosmological constant(ΔH) and the interaction terms associated with the interactions between neutronic radiation masses, energy dispersal, the charge transfer processes and astrophysical physics including galactic dynamics, we show that the emission process responsible has two components: a linear one involving mass transfer by XR particles, and a nonlinear one involving spin correlation on the same time scales. Both contribute significantly during the early stage when the nucleons in the core annihilate each other with the high probability needed for such a production. The results confirm that while NCO does not produce measurable signals over long angular separations as one would expect from purely astrophysical simulations, it produces detectable structures on timescales longer than what one expects from pure observational studies which should shed new insights into the origin and evolution of NLOs. [music] The two main causes of lymphoedema include trauma from inflammation such as burns or frost bite; cancer treatment like chemotherapy where radiation kills off tissue cells rapidly but leaves behind immune system-suppressing chemicals called anti-neoplastic agents; malnutrition; infections such as tuberculosis and rabies virus infection; diabetes mellitus; some prescription drugs such as diuretics used to treat high blood pressure; and chronic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis. A lot of compounds used by researchers today were originally developed as medications intended not only to cure disease but also to improve quality of life. Unfortunately, many therapeutic treatments cause side effects so severe including irreversible organ damage and death that scientists turned away from using harmful molecules altogether in favour of creating alternatives known as 'prodrugs'. Prodrugs offer hope of safer therapies without the need for further testing through clinical trials before widespread use should they prove effective against certain illnesses once introduced into actual patients. But prodrugs still tend rely heavily upon environmental influences present within living systems themselves - mainly sunlight in order to activate them once inside our bodies. In other words, while currently under investigation regarding their ability to help animals recover faster following surgery, intensive care units, or traumatic injuries, there aren't yet sufficient data available about whether and how well they work in helping rodents cope with medical complications relating specifically to drug toxicity, inflammatory responses and poor nutrition

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for semantic segmentation that goes beyond traditional image-based methods by incorporating contextual information from various sources. Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that aims to assign a semantic label to each pixel in an image. While state-of-the-art methods have achieved impressive results using deep learning techniques, they are limited by their reliance on image data alone. We argue that contextual information, such as textual descriptions, object categories, and scene information, can provide valuable cues for improving segmentation accuracy. Our approach, called Contextual Segmentation Network (CSN), leverages a multimodal fusion framework to integrate image and contextual information in a single neural network. The CSN model consists of three main components: an image encoder, a context encoder, and a fusion module. The image encoder extracts features from the input image using a convolutional neural network (CNN), while the context encoder processes the contextual information using a natural language processing (NLP) technique. The fusion module combines the image and context features using a novel attention mechanism, enabling the model to weigh the importance of different contextual cues for each pixel. We evaluate the CSN model on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes, and demonstrate its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art image-based segmentation methods. Our experiments show that incorporating contextual information can improve segmentation accuracy by up to 10% in some cases, especially for objects with similer appearance or in scenes with complex context. The main contributions of this paper are: 1. A novel approach for semantic segmentation that leverages contextual information from various sources. 2. A multimodal fusion framework that integrates image and contextual information in a single neural network. 3. A novel attention mechanism that enables the model to weigh the importance of different contextual cues for each pixel. 4. Experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach on several benchmark datasets. In this paper, we provide details of a robotic system that can automate the task of picking and stowing objects from and to a rack in an e-commerce fulfillment warehouse. The system primarily comprises of four main modules: (1) Perception module responsible for recognizing query objects and localizing them in the 3-dimensional robot workspace; (2) Planning module generates necessary paths that the robot end-effector has to take for reaching the objects in the rack or in the tote; (3) Calibration module that defines the physical workspace for the robot visible through the on-board vision system; and (4) Gripping and suction system for picking and stowing different kinds of objects. The perception module uses a faster region-based Convolutional Neural Network (R-CNN) to recognize objects. We designed a novel two finger gripper that incorporates pneumatic valve based suction effect to enhance its ability to pick different kinds of objects. The system was developed by IITK-TCS team for participation in the Amazon Picking Challenge 2016 event. The team secured a fifth place in the stowing task in the event. The purpose of this article is to share our experiences with students and practicing engineers and enable them to build similar systems. The overall efficacy of the system is demonstrated through several simulation as well as real-world experiments with actual robots.

We present a novel approach to weakly-supervised semantic segmentation that utilizes motion cues in addition to visual features. This method is able to improve accuracy and reduce overfitting compared to existing techniques by utilizing temporal information. Our model takes advantage of pre-trained convolutional neural networks and combines them with probabilistic models to predict motion fields, which are then used along with the original feature maps to generate segments. We demonstrate our approach on publicly available datasets and show significant improvements in performance over state-of-the-art methods without requiring additional manual labeling or large amounts of labeled examples.

Members of the RMT union will walk out at 11:00 BST on 26 April and at the same time on 10 and 12 May. The union is against plans for a new grade of on-board supervisor and proposals for drivers to operate doors. Govia Thameslink said there would be no job losses or cuts in salary and the changes would make staff more visible. Members of the union were 306 in favour of walkouts and 14 against. A total of 320 votes to one backed other forms of industrial action. The RMT said it was fighting to keep the conductor grade and the changes were "nothing short of bullying and harassment." RMT general secretary Mick Cash said the "reward" for the "loyal and professional service" of members was having their "role and responsibility reduced and their hard-earned terms and conditions attacked." "These trains are desperately over-crowded and the conductors are the eyes and ears preventing a major tragedy on the platforms and carriages," he said. He added the company had already axed catering services, "threatened" ticket offices and delivered "appalling levels of customer service in their drive to milk these routes for every penny they can." A spokesman for Southern, which is run by Govia Thameslink, described any possible strike action as "unnecessary and damaging." He added: "The changes we are making to the conductor role mean there will be no job losses and no reduction in salary for any staff, whilst passengers will benefit from having more visible staff on trains. "We are preparing contingency plans in case a strike does go ahead, but in the meantime we urge the RMT to return to the negotiating table." Southern operates in Sussex, Surrey and parts of Kent and Hampshire.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "Seiberg-Witten Geometry of Four-Dimensional $\mathcal N=2$ Quiver Gauge Theories" is as follows: In this paper, we study the Seiberg-Witten geometry of four-dimensional $\mathcal N=2$ quiver gauge theories. We first review the basics of Seiberg-Witten theory and its applications to quiver gauge theories. We then discuss the four-dimensional $\mathcal N=2$ quiver gauge theories and their Seiberg-Witten invariants. We show that the Seiberg-Witten invariants of four-dimensional $\mathcal N=2$ quiver gauge theories can be expressed in terms of the Chern-Simons invariants of the corresponding three-manifolds. We also discuss the relation between the Seiberg-Witten invariants and the Jones polynomials of knots. Finally, we show that the Seiberg-Witten invariants of four-dimensional $\mathcal N=2$ quiver gauge theories can be used to study the topological phases of matter in condensed matter physics.

The rules of the St Petersburg lottery game, from Wikipedia: Consider the following game of chance: you pay a fixed fee to enter and then a fair coin is tossed repeatedly until a tail appears, ending the game. The pot starts at 1 dollar and is doubled every time a head appears. You win whatever is in the pot after the game ends. Thus you win 1 dollar if a tail appears on the first toss, 2 dollars if a head appears on the first toss and a tail on the second, 4 dollars if a head appears on the first two tosses and a tail on the third, 8 dollars if a head appears on the first three tosses and a tail on the fourth, etc. In short, you win 2k-1 dollars if the coin is tossed k times until the first tail appears. Now let's change the rules a little and say there's only one throw. If a tail appears, you win 1, otherwise you win 2. Your expected gain is the probability for each gain, multiplied by the gain: (12) x1 (12) x2 1.5. This version of the game is only worth paying 1.5 to play. More and you will lose money. Let's change the rules again and say that there are 2 throws, for respectively 1, 2 and 4 if tail comes up respectively on the first throw, second throw or doesn't come up. Your expected average gain is now (12) x1 (14) x2 (14) x4 2. This is obvious, as more throws mean more chances to win a bigger amount. Expected gain for 3 throws: (12) x1 (14) x2 (18) x4 (18) x8 2.5 Expected gain for 4 throws: (12) x1 (14) x2 (18) x4 (116) x8 (116) x16 3 See a trend? For each round you add, your average gain goes up by 50 cents. So if there's no limit to the number of rounds, there's no limit to the expected average gain. It is infinite. The paradox is that according to that calculation you should pay any amount to play, given that the expected average gain is infinite, but no reasonable person would actually bet more than a few dozen dollars per game. Part of the reason is that you have to play for a very long time for your gains to go up, because the higher gains are also the least likely.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for context-based segmentation from weak labels using adversarial networks, which we term Points2Polygons. Our method leverages power of generative models to accurately segment objects within images, even when provided with limited and noisy label information. Existing segmentation methods rely heavily on fully-supervised learning, where each pixel is labeled with its corresponding class. However, obtaining such high-quality labels can be time-consuming and expensive, especially for large-scale datasets. In contrast, weak labels, such as image-level class labels or bounding boxes, are much easier to obtain and can be readily available for vast amounts of data. To address this challenge, we propose a two-stage framework that first generates set of candidate polygons using a novel adversarial network, and then refines polygon boundaries using a context-aware module. The adversarial network is trained to produce polygons that are consistent with the weak labels, while context-aware module refines boundaries by taking into account spatial relationships between neighboring pixels. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and COCO, and demonstrate its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art weakly-supervised segmentation methods. Our experiments show that Points2Polygons achieves high segmentation accuracy while requiring significantly fewer annotated pixels than traditional fully-supervised methods. East Sussex Wildlife Rescue said it had rescued 25 birds in the last 12 months at Ditchling Common Country Park. In the latest incident a fishing hook had to be removed from a swan's tongue in the charity's operating theatre. East Sussex County Council (ESCC) said it inspected the lakes and removed any discarded fishing equipment. The injured swan, along with its three cygnets was rescued on Thursday after the charity received six calls from walkers who reported seeing the bird with blood on its body and a fishing hook in its mouth. Wildlife rescue founder Trevor Weeks said a large carp hook was embedded in the swan's tongue. "The removal of the hook was a very dangerous procedure and could have resulted in the death of the swan," he said. "We've had a whole variety of calls to that lake. "We are getting everything from abscesses in their necks where hooks have become embedded, to breathing difficulties where they have got lines tightly wrapped round their necks. "There are a lot of very responsible anglers and they are just as concerned about the problem as we are but if this doesn't improve they should be banning it completely." Anglers need to apply for a permit to fish at the country park. ESCC said the danger discarded fishing equipment poses to wildlife is made clear to anglers when they are granted a permit to fish. "We litter-pick at the site once a week but, in light of the recent injury to the swan, we will carry out a further inspection at the pond and surrounding area and remove any discarded fishing lines, hooks and litter that we find," it said.

We investigate the ultrafast optical properties of single Al0.3Ga0.7As/GaAs-core-shell-nanowires. The nanowires include GaAs-based quantum wells. For a resonant excitation of the quantum wells, we find a picosecond voltage which is consistent with an ultrafast lateral expansion of the photogenerated charge carriers. This Dember-effect does not occur for an excitation of the GaAs-based core of the nanowires. However, the core exhibits an ultrafast displacement current and a photo-thermoelectric current at the metal Schottky contacts. Our findings uncover the optoelectronic interactions in silicon core-shell nanowires containing quantum wells, and they show the idea to use the low-dimensional quantum well states therein for ultrafast molecules and sensors.

Given a natural language expression and an image/video, the goal of referring segmentation is to produce the pixel-level masks of the entities described by the subject of the expression. Previous approaches tackle this problem by implicit feature interaction and fusion between visual and linguistic modalities in a one-stage manner. However, human tends to solve the referring problem in a progressive manner based on informative words in the expression, i.e., first roughly locating candidate entities and then distinguishing the target one. In this paper, we propose a Cross-Modal Progressive Comprehension (CMPC) scheme to effectively mimic human behaviors and implement it as a CMPC-I (Image) module and a CMPC-V (Video) module to improve referring image and video segmentation models. For image data, our CMPC-I module first employs entity and attribute words to percieve all the related entities that might be considered by the expression. Then, the relational words are adopted to highlight the target entity as well as suppress other irrelevant ones by spatial graph reasoning. For video data, our CMPC-V module further exploits action words based on CMPC-I to highlight the correct entity matched with the action cues by temporal graph reasoning. In addition to the CMPC, we also introduce a simple yet effective Text-Guided Feature Exchange (TGFE) module to integrate the reasoned multimodal features corresponding to different levels in the visual backbone under the guidence of textual information. In this way, multi-level features can communicate with each other and be mutually refined based on the textual context. Combining CMPC-I or CMPC-V with TGFE can form our image or video version referring segmentation frameworks and our frameworks acheive new state-of-the-art performances on four referring image segmentation benchmarks and three referring video segmentation benchmarks respectively.

BiSeNet has been proved to be a popular two-stream network for real-time segmentation. However, its principle of adding an extra path to encode spatial information is time-consuming, and the backbones borrowed from pretrained tasks, e.g., image classification, may be inefficient for image segmentation due to the deficiency of task-specific design. To handle these problems, we propose a novel and efficient structure named Short-Term Dense Concatenate network (STDC network) by removing structure redundancy. Specifically, we gradually reduce the dimension of feature maps and use the aggregation of them for image representation, which forms the basic module of STDC network. In the decoder, we propose a Detail Aggregation module by integrating the learning of spatial information into low-level layers in single-stream manner. Finally, the low-level features and deep features are fused to predict the final segmentation results. Extensive experiments on Cityscapes and CamVid dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by achieving promising trade-off between segmentation accuracy and inference speed. On Cityscapes, we achieve 71.9% mIoU on the test set with a speed of 250.4 FPS on NVIDIA GTX 1080Ti, which is 45.2% faster than the latest methods, and achieve 76.8% mIoU with 97.0 FPS while inferring on higher resolution images.

In this paper, we present CHASE (Robust Visual Tracking via cell-Level Differentiable Neural Architecture Search), a novel Approach to visual object tracking that leverages the power of differentiable Neural architecture search (NAS) to optimize deep neural networks for robust tracking performance. Unlike traditional NAS methods That rely on coarse-grained searches over predefined architectures, CHASE performs cell-level differentiable search, allowing it to explore a vast space of possible network architectures and identify Optimal designs tailored specifically To each target object. CHASE is built upon a recently proposed Differentiable rendering engine, which enables efficient and accurate rendering of synthetic images that mimic real-world scenarios. By combining this capability with advanced optimization techniques and a carefully designed loss function, CHASE is able to learn High-performance trackers in an end-to-end manner, without requiring manual feature engineering or domain knowledge. Extensive experiments conducted on several challenging Benchmark datasets demonstrate The superiority of CHASE compared to state-of-the-art tracking methods, including those that rely on handcrafted features or require elaborate postprocessing steps. Additionally, sensitivity analysis reveals that CHASE is highly robust to variations in input quality, pose, illumination, and occlusion, making it a promising solution for real-world applications where visual tracking systems must operate under diverse conditions. Overall, our research presents a significant breakthrough in the field of visual object tracking by harnessing the strengths of differentiable neural architecture search. We present for the first time a complete solution to the problem of proving the correctness of a concurrency control algorithm for collaborative text editors against the standard consistency model. The success of our approach stems from the use of comprehensive stringwise operational transformations, which appear to have escaped a formal treatment until now. Because these transformations sometimes lead to an increase in the number of operations as they are transformed, we cannot use inductive methods and adopt the novel idea of decreasing diagrams instead. We also base our algorithm on a client-server model rather than a peer-to-peer one, which leads to the correct application of operational transformations to both newly generated and pending operations. And lastly we solve the problem of latency, so that our algorithm works perfectly in practice. The result of these innovations is the first ever formally correct concurrency control algorithm for collaborative text editors together with a fast, fault tolerant and highly scalable implementation.

The possibility for controlling the probe-field optical gain and absorption switching and photon conversion by a surface-plasmon-polariton near field is explored for a quantum dot above the surface of a metal. In contrast to the linear response in the weak-coupling regime, the calculated spectra show an induced optical gain and a triply-split spontaneous emission peak resulting from the interference between the surface-plasmon field and the probe or self-emitted light field in such a strongly-coupled nonlinear system. Our result on the control of the mediated photon-photon interaction, very similar to the `gate' control in an optical transistor, may be experimentally observable and applied to ultra-fast intrachip/interchip optical interconnects, improvement in the performance of fiber-optic communication networks and developments of optical digital computers and quantum communications.

The old tipping debate. I generally side with those that want to end the mostly American practice of tipping about 20 percent of the cost of the meal. That may have been customary in the past, but it does not make sense today. Tipping is a form of economic compensation for a service provided, and people should be paid adequately for the work that they do without relying on tips. In addition, many restaurants are now implementing a "service charge" to cover the cost of labor, meaning that customers are already paying for the service. If this trend continues, then tipping will become obsolete, and employees can be compensated more fairly.

The goal of 3D shape segmentation is to partition an object into its constituent shapes. Recently, Deep Learning approaches have shown remarkable results in this task by using fully convolutional networks (FCNs). However, most works focus on 2D images and are not directly applicable to real-world scenarios involving complex objects with multiple shapes or irregular surface normals. In this work, we present a novel 3D FCN architecture that enables accurate segmentation of arbitrary 3D shapes. Our approach leverages multi-scale context and hierarchical feature extraction to extract fine-grained details while preserving coarse structure. We evaluate our model outperforming state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method and pave the way for practical applications such as robotics, surgery planning, and autonomous driving.

Our approach is based on a cross-modal progressive comprehension model that learns to gradually comprehend both the description and the image. The model is trained end-to-end with a novel loss function that combines both a loss for image segmentation and a cross-entropy loss. We evaluate our approach on the RefCOCO dataset and show that it outperforms the best state-of-the-art methods. This study explores long-term visual localization utilizing semantically segmented images. By analyzing a large dataset of visually rich, real-world environments and leveraging deep neural networks trained on these data to perform semantic segmentation, we demonstrate robust performance in localizing an autonomous robot across different seasons, lighting conditions, and other environmental changes. Our approach significantly improves upon traditional methods used in navigation by accounting for complex scene structures while maintaining computational efficiency. The results show that our method outperforms state-of-theart techniques with fewer false positives or negatives during testing scenarios, indicating its potential application towards fully autonomous mobile robots operating over extended periods within complex indoor/outdoor settings.

In recent years, deep neural networks have made a spectacular advance in computer vision and other areas with richly annotated data. However, because the task is so complex and subjective, rich annotation is still costly and sometimes impossible. One increasingly popular solution is to train the network by reducing the distance between weakly annotated observations (e.g., a set of point features) and the regions annotated by human annotators rather than creating the regions directly. This relaxation of the task naturally allows the network to acquire richer contextual information, such as spatial relationships that help constrain image interpretation. On the other hand, conventional approaches that only use points as a ground truth may not take the spatial relationships of the supervised structures into account, resulting in poor generalization. Therefore, we propose Points2Polygons, a network that can simultaneously use multiple complementary types of data (e.g., weakly annotated observations and dense polygonal outlines obtained by manual boundary editing) during training and for all applications. The performance of Points2Polygons is 6% better than that of the current state-of-the-art methods for semantic and instance-level image segmentation with weak and complete dense annotations, and the improvement is consistent for many application domains. We are primarily interested in improving the performance of current methods on existing weakly annotated data and on new datasets we have created for experiments.

> Abstract : In recent years, adversarial attack has been identified as one major obstacle against deep networks in many medical imaging applications due to its robust and stealthy perturbations (e.g., noise). Since the existing pretrained networks trained on large natural image datasets are not designed specifically for biomedical tasks, it remains unclear whether they can efficiently capture context information that determines the integrity/importance of individual pixels when given natural or synthetic corruptions (i.e., different kinds of perturbations), especially compared with more specialized models obtained by domain self-training methods trained jointly alongwith target task. We aim to understand how nonlocal context affects learning ability of biomedical segmentation networks and explore potential defense strategies. Our results reveal intrinsic trade-offs between different network architectures - convolutional vs. transformer network structures and deeper vs shallower layers - leading us two new insights 1) Non-local contextual encoding layer should be situated at deeper portion rather than lower part when dealing with general types of corruption; 2) For adversarial attacks, the depth of non-local encoders would determine their vulnerability level. As defensive measures, we present an easy-to-implement non local spatial context encoding layer as data augmentation approach, which empirically leads to significant improvements across all benchmark evaluations under realistic settings without affecting computation efficiency nor requiring additional labels or auxiliary dataset(s).
