The separability problem for word languages of a class $\mathcal{C}$ by languages of a class $\mathcal{S}$ asks, for two given languages $I$ and $E$ from $\mathcal{C}$, whether there exists a language $S$ from $\mathcal{S}$ that includes $I$ and excludes $E$, that is, $I \subseteq S$ and $S\cap E = \emptyset$. In this work, we assume some mild closure properties for $\mathcal{C}$ and study for which such classes separability by a piecewise testable language (PTL) is decidable. We characterize these classes in terms of decidability of (two variants of) an unboundedness problem. From this, we deduce that separability by PTL is decidable for a number of language classes, such as the context-free languages and languages of labeled vector addition systems. Furthermore, it follows that separability by PTL is decidable if and only if one can compute for any language of the class its downward closure wrt. the scattered substring ordering (i.e., if the set of scattered substrings of any language of the class is effectively regular). The obtained decidability results contrast some undecidability results. In fact, for all (non-regular) language classes that we present as examples with decidable separability, it is undecidable whether a given language is a PTL itself. Our characterization involves a result of independent interest, which states that for any kind of languages $I$ and $E$, non-separability by PTL is equivalent to the existence of common patterns in $I$ and $E$.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to medical image segmentation utilizing a spatial guided self-supervised cluster network (SGSCN). Our approach uses the inherent conceptual structure in medical images to develop clustering representations without the need for annotated information. The SGSCN model consists of a convolutional neural network (CNN) accompanied by a spatially-aware clustering module. The CNN encodes the input image into a set of feature maps, which are then used to compute a visual correlation graph. The spatially- aware clustering module partitions the graphs into different clusters, where each cluster corresponds to a particular class label. We evaluate our approach on other publicly accessible clinical imaging datasets, including MRI brain scans and CT lung scans. Experimental findings show that SGSCN outperforms conventional supervised learning methods, as well as state-of-the art self-supervised techniques, in terms of segmentation accuracy. Instead, we demonstrate the efficacy of our technique in situations where annotations are limited or impossible to provide. CGSCN has significant consequences for medical image analysis tasks, especially in cases where annotated information is scarce or challenging to provide. Our method offers a flexible and reliable way to segment medical images without relying on manual annotation effort. This can possibly accelerate the implementation of AI technologies for other clinical applications, such as cancer treatment, medication planning, and surveillance.

"Don't Torture a Duckling" is one of the coolest Italian horror films I've ever seen, and I've seen my share. Released in 1972 and directed by the maestro of giallo, Lucio Fulci, this film offers that delightful blend of mystery, gore and social criticism that made Italian classics of the time stand out. Set in a small, rural village in southern Italy, the film follows the horrific serial murders of young children. The local community is riddled with superstition, religious fervor, and palpable tension. It's a slow burn but that's what makes it even more exciting. Unlike other giallo films, Fulci focused on creating a dark atmosphere, exquisite cinematography, and well-developed characters. The acting is on point, especially from Florinda Bolkan who plays the mysterious Maciara, a woman accused of witchcraft. Her performance is as intense as it is delicate, and you can't help but feel a connection with her. The soundtrack by Riz Ortolani is hauntingly beautiful, perfectly encapsulating the eerie atmosphere of the film. What sets "Don't Torture a Duckling" apart from other Italian horror films of the time is its social commentary. Fulci explores themes of religious fanaticism, paranoia, and mob mentality in a way that makes you question the true nature of evil. While "Don't Torture a Duckling" may lack some of the more over-the-top scenes of its gory contemporaries, it compensates with a compelling story, interesting characters, and a chilling atmosphere. It's a hidden gem worthy of discovery for fans of classic Italian horror and a testament to the genius of Lucio Fulci. If you haven't seen this masterpiece yet, do yourself a favor and dive into this twisted tale of mystery, religion and murder.

IMDADM2, a peptide hormone, has diverse physiological roles such as expanding blood vessels, managing hormone release, and promoting cell growth. Earlier research has indicated that IMDADM2 could potentially play a part in the physiological processes of reproduction such as implantation and placentation. There is a certain amount of proof indicating the link between IMDADM2 and the process of trophoblast invasion in human pregnancy, which involves implantation and placentation. Research conducted outside of a living organism has shown that IMDADM2 encourages the movement and penetration of trophoblasts, which are necessary actions for the implantation process to be successful and for the placenta to develop. Moreover, IMDADM2 has been discovered to govern the generation of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), which play a crucial role in breaking down and restructuring the extracellular matrix throughout trophoblast penetration. Moreover, research has indicated that the expression of IMDADM2 is increased in endometrial tissues of humans during the implantation phase and in placental tissues throughout the entire pregnancy period. It proposes that IMDADM2 may have a possible function in controlling the uterus' ability to receive and the development of the placenta. Further investigation is required to comprehensively comprehend the ways in which IMDADM2 aids in implantation and placentation during human gestation, and to establish its importance in reproductive medical conditions like recurring miscarriage or preeclampsia.

In this paper, we demonstrate control over the light absorption and emission properties of quantum dots (QDs) using a surface-plasmon field. By placing QDs in close proximity to a metal surface, we can manipulate the interaction between the QDs' electronic transitions and the surface plasmons, leading to enhanced light absorption and emission. We experimentally observe a significant enhancement in the QDs' optical response when they are coupled to the surface-plasmon field, resulting in increased absorption and emission intensity. The extracted energy transfer efficiency reveals that the coupling between the QDs and the surface plasmons plays a key role in the observed enhancement. Furthermore, we show that the strength of the surface-plasmon field can be controlled by changing the distance between the QDs and the metal surface, allowing for fine-tuning of the QDs' optical properties. This tunability offers great potential for applications such as ultracompact optoelectronic devices, sensing systems, and photovoltaic cells. Our results provide new insights into the interaction between QDs and surface plasmons, paving the way for further exploitation of this phenomenon in various fields. We believe that our findings will have significant impacts on both fundamental research and practical applications in nanophotonics and related areas.

This work is motivated by our ongoing efforts to develop multi-domain segmentation of low and high mass knee osteoarthritis (OA), which has led us to search within the human brain to find relevant features. The current state-of-the-art approaches to the problem are either limited by their low coverage or low volume, often leading them to fail when used with dense subfolded volumes of images. We have developed learning cost functions for multi domain learning in large, high-volume datasets (i.e., those exceeding 4-6 million voxels). Our approach allows for rapid analysis by trained neural networks that converge quickly over large data sets without sacrificing accuracy. We show the utility of the method to understand joint anatomy, determine optimal labeling strategies for clinical decision making, generate new models that reduce both computational time and error during the next training epoch, identify weakly correlated regions, and identify local predictors of joint structure using MR image labeling. To date, we have only analyzed 2.5 trillion labeled steps (one of four times larger than most previous experiments) at a resolution of 8×8 matrix. While it's still quite early days as far as this type of deep learning goes, I think there is great potential here due to its ability to look beyond known anatomical signatures that will give researchers more information about an individual patient than they could ever learn through traditional methods with less precision (as explained below the fold!). Additionally, in the future, we may be able to leverage various advanced techniques like multi-scale deep learning in order to accomplish what these earlier papers focused on, i.e., how best to label multiple subjects into discrete anatomic categories based upon how each subject performs different tasks within a given study.

We propose a novel approach for a robust semantic segmentation of images taken under adverse weather conditions. Our method is based on a fast image segmentation method, which is able to divide an image into homogeneous regions. The division is made by means of a coarse-to-fine method, where the coarse segmentation is achieved by a fast and robust method, and the fine segmentation by a more accurate but less fast one. The coarse segmentation is used to obtain a set of candidate regions, and the fine one is used to select the best candidate region for each pixel. We have evaluated our method on the Cityscapes dataset, and the results show that it can achieve a high accuracy even in adverse weather conditions. The Cityscapes dataset is composed of a set of high-quality images, which are labeled with a pixel-wise semantic annotation. It was designed to be challenging, with a wide variety of weather conditions and object classes. The dataset is available to the public and can be used for research and development of semantic segmentation methods. The dataset contains a total of 5000 images with a resolution of 2048 by 1024 pixels. The images are annotated with 19 object classes, such as pavement, building, and vegetation, and are divided into a training, a test, and a development set for the evaluation of semantic segmentation methods. The Cityscapes dataset is a useful resource for the research and development of semantic segmentation methods, providing a large and diverse set of images with a pixel-wise semantic annotation. The scenes in the images vary in the weather conditions and object classes. This is a novel approach for robust semantic segmentation in adverse weather conditions. It is based on a fast and robust video-segmentation method, which can divide a sequence into a set of homogeneous regions. The division is performed by means of a coarse-to-fine method, where the coarse division is performed by a fast and robust method, and the fine division by a more accurate but slower one.

This research investigates cross-modal progressive comprehension, a process that involves understanding and interpreting visual information by combining it with linguistic cues. The aim of this study is to develop an algorithm capable of referring segmentation in natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Using state-of-the-art machine learning models such as deep neural networks, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), long short term memory(LSTM)and other tools from computer vision we analyse image data sets like MS COCO dataset which contain segmented objects along side captions. We evaluate our approach on various metrics including Accuracy & Recall rate which show significant performance improvement over baseline methods. This suggests that using both modalities together can enhance object recognition accuracy leading towards better NLP results specifically while dealing text based problems regarding Image captioning,Visual Query etc where localization plays important role.

The man smiled. "Yeah. It's just that you looked like you were dreaming of fireflies." "How can you tell that, just from a glance?" asked Kelly, leaning forward and catching the scent of his cologne, like leather and pine, masking the subway stench of too many unmentionable things. "Can't imagine a girl like you dreaming of anything less than pure magic," he said with a lopsided grin. "That's some line," said Kelly. "How often does it work?" "I don't know. Never seen a girl worth trying it on before." Now it was Kelly's turn to smile. "It wasn't fireflies," she admitted. "But I was sitting here dreaming. I do that a lot these days." "Kind of dream you'd be willing to share with a stranger?" Kelly paused and turned the thought over in her head. "Yeah. I think so. In fact, I think it's one of those dreams I'd only be willing to share with a stranger." "That dangerous, huh?" "Maybe." Kelly reoriented herself so that she was facing him fully. Her ankle brushed against the side of his calf, still stretched across the way. After an instinctual jump, she let it rest there, amused by the brief and impersonal - but still somehow too intimate - touch. "See, I was dreaming about going off somewhere and leaving everything in the city behind. All the ex-boyfriends, the crappy job, the roommate, the friends..... just letting them go. Title: RLCorrector: Reinforced Proofreading for Connectomics Image Segmentation Abstract: In this study, we propose a novel deep learning-based method called RLCorrector that employs reinforcement learning to improve image segmentation accuracy in connectomics experiments. The proposed system leverages a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning methods to extract relevant features from images and generate improved segmentations. We demonstrate effectiveness by applying it on real brain imaging data and show improved segmentations with significant reduction in errors compared to traditional approaches. Our results highlight potential of combining reinforcement learning with transfer learning techniques for improving image processing tasks in life sciences domains. Keywords: Reinforcement Learning, Image Transformation, Neural Networks, Deep Learning

When you start making 5 million a year you start spending a lot more. The problems start when you are no longer making 5 million a year but you keep getting offers for projects that don't pay enough to justify the expense of living in New York City or buying your own homes. Even if it is just a small percentage, some companies and businesses will try their best not to let employees take advantage of this new paradigm; however, there have been successful scams. In short, I can imagine how many people consider this as an opportunity to make money by simply selling their services. It's easy to see why - after all, the work from home job market has opened up so much potential. However, inside most jobs like those mentioned above, they give very few advantages to freelancers over regular workers, except maybe being able to work remotely or without having to leave their children behind. For example, how does someone who works long hours, starts early every day, and doesn't get much sleep at night become motivated to be productive? If working on-site gives them less distraction or anxiety than going home to face another day of raising a family, what makes anyone think they would want to part ways with these benefits in order to work full time for a company? The problem is, there isn't anything wrong with fulfilling one's personal needs, but we need to remember that our overall satisfaction levels don't come solely from the things we do for ourselves. They also come through the experiences and connections we form along the way. When we stop meeting others halfway and create opportunities for others themselves, we learn something about them too: we gain valuable life skills which can then help us create value for society at large. That's true whether it's a parent teaching their child self-reliance or a business leader helping struggling entrepreneurs find success (and ultimately happiness).

In this paper, we present CHASE, a novel approach to visual tracking that leverages the power of differentiable neural architecture search (NAS) to optimise the tracking performance. Unlike traditional tracking methods that rely on hand-crafted features and pre-defined architectures, CHASE uses a cell-level differentiable neural network to learn a robust and adaptive representation of the target object. The proposed method consists of two main components: a cell-level differentiable neural network, and a tracking loss function that is designed to optimise the tracking performance. The cell-level differentiable neural network is trained to learn a robust representation of the target object by optimising a novel tracking loss function that encourages the network to produce a stable output in the presence of occlusions, illumination changes, and other challenges. The tracking loss function is designed to be differentiable with respect to the network's architecture, allowing us to use backpropagation to optimise the network's parametres. We use a combination of gradient descent and evolution strategies to search for the optimal architecture that maximises the tracking performance. We evaluate CHASE on several challenging benchmarks, including the PASCAL Visual Object Tracking (VOT) dataset, the Temple-Color-Tracking (TCT) dataset, and the LaSalle-Color-Tracking (LCT) dataset. Our experiments show that CHASE outperforms several state-of-the-art tracking methods, including deep learning-based methods, and achieves a high success rate in various challenging scenarios. The main contribution of this paper is the introduction of a novel differentiable neural architecture search method for visual tracking, which allows the network to adapt to changing object appearance and learn a robust representation of the target object. The proposed method has important implications for a wide range of applications, including object tracking in videos, autonneomous driving, and robotics.

There's a part of your brain, lets call him bob. Bob is a very particular fellow, in fact so particular that when he see something he doesn't like he lets EVERYBODY know. Bob only likes things that fit within his view of reality. So if you're playing a game and a graphics glitch occurs, he lets you know, a robot that almost looks like a person but doesn't quite, he lets you know. But when you are asleep, Bob sleeps with you whereas the rest of the brain doesn't.,When we are dreaming an area of the brain known as the prefrontal cortex is not active. This is the area we use for regulating emotional responses, critical thinking, judgement, planning into the future and rational and logic based decisions. This part of the brain is considered to play a big role in human intelligence. This is also the part of the brain where all our conscious decisions are made. Without the prefrontal cortex we can not be conscious! We are still not exactly sure why we we dream, but from a Neuroscience point of view, dreams are more then likely a product of memory encoding while we sleep. The hippocampus reruns the data we took in that day and refires the neuropathways involved with a particular memories over and over again so in the future those neuropathways are more likely to fire in sync again, resulting in a long term memory. Without the prefrontal cortex to catch the weird scenarios that arise in our dreams, due to this memory encoding process, we accept the dream as normal reality.

Semantic segmentation is a critical task in computer vision that involves assigning a label to each pixel in an image based on its semantic meaning. While recent advances in deep learning have led to significant improvements in image-based semantic segmentation, there are still challenges in accurately segmenting objects in complex scenes with ambiguous or occluded regions. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to mining contextual information beyond image for semantic segmentation. Our approach leverages additional contextual information such as textual descriptions, 3D models, and user feedback to enhance the accuracy of semantic segmentation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets and show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art image-based semantic segmentation methods. Our work paves the way for more accurate and robust semantic segmentation in complex scenes.

The woman, 37-year-old Wu Shuoyan, is alleged to have been killed last May simply for refusing to hand over her phone number to cult members. The murder, filmed on CCTV , occurred in a McDonald's restaurant in Zhaoyuan, Shandong Province. Last week, the court heard how more than 40 members of the Eastern Lightning sect, who claim to be "the second coming of Christ," had gathered outside the fast food outlet and were harassing customers for their phone numbers. The tragedy unfolded when Ms Wu refused to hand over her contact details, instead calling the police. She was then attacked by five women with steel rods and severely beaten on the head. Ms Wu later died in hospital. One of the defendants, Zhang Lidong, told the court that he did not regret killing the woman because she had insulted God. "I wish I could do it again," he said. "It's not a crime. It's justified." He claimed that Ms Wu had been taken over by evil spirits, which made him believe that she deserved to die. Zhang was one of five people charged with murder last year. Three others have since been charged as accessories to the crime. In May this year, another member of the cult in Shijiazhuang, Hebei Province, confessed to murdering a doctor who had also refused to give his phone number to the group. Chen Qianming, 27, admitted to stabbing 49-year-old Dr Shen Yang in the heart and chest after being unable to convince him to join the sect. The attack took place in October 2013, but the suspect did not turn himself into police until March this year.

This review examines recent developments in multi-fidelity modeling, a technique that utilises multiple levels of computational fidelity to reduce uncertainty and improve predictive accuracy. By investigating various applications across different disciplines, we highlight how these models can be tailored to suit specific purposes while maintaining their fundamental principles. We also discuss challenges faced by practitioners when implementing multi-fidelity approaches and propose potential solutions which could enhance their usefulness further. Overall, this study provides insights into current advancements within multilevel simulation methodology and underscores its relevance as an emerging toolset applicable across diverse domains of research.
